News.title: Families' anger at jailed funeral boss's apology letter
News.content:
Natalie Smith's grandfather Norman Bridger was one of the bodies found at Legacy.

He had been there for 11 months and was 95 when he died, with a funeral held for him before they found out his body was still at the site.

Smith said Bush's letter was a "tick box exercise to try and make himself look like he'd approached the families".

She said she reacted with "disbelief" when she received the letter, which contained "no real substance, no emotion, nothing".

"They're just words and there was nothing behind them," she said, adding she would never forgive Bush for what he had done.

Robert Bush's letter in full:

To everyone who has been affected by my actions.

"I have spent a great deal of time thinking about the events that [sic] wish to say something directly to you.

"I know that many of you entrusted me and my business with the care of someone you loved during one of the most difficult times in your lives.

"I recognise that what happened has caused distress, upset and uncertainty for many families. I am deeply sorry.

"There are no words that can undo what has happened or take away the pain that many of you have experienced. I understand that this has affected not only your confidence in me, but also memories surrounding the loss of those closest to you.

"I accept responsibility for my failures. Looking back, I know that I should have acted differently and much sooner. I regret that I did not do so.

"I do not expect forgiveness, nor do I write this letter in the hope of reducing the seriousness of what has happened.

"I simply wanted you to know that I genuinely regret the consequences of my actions, and the impact they have had on so many people.

"I appreciate that every family's experience has been different, and I respect that some people may never wish to accept my apology. That is entirely understandable.

"I hope that, in time, each of you can find some peace and remember your loved one for who they were rather than for the circumstances that have followed. I am truly sorry."

If you have been affected by issues surrounding bereavement, information is available via BBC Action Line, including contact details of organisations that can help.

Listen to highlights from Hull and East Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, watch the latest episode of Look North.

News.title: Emmerdale actor Lawrence Robb joins Strictly line-up
News.content:
Emmerdale actor Lawrence Robb is the latest star to join the line-up for this year's Strictly Come Dancing.

Robb has played Mackenzie 'Mack' Boyd in the ITV soap since 2020, and has also appeared opposite Billie Piper in I Hate Suzie and in stage productions such as Legally Blonde The Musical.

In a statement, the actor joked: "I don't know who's more excited about this, me or my mother.

"I can't quite believe that I am going to be getting my dancing shoes on this September on one of my favourite shows of all time."

He added: "It's a dream come true, and I can't wait to bring my all to ballroom. Wish me luck, and any advice is very welcome - trust me I'll need it!"

Robb is the 12th celebrity to be confirmed for this year's series, joining stars including Delta Goodrem, Lacey Turner, Dani Dyer, Will Best, Jaime Winstone and Dame Sarah Storey.

More contestants are set to be announced in the coming weeks, with 15 expected in the final line-up. Scroll down to see the rest of this year's line-up so far:

News.title: Mark Hughes' son died of sudden adult death syndrome
News.content:
The son of former Manchester United footballer Mark Hughes died from sudden adult death syndrome, a coroner has found.

Alex Hughes was found collapsed at his home in Macclesfield, Cheshire, on 19 June by his two sons.

The 38-year-old, who followed his ex-Wales international father into football and held roles in recruitment at Grimsby Town, Manchester City and other clubs, could not be revived by paramedics, his inquest heard.

Following his death, Mark Hughes and his wife Jill said they were "totally heartbroken by the sudden and unexpected loss of our beloved son".

Sudden adult death syndrome (SADS) - also known as sudden arrhythmic syndrome - is diagnosed when the cause of death cannot be explained in a post-mortem examination because the structure of the heart appears normal.

It affects about 500 people in the UK every year.

The British Heart Foundation said SADS "usually happens when a dangerously abnormal heart rhythm goes untreated and leads to a cardiac arrest".

The foundation added that inherited heart conditions are "often the cause of SADS if the person who has it doesn't know they do".

News.title: Owner of bike maker Raleigh files for insolvency
News.content:
The company that owns iconic Nottingham bike manufacturer Raleigh has begun insolvency proceedings.

Accell, based in the Netherlands, bought Raleigh for $100m in 2012 but said on Wednesday it had "exhausted all the available options" and was "no longer able to meet its financial obligations".

It comes after a difficult period for Raleigh, which saw redundancies in 2024 and losses of Â£30m in accounts released the following year.

Jonas Nilsson, chief executive of Accell, said it was "a deeply sad and frustrating situation".

News.title: Walk-in mental health centres to open in banks and libraries across England
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "Nobody should be left to struggle with their mental health alone. But every day, thousands of people are waiting months for help, then finding the only door open to them is a busy A&E.

"These new centres will be a lifeline for so many," he said.

"They will bring NHS services closer to home, making it easier to get support before problems get worse and ensuring those in crisis get the right care in the right place."

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper added: "This is how we can turn the tide on mental ill health - preventing more people from reaching crisis, cutting waits for care, and building an NHS which is there for everyone when they need it.â

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Cooper said there would be a "continual programme" of rolling out these mental health centres - with the first ones set to open this autumn.

"It will take a bit of time in some areas but 100 right across the country I think will make a real difference to getting people mental health support early," she said, adding that "prevention can be much more effective to provide healthcare".

She said the government has already increased mental health staffing, but said "what these services are going to be doing is bringing together existing teams of staff to work together in a different way".

The chief executive of the Centre for Mental Health, Andy Bell, said he welcomed the announcement on the whole - although was concerned that the mental health emergency departments had not been properly tested yet.

He also said children and young people, who will be able to use these services, needed their own dedicated hubs.

But he said he was "delighted" that the government was taking action on mental health after it had been neglected by successive governments for too long.

"This must now be backed up by investment, most crucially in the workforce needed to provide effective mental health care," he said.

Stephen Jones, of the Royal College of Nursing, said he agreed investment in staff would be crucial if the new centres were going to cope with demand.

"More services closer to people's homes are a crucial step towards more humane care," he said.

But he added: "To succeed, both will need specialist mental health nurses at the centre."

The Department of Health said that the initiative is backed by Â£343m and the first sites will open in autumn this year, with "further facilities following from March 2027".

News.title: Reform pledges to reward public for illegal working tip-offs
News.content:
Reform UK says it would pay members of the public for tip-offs that lead to successful prosecutions of High Street shops employing illegal workers if it gained power.

The party's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said financial rewards under a "Turkish barbers tip line" would be paid from larger fines it would impose on firms using illegal employees.

It has pledged to fine larger firms up to 10% of their global revenues, and imprison the bosses of companies employing illegal migrants.

The Home Office said it was already increasing penalties for companies hiring illegal workers. A source within the department called some of Reform's proposals "empty posturing".

Reform said that if it won the next general election, it would make chief executives and directors of large companies profiting from illegal workers personally and criminally liable.

That would be regardless of their knowledge of workers' legal status.

The party said this would be similar to the personal liability of senior managers for the financial misconduct of their firms under Financial Conduct Authority rules.

Reform said it would also introduce a tip line for the public to report suspected illegal working or organised criminal activity.

Speaking at a news conference to unveil the policy, Yusuf said Reform would make it a legal duty for local authorities to investigate every "credible report" they receive.

He said the reward scheme would emulate a system in the United States that rewards whistleblowers with a share of fines imposed after successful prosecutions of serious financial crime.

He added: "In terms of the exact percentage, that would be in the final legislation that we pass."

News.title: Half of vaccines are binned - 'fridge-free' versions could change that
News.content:
Prof Saul Faust, the director of the NIHR Clinical Research Facility in Southampton, said it gave "equivalent" immune responses to the conventional vaccine as well as being "safe and well tolerated" in the early stage studies.

Faust added: "This obviously has potential to remove cold chain dependence, reduce wastage and improve access."

A larger trial involving 160 people is already due to start in the coming months.

This would be the final stage of research as the original vaccine is already approved and licensed so there is no requirement to perform large-stage trials needed for a novel vaccine.

The studies are being done to meet the World Health Organization's (WHO) goal of a vaccine that survives at 30C and 75% relative humidity.

But the research team say separate data shows the components of their vaccine also survive cycling between temperatures of -20C and +40C. That could mean the vaccine being viable after transport in a cold aircraft hold and then in the back of a truck in the heat.

There is not one single reason vaccines are wasted and disposed of, but the WHO estimates this is the fate of half of all vaccines globally. This can include damage in transport, passing the expiration date, and unused doses from multi-dose vials, but a major factor are failures in the cold chain.

News.title: When your child is dying you shouldn't have to beg for help
News.content:
One of the main problems the Cookstown family experienced was taking Lila out in the car, which had a huge impact on family life and their ability to attend hospital appointments.

In Northern Ireland, a child cannot qualify for the higher rate mobility component of Disability Living Allowance (DLA), external - which is required for the Motability Scheme - until they reach three years of age as it depends on a child's ability to walk.

Lila could not roll, sit, or stand and, according to a paediatric physiotherapist, was completely dependent for all care.

She received a specialised buggy, but the family still needed a wheelchair-accessible vehicle to transport her and the buggy.

Hayley said this was "denied" to Lila "due to her age, not clinical need".

Robert said not having a safe vehicle to transport his daughter in was "terrible" and he had to sit in the back of the car and hold Lila's head up "just so she could breathe".

A charity which helps disabled children did step in to assist and provided the family with a wheelchair-accessible vehicle, just before Lila's second birthday. Her father said that was a "lifeline".

"She was able to be safe and she got the life that she deserved eventually because she was fit to get out of the house," her mother said.

Lila's third birthday would have been on 1 August.

The family spent what turned out to be Lila's final weeks of life filling in forms so she did not miss the deadline for applying for mobility DLA before her third birthday.

Hayley said she felt her daughter was not "entitled to basic human rights that other kids are entitled to because she was born different".

"I would like the departments to work with healthcare professionals and look at diagnosis and clinical need and the expert opinions of medical professionals rather than age and a birthday," she said.

The Football Association remains steadfast in its belief that Gianni Infantino is no longer the right leader for Fifa, despite the global football body declaring its "full support" for its president on Wednesday night.

FA sources had previously indicated their intention to send a letter to Fifa, confirming the withdrawal of support for Infantino's re-election bid at next year’s Congress.

This position is understood to be unchanged, even after Fifa and Infantino issued an apology to national associations regarding their handling of a proposal to involve private investors in a company overseeing the World Cup and other competitions.

The Football Association of Wales (FAW) has publicly withdrawn its backing, alongside the FAs of Serbia, Sweden, and Finland. Sources close to the matter suggested Fifa’s recent statement has only intensified the anger among Infantino’s opponents, predicting "open warfare" at the highest echelons of world football politics.

open image in gallery FA chief executive Mark Bullingham (left) next to Infantino (centre) ( PA )

Even before Wednesday’s declaration, Fifa Council members were understood to be working to secure the 19-strong majority required to demand a meeting with Infantino.

This gathering would aim to hold him accountable for the private investor plan and the Folarin Balogun case. Members are understood to be prepared to initiate a ‘governance boycott’ of Council meetings – a move that would effectively paralyse Fifa – if they fail to achieve the necessary majority or if Infantino refuses their request for a meeting despite it being duly supported.

Fifa’s statement affirmed that Infantino had the "full support" of its management board members present at Wednesday’s meeting in Rabat, Morocco, underscoring his clear intent to remain in charge despite mounting opposition.

The statement acknowledged that "mistakes were acknowledged" in the handling of the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, clarifying it was "not the intention" for the Fifa Council or member associations to "feel excluded" from the process.

While a review into the FFE proposal’s handling was promised, the statement insisted that "everything that was done was done in full compliance with the Fifa regulatory framework."

It also warned that Fifa "will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation."

Meanwhile, Prince Ali Bin Al Hussein, president of the Jordanian Football Association, accused Fifa of "blackmail" in a post on X on Tuesday. He claimed Fifa had promised assistance with financial recovery during the World Cup if the JFA supported Infantino.

open image in gallery Prince Ali Bin Al Hussein accused Fifa of blackmail earlier this week ( AFP/Getty )

Fifa is aware of this allegation but has yet to comment, nor has it addressed The Guardian’s report on Wednesday alleging Fifa’s central role in discussions to develop the European Super League in 2020, which was at one point reportedly set to be named the ‘Fifa Super League’.

Fifa did, however, deny a report in The Times on Wednesday that Infantino had promised Morocco the right to host the 2030 World Cup final. The organisation stated that a decision on the matter would be made "in due course”, noting Morocco is one of three main co-hosts for the tournament, alongside Spain and Portugal.

Uefa was among three continental confederations that publicly rejected Infantino’s private investor proposal last week, even threatening to boycott Fifa competitions, including the World Cup, until it was abandoned.

Despite Infantino confirming the plan would not proceed last Saturday, Uefa issued a further statement affirming it had "lost confidence" in the Swiss. Uefa has not yet commented on Fifa’s statement published on Wednesday.

Hackers tried to break into at least 30 municipal water systems in Minnesota on July 26-27, 2026. Since then, Michigan and five other states have reported similar cyberattacks.

The attackers did not try to infiltrate the computers that utility offices use. Instead, they tried to seize control of small computers in equipment like pumps and valves that deliver drinking water to millions of people.

The utilities countered the attacks by shutting down the control computers and sending personnel out into the field to operate equipment manually. Utility officials have said that water remained safe to drink.

As a scholar who researches cyber conflict, I find that the methods used in these incidents are typical of international cyberattacks. Initial suspicion has fallen on hackers allegedly aligned with Iran, but the U.S. government has yet to attribute the attack to anyone.

How can someone from far away seize control of a water system and possibly shut off the flow or taint the water?

open image in gallery The utilities countered the attacks by shutting down the control computers and sending personnel out into the field to operate equipment manually ( AP )

Controlling the water machinery

There are about 152,000 public drinking water systems in the United States, according to the federal government. A municipality gets its water from lakes, reservoirs, rivers or underground aquifers.

Pumps move water through pipes to a treatment plant that filters and disinfects it. More pumps push the treated water into storage tanks, then through distribution pipes to homes and businesses. The entire system can span many square miles.

The hackers accessed small computers called programmable logic controllers at the water systems that operate all sorts of industrial equipment. The programmable logic controllers read sensors that measure conditions such as water pressure, water chemistry, tank levels and equipment status, and automatically operate pumps, valves and alarms. A household thermostat is a useful comparison: It reads the temperature and tells the heating or cooling system what to do.

The programmable logic controllers also transmit operational data to a utility’s central computer system. Workers use dashboards to monitor the information and send commands back to the controllers. The two-way communications can travel through wired networks, over radio or cellular links, or through internet connections.

Many utilities operate with small staffs, so remote connections allow an employee to monitor a distant pump or tank, receive an alarm after hours or let a vendor diagnose equipment without traveling to every site.

Controllers that use the internet may access it directly, or go through protective firewalls, secure gateways or virtual private networks. Direct access is more vulnerable because there are fewer defensive barriers. A hacker can find a controller by scanning the internet and finding its Internet Protocol, or IP, address, then try a weak or stolen password or exploit a known security flaw.

To reach a controller through a secure gateway or encrypted service, a hacker would have to steal remote-access credentials, or break into the gateway or private network, or get control of an operator’s workstation. The hacker could then use that foothold to reach the controller.

Attempted access can also be part of an intruder’s longer-term strategy to collect information, test defenses or establish entry for a later date.

How an attack works

Attacks on industrial control systems often follow a familiar sequence. Infiltration often begins with a quiet search for access. Attackers scan internet addresses for controllers, dashboards and outside companies that provide remote access services, looking for targets that are linked directly to the internet.

Next, the attacker looks for a default or stolen password to log in, an unpatched vulnerability or a misconfigured remote-access service. Sophisticated malware is not always necessary: In 2023, U.S. officials reported that Iranian-linked hackers targeted internet-connected Unitronics programmable logic controllers used by water utilities. Some utilities were still using the manufacturer’s default password, according to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

Finally, the attacker exploits the access they have gained. This could mean changing a password, issuing commands or attempting to alter the controller’s software. Researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology note that an intruder could replace legitimate control instructions with malicious commands. An attacker could also sneak into an office computer through phishing, then access the controller network.

Industrial equipment in service for decades is extremely vulnerable because it may not support modern security features, and utilities may delay updates because they want to avoid interrupting operations.

Reports thus far indicate that hackers accessed the Minnesota water systems through controllers that communicate over the internet directly. A July 30 FBI and Environmental Protection Agency advisory stated that attackers remotely accessed Rockwell Automation MicroLogix programmable logic controllers that were connected directly to the internet, and changed their IP addresses and passwords.

About the author William Akoto is an Assistant Professor of Global Security, American University School of International Service. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

Defensive moves that utilities can take

The most immediate step that utilities can take to protect themselves is to remove controllers and human dashboards from direct connection to the internet. Following the Minnesota attacks, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urged water utilities to place this equipment behind properly configured firewalls and other safeguards.

When remote access is necessary, utilities should route communications through a secure gateway or VPN, require multiple levels of authentication, and limit how much access each user has. Utilities should change default passwords, disable unused remote-access services and install vendor-approved updates to connected equipment.

In their guidance on internet-exposed dashboards, the cybersecurity agency also recommends separating operational networks from email and other business systems. This measure makes it harder for attackers to move between the two systems.

Finally, utilities should back up controller programs, log remote-access activity and practice restoring systems and operating manually.

A matter of resources

Rural water utilities with limited resources are a significant vulnerability in the United States’ critical infrastructure.

A group of volunteer cybersecurity experts is providing guidance to water utilities, but their reach is limited. Smaller utilities may need government funding or shared cybersecurity services to be able to defend themselves.

Dr. Anthony Fauci’s cell phone is now in the hands of Republicans pushing to charge him with contempt of Congress after he refused to answer questions about his actions during the COVID-19 pandemic at a hearing last week.

Fauci repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right during testimony last week, declining to answer more than 100 times, with Republican Senator Rand Paul leading the charge against the infectious disease expert.

The Senate Homeland Security Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations has obtained a copy of the doctor’s iPhone, The Wall Street Journal first reported, which Republicans hope could shed more light on the matter. The Republican-led committee already has copies of Fauci’s private journals, publicly released last week.

Fauci used the iPhone while he was director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases during the Trump administration, his spokesperson told the WSJ. The revelation of the cell phone comes as the committee is about to hold a vote on whether to hold Fauci in contempt for not answering questions at last week’s hearing.

The doctor helped lead the nation’s response to the pandemic and is accused by Paul of not being forthcoming about the potential origins of the virus, in addition to guidance he gave on vaccine mandates and social distancing. He has vigorously denied the allegations.

Dr. Anthony Fauci’s cell phone is now in the hands of Republicans pushing to charge him with contempt of Congress after he refused to answer questions about his actions during the COVID-19 pandemic at a hearing last week ( Reuters )

He stayed in government during the first year of the Biden administration and was pardoned by former President Joe Biden as one of the Democrat’s final acts in office.

Concerned that the doctor could become a future target of Republicans, Biden issued a preemptive pardon for Fauci that effectively blocked federal criminal prosecutions for any official conduct between 2014 and 2025, a period covering his response to the pandemic.

Fauci noted the pardon does not protect him from possible state prosecutions or from any allegations of false testimony before Congress.

Paul threatened that Fauci would face “consequences” for asserting his Fifth Amendment right after the infectious disease expert blasted the Republican lawmaker for his “unhinged obsession” with him.

Fauci “didn’t need to hide behind the Fifth Amendment, and maybe the Fifth Amendment doesn’t attach when you have a pardon in place ,” Paul told reporters after the hearing.

Before the hearing, Fauci said he still faced potential legal risks despite the pardon. In a statement, he accused Paul of trying to force him into saying “something, anything” that could fulfill the senator's repeated pledge to see him “behind bars.”

Paul said Wednesday he does not plan to immediately seek a full Senate contempt vote, acknowledging such resolutions often fail to secure the required 60 votes. Instead, he said the committee will first vote on sending a recommendation to federal prosecutors, with the possibility of a Senate vote later if necessary.

The Associated Press contributed reporting

News.content:

The protest group at the centre of the deadly unrest in Pakistan-administered Kashmir denied receiving any backing from India, challenging Islamabad to show evidence for such allegations and insisting its campaign was driven by demands for democratic rights rather than foreign interests.

In an interview with The Independent, SA Khan, a member of the advisory council of the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee, said his coalition of civil society and political organisations was “not answerable to India” and rejected accusations that it was financed or directed by Delhi.

Pakistan-administered Kashmir is in the grip of its worst political unrest in years, with deadly violence, an internet blackout, and allegations of police brutality overshadowing regional elections.

What began as demonstrations over soaring costs of electricity and essential commodities has evolved into a movement demanding political reforms, representative government, and greater accountability.

open image in gallery Pakistan Frontier Constabulary personnel stand guard along a street in Muzaffarabad on the eve of the first phase of regional election on 26 July 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Since the protests started earlier this year, Islamabad has repeatedly alleged that the Awami Action Committee is backed by the rival country and has portrayed it as an armed group seeking to disrupt elections.

It even banned the organisation under anti-terrorism laws in June.

This month, federal information minister Attaullah Tarar claimed an investigation had uncovered an India-linked digital disinformation network that financed and amplified online campaigns associated with the banned group.

He said security agencies had arrested a digital-marketing service provider allegedly linked to India, while investigators found payments for promoting social media content in Pakistan had been routed through payment gateways originating in India.

Mr Khan dismissed the allegations. "JKJAAC categorically rejects the allegation that it is sponsored, financed or controlled by India," he told The Independent. "It is an indigenous civil-rights movement rooted in local concerns about electricity prices, essential commodities, governance, public resources, implementation of signed agreements and political representation."

His remarks came after India's foreign ministry dismissed the recent elections as a "complete farce".

Mr Khan argued that Delhi's statement did not establish a relationship between India and the movement as he called on the government to disclose “credible evidence of foreign financing”.

"A statement by the Indian government about the elections does not establish an organisational, financial or operational relationship with JKJAAC,” he said.

“Foreign governments may comment on events for their own political purposes. JKJAAC doesn’t control those statements and should not be judged by them."

open image in gallery A motorcyclist navigates a road barricaded by supporters of the outlawed Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee in Muzaffarabad ( AP )

A prolonged internet blackout and restrictions on journalists have hampered independent reporting from Pakistan-administered Kashmir amid allegations of brutalities committed by the security forces.

Pakistani authorities have insisted that security forces acted lawfully against violent protesters who attacked police and paramilitary personnel, releasing videos they said showed armed demonstrators and maintaining that several security officers were killed in the unrest.

Mr Khan, however, insisted that the movement remained committed to peaceful protest. "JKJAAC rejects the description of the movement as an armed organisation,” he added. “Its declared policy is peaceful and non-violent.”

Mr Khan also called for an independent examination of the government's evidence.

At the heart of the unrest is the demand to do away with the 12 seats reserved in the regional legislature for refugees from India-administered Kashmir.

The Awami Action Committee argues that legislators who do not live in the territory should not be in any position to determine who forms the government in the semi-autonomous region. “Our movement is centred on Haq-e-Hukmrani, the people's right to participate meaningfully in governing themselves, and Haq-e-Malkiat, the right to equitable ownership, management, and benefit from public resources," Mr Khan said.

open image in gallery A woman casts her ballot during the second phase of regional elections in Muzaffarabad ( AFP/Getty )

Mr Khan insisted the movement was not seeking to strip refugees of political rights. "The issue is not whether refugees and displaced State Subjects deserve recognition and representation. They do," he said.

“The concern is that 12 members of the legislative assembly are elected from constituencies outside Azad Jammu Kashmir by voters living elsewhere in Pakistan, yet those members can determine who forms the government inside AJK."

Mr Khan said the movement was open to reforms that would preserve refugee representation while addressing disparities in voting power and territorial accountability.

"These aren’t abstract constitutional questions," he said. "They affect whether families can afford electricity and food, whether young people can find work, whether public money is spent on communities, whether residents have a meaningful voice in the institutions governing them."

According to documentation supplied to the Awami Action Committee by the Jammu Kashmir Human Rights Observatory, at least 88 civilians had been killed in the unrest until 3 August.

Amnesty International, however, said in a report published in late July that at least 40 people, including 34 civilians and six security personnel, had been killed.

"We cannot responsibly say that every deceased person was a formally registered JKJAAC supporter. Many were protesters, local residents, or participants in the wider civil-rights mobilisation," Mr Khan said.

open image in gallery A motorcyclist rides along a blocked road following clashes between protesters and security personnel in Muzaffarabad on 1 August 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

He said there was still "no reliable" final injury count because of limited access to hospitals, families and official records.

Mr Khan said his group regretted every death, including of police and paramilitary personnel.

"JKJAAC regrets the deaths of civilians, police officers, and paramilitary personnel and extends sympathy to all affected families. No family should lose a relative because a political dispute was allowed to become violent."

At the same time, Mr Khan rejected attempts to hold the entire movement responsible for the deaths of security personnel, insisting on individual accountability rather than collective blame. "If evidence establishes that an individual committed a killing, that person should face lawful proceedings. JKJAAC will not defend criminal violence."

open image in gallery Army personnel patrol outside a polling station in Mirpur, Pakistan-administered Kashmir, on 27 July 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Mr Khan accused Pakistani authorities of treating the dispute primarily as a security issue rather than addressing its political and civil-rights dimensions.

"We regard this as a political and civil-rights dispute that has been securitised rather than resolved," he said.

Looking ahead, Mr Khan said the group saw two possible paths: further escalation or a return to negotiations.

"One is continued securitisation, further deaths, deeper public anger and long-term damage to trust," he said.

"The other is reciprocal de-escalation and serious negotiation."

News.title: Rights groups accuse Israel of targeting and killing Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil

Global and Lebanese rights groups on Thursday accused Israel of intentionally targeting and killing Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil earlier this year and obstructing medical workers from reaching her as she lay critically wounded.

Khalil, a longtime correspondent for Lebanese newspaper Al-Akhbar in southern Lebanon, was killed in an Israeli strike in April in the village of al-Tiri, about 8 kilometers (5 miles) from the border with Israel, while covering the war between Israel and the Hezbollah militant group. She was one of 11 journalists killed in Israeli strikes in Lebanon since 2023.

Khalil’s colleague, freelance photographer and video journalist Zeinab Faraj, was wounded in the strikes.

International rights groups Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch, alongside Lebanese watchdog group Legal Agenda and the Union of Journalists in Lebanon, told reporters in a joint press conference in Beirut on Thursday that they reached this conclusion after corroborating information from photos, videos, satellite imagery, testimonies from eyewitnesses and officials, and conversations over WhatsApp.

They also said Israel was aware of Khalil and Faraj’s presence and that Israeli drones were flying low over the two before they took refuge in a building and that the Israeli military should have been aware that they were women and journalists.

The rights groups said Israel received multiple calls from Lebanese authorities and the United Nations peacekeeping mission in Lebanon, UNIFIL, to allow paramedics to access the site throughout the day.

“These strikes are considered direct attacks on civilians, which are considered war crimes,” said Amnesty Lebanon Researcher Sahar Mandour. “This does not change based on the Israeli military classification of this area as a no-go zone. It is a civilian area.”

The Israeli military said in a statement Thursday its own preliminary inquiry concluded that Khalil was killed in a series of strikes aimed at Hezbollah members, and once the investigation is completed, it will be sent to its legal branch for review.

Israel has previously denied targeting journalists.

The April strikes took place less than a week after a fragile truce went into effect between Israel and Hezbollah, and the journalist was deployed to report on the situation in battered villages. Her death was met with outrage across Lebanon.

The rights group said Thursday an initial Israeli strike killed two people in a car as they drove in front of the two journalists. A second strike hit the journalists’ car after they pulled over and took refuge by the entrance of a building nearby, lightly wounding them. They made their way inside the building, an abandoned store that sold local preserved food, before a third strike hit the building.

Lebanese Red Cross paramedics were eventually given clearance to enter the scene and were able to pull Faraj out alive but said they were fired at by Israeli troops when they tried to get to Khalil, who was buried under the rubble.

She remained alive for several hours, succumbing to her wounds, the report said, and the Israeli military soon after gave clearance for the medical workers to take her.

The coroner's report said that Khalil died in the evening from cardiac arrest due to head trauma and severe bleeding, hours after paramedics initially entered the area and were turned away, said Human Rights Watch's Lebanon Researcher Ramzi Kaiss.

“Khalil was likely alive when paramedics were forced away,” Kaiss said.

Amal Khalil is remembered for being present in large parts of southern Lebanon to try to shed light on life there, despite the risks. Her work in the area is widely respected across Lebanon's media landscape.

Over 4,000 people were killed in Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon, and over one million people displaced since the latest Israel-Hezbollah war began on March 2. Hezbollah fired rockets across the border two days after the U.S. and Iran attacked Iran.

—

Associated Press writer Sam Metz in Jerusalem contributed to this report.

Los Angeles County health officials have issued a public health alert after someone with an infectious case of measles visited Universal Studios Hollywood last month, potentially exposing numerous park-goers to the highly contagious virus.

The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health confirmed that anyone present at the theme park on Sunday, July 26, between 10 a.m. and 9 p.m., may have been exposed.

Officials are currently investigating other potential exposure sites. Individuals who visited during this timeframe are advised to monitor themselves for symptoms until August 16.

While those who have previously contracted measles or received the recommended measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine are generally protected, health officials still recommend vigilance for symptoms. Unvaccinated individuals or those with an unknown vaccination status face a significantly higher risk of infection.

Unvaccinated individuals or those with an unknown vaccination status face a significantly higher risk of infection ( Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images )

"As measles cases increase, it is important that residents take steps to make sure they are fully protected," Los Angeles County Health Officer Dr. Muntu Davis said in a statement. "The MMR vaccine is the safest and most reliable way to prevent measles and protect yourself, your family and your community."

Health officials urged residents to review their vaccination records, particularly before traveling, and to contact a health care provider if they are pregnant, immunocompromised, have an infant younger than 12 months who may have been exposed or are otherwise at higher risk.

Anyone who develops symptoms including fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes or a rash should stay home, avoid school, work and public gatherings, and contact a health care provider before visiting a medical facility, officials said.

Measles spreads through the air when an infected person breathes, talks, coughs or sneezes, and the virus can remain in the air or on surfaces for several hours after the infected person has left an area. According to the department, two doses of the MMR vaccine are about 97 percent effective at preventing the disease.

As of July 31, 2,371 measles cases have been reported nationwide this year, according to county health officials. Most of the cases are linked to outbreaks that began in 2025 and 2026. Los Angeles County last reported a measles case on July 21.

A stark new assessment has revealed that a mere 14 per cent of England's rivers, lakes, and coastal waters are currently in good ecological health.

The findings come from the Environment Agency's first update in six years, conducted under retained EU legislation governing water quality.

This comprehensive evaluation scrutinised 4,658 of the country's rivers, lakes, estuaries, canals, and coastal waters, measuring their health against a range of standards including wildlife populations, overall water quality, and the condition of physical habitats.

The report indicates that just 14.3 per cent of surface water bodies achieved an overall good ecological status in 2025, with widespread issues attributed to sewage spills, agricultural nutrient runoff, and pollutants emanating from urban areas and roads, such as litter, petrol, and garden pesticides. Alarmingly, only 15 per cent of rivers meet or exceed good ecological status, according to the figures.

They also reveal England’s water bodies are falling far short of the Government target to restore 75% to good ecological status by 2027.

open image in gallery The report indicates that just 14.3 per cent of surface water bodies achieved an overall good ecological status in 2025, with widespread issues attributed to sewage spills. ( PA )

In response to the latest data campaigners warned “nothing has changed” despite repeated Government promises, and said England’s rivers were among the filthiest in Europe, poisoned by sewage and industrial-scale agriculture.

The 2025 figures are slightly down from the 16.3% achieving good status in the last assessment in 2019, although the Environment Agency said they were not directly comparable as it had updated its methods, used a wider set of data and focused on places it suspected had problems.

But the EA said the analysis showed that “too many water bodies are not achieving the standards we want to see” and it would use the data to direct action from companies, farmers, businesses and councils to improve the state of England’s waterways and lakes.

And every single surface water body continues to fail to meet a “good” chemical status, largely due to persistent chemicals in the environment including former flame retardants and “PFOS”- a former stain repellent and firefighting chemicals.

These substances are now banned or heavily restricted in the UK but break down very slowly and persist in the environment for decades.

The rules mean that classification of water bodies is done on a “one out, all out” so that if a river, lake or estuary fails to meet good status in one of the elements it is assessed on – from fish, invertebrate and plant life to phosphate, ammonia and oxygen levels – it will fail to meet good ecological status overall.

The data show more than four fifths (82%) of individual indicators were good or high status, which the EA described as “encouraging”.

The 2025 dataset shows two thirds (65.4%) of water bodies achieve moderate ecological status, while 17% are poor, 3.1% are bad and just 0.1% achieve high status.

open image in gallery The EA said the analysis showed that “too many water bodies are not achieving the standards we want to see.” ( Getty )

The assessment also looks at groundwater and finds that 41% achieve good status, compared to 37% in 2019.

Chairman of the Environment Agency Alan Lovell said the Water Environment (Water Framework Directive) classifications helped officials understand where water bodies were improving and where further action was needed.

“The results show that too many water bodies are still not achieving the standards we want to see.

“We share the public’s ambition for faster progress which is why we are transforming our enforcement work with better data, stronger powers and our largest ever enforcement workforce.”

He added: “We are using all our evidence to direct sustained improvement action from water companies, farmers, businesses and councils.”

The agency pointed to improvements in phosphate levels in the River Roch to a “good” classification, following a catchment permit that required sewage treatment works upstream of the Manchester Ship Canal to remove more phosphate, improving the canal and other connected waters.

The EA also said it had stepped up its inspections of water company sites, and would be further increasing farm inspections from 4,000 to 6,000 a year over the next three years.

Environment Secretary Angela Eagle said the results underlined the need for “wholesale change” across the water sector.

“Our local communities deserve to have clean local rivers and lakes,” she said.

“We’ve already introduced landmark legislation to hold water companies to account, secured record investment to help fix infrastructure, and are laser focused on long term reforms that will prevent future failures.

“We will drive forward a system that puts the public interest first with higher standards, better performance and cleaner waterways.”

open image in gallery Environment Secretary Angela Eagle said the results underlined the need for “wholesale change” across the water sector. ( Getty )

But chief executive of environmental charity River Action James Wallace said, “Despite successive Governments’ promises, nothing has changed.

“Our rivers remain among the filthiest in Europe, poisoned by sewage from polluting, profit-driven water companies and by industrial-scale agriculture, including chicken manure runoff from intensive poultry units that rear tens of millions of birds for fast-food chains and supermarkets.”

And he said: “If the Government is serious about restoring our rivers, it must use the upcoming Clean Water Bill to take back control of water companies from private profiteers and ensure they are owned and operated for public benefit, environmental protection and public health.

“It must also tackle agricultural pollution with the same urgency, holding the biggest polluters to account, supporting the transition to nature-friendly agriculture and ending the regulatory failures that have allowed our rivers to become open sewers.”

A spokesperson for industry body Water UK said: “As the Environment Agency has made clear, the health of rivers, lakes and waterways is shaped by many different factors, including agricultural nutrients and urban and transport run-off, as well as sewage.

“Water companies are investing a record £22 billion in environmental improvements by 2030.

“This will be the largest amount of money ever spent on the natural environment, and will help to secure our water supplies, support economic growth and end sewage entering our rivers and seas.”

News.title: El Nino could cause explosion of rabid seals, animal health experts warn
News.content:
This year’s El Nino weather event risks propelling an outbreak of rabid seals around the world, the world’s animal health body has warned.

Countries in South America and Australasia are being urged to look for signs the deadly infectious disease has reached their waters, only two years after it was first confirmed in South Africa.

The 2024 discovery of rabies in South Africa’s Cape fur seals was the first significant outbreak ever found in marine mammals and has been described as a “significant shift in rabies ecology”.

More than 100 cases have been confirmed in South Africa and Namibia since then, raising fears that aggressive rabid seals could infect humans, pets and other wildlife.

Changing patterns in fish stocks caused by the El Nino phenomenon now potentially risk widening the spread, as uninfected seal populations migrate for food and come into contact with rabid colleagues.

Scientists believe warming sea temperatures off Antarctica could send seal populations northwards into Southern African waters, where they could be exposed to rabies.

They could then return to their home waters, taking the virus with them and infecting other seal populations.

News.title: ​Arteta’s ‘dynasty’ dream collides with Arsenal’s harsh reality
News.content:
Arsenal 1 Real Betis 3

Mikel Arteta says he wants to create a “dynasty” at Arsenal as he threw down the gauntlet to his players to retain their Premier League title and reach a “different level”.

Arsenal are on the verge of completing a £75m deal for Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimãraes from Newcastle and have not given up hope of landing Real Madrid winger Vinícius Júnior, who has been offered an improved contract by the Spanish giants.

The Premier League champions slumped to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night, when they paid the price for individual errors and a lethargic, sloppy defensive display.

But that did little to quell Arteta’s ambitions for the new season. “I’m even more excited [about this season], and we’re going to go and attack every possible title because that’s the ambition that we have,” he said.

“We know that we have the ability. We will go from a strength to a strength as well, whether it’s with the players that we have to take them to a different level, and with the market that is still open to recruit as well, so we are very optimistic about it.

“All the work that we’ve done – that I’ve done through the summer – is to understand what we need to do to win again and to create a dynasty in this football club. That’s the aim.”

Despite Arteta’s bullishness, he conceded Arsenal would have to be a lot better than they were against Betis. When asked about the mood in the dressing room, he said: “Very upset, given a hard time. They are fuming, but this is good. That’s what we need.”

Telegraph Sport analyses some of the talking points from a disappointing evening at the Aviva Stadium.

No Saliba a concern

The importance of goalkeeper David Raya and centre-backs William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhães to Arsenal hardly needs overstating. Their title success was built on the foundations provided by that triumvirate at the back.

Raya has yet to report back from holiday after Spain’s World Cup triumph and Saliba is facing an extended spell on the sidelines with a back injury. Gabriel did appear for the second half but, watching this, Arteta is unlikely to have been dissuaded from the belief he needs another top defender to compensate for the loss of Saliba.

It may have been only Arsenal’s second game of pre-season, so a degree of legginess was understandable.

But the ease with which they were cut open and overloaded by the Spanish side, and the volume of individual errors, did not sit comfortably with Arteta with just over a fortnight until they kick off their title defence at home to newly promoted Coventry City.

Only once in 63 matches last season did Arsenal concede three goals in a single game but they were fortunate Betis did not score more. “In the first half there are two different things: to play well and to compete,” said Arteta, who saw his side trail 3-1 at the interval.

News.title: Ebola outbreak outpacing containment effort, WHO chief warns
News.content:
Caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there are no vaccines or treatments, it has been extremely difficult to contain, according to experts on the ground.

“The outbreak is spreading faster than our scale-up of the response, with new cases doubling in some hotspots over the past week alone,” Dr Tedros said on X.

Part of the difficulty is that the virus was circulating undetected for weeks before the outbreak was formally declared in mid-May, leaving health officials even now racing to catch up with the spread.

Prof Placide Mbala, director of research, clinical trials and innovation at Africa CDC, told the Telegraph: “It’s mostly the fact we arrived a bit late. It took us some time before we detected this virus outbreak. And when we detected the outbreak, we already had a total of I can say more than 200 suspected cases. It’s been difficult to catch up. That’s where we are.”

While the DRC has a wealth of experience in tackling haemorrhagic fever outbreaks, the effects of that initial delay are still being felt.

Prof Mbala said: “We have some experience dealing with the cases, the labs, the communication, the infection prevention and control.

“We have some experience... But my observation is that we were very slow, and it’s why we’re in this situation.

“We are slow detecting the people, slow responding, we are slow deploying people, we are slow to recruit the community healthcare workers to improve contact tracing, we are slow to deploy the safe burials.”

DRC’s largest outbreak had previously been from 2018 to 2020, when 3,481 cases were recorded.

The West Africa outbreak recorded 28,616 cases and 11,310 deaths according to the WHO.

Prof Mbala said insecurity was also severely hampering attempts to curb the virus. The outbreak epicentre is in Ituri province, which has been wracked by ethnic strife for decades and is also home to militias competing to control mining.

He said: “There are many, many mining groups controlling most of the mining places. We have a big issue with those places, because they are places where the response team cannot go.”

Medics and aid workers have also been undermined by violent public distrust of their efforts.

Locals in the area have either doubted the existence of the virus, or have accused health teams of deliberately spreading the infection, or somehow benefiting from it.

More than a dozen health facilities have been set alight and several health workers have been killed.

Prof Mbala said: “The local people, they also sometimes are very upset, because they believe that it’s a kind of a business, and people who are coming here, they are getting a lot of money, [so] don’t want this disease to stop.”

He said he hoped that immunity was starting to rise in some areas and this would start to curb transmission.

However there was also a risk that people fleeing the outbreak would spread the virus further afield.

He said: “The second scenario is the fact we are seeing people moving from the affected area to new areas, to run away from the response team because they do not want to go to the treatment centre.

“And in complicity with their family members living in other areas, they are now the ones who are spreading the disease to new areas

“So we’ll see new places affected because people are moving around from the affected zone to the non-affected zone.”

News.title: Mykhailo Mudryk returns as Chelsea slip to Juventus defeat
News.content:
Chelsea 0 Juventus 1

Mykhailo Mudryk made his first Chelsea appearance since November 2024 as Xabi Alonso’s team succumbed to their second pre-season defeat.

Mudryk replaced Nicolas Jackson in the 82nd minute against Juventus, marking his return to competitive football after a long doping ban that was resolved this week thanks to changes in Wada regulations.

There were a couple of crosses delivered from the left flank by the Ukrainian winger, who could yet leave Chelsea on loan or on a permanent basis before the close of the transfer window.

Juventus were the victors though, thanks to a sumptuous 68th-minute goal by Kosovo winger Edon Zhegrova.

Alonso had 21 players on his bench, and made 12 second-half substitutions.

Levi Colwill and Cole Palmer featured in the defeat by 10-man Spurs on Saturday, but sat this game out as they continue to build fitness. Danny Welbeck did start though, reunited with former Brighton team-mate Joao Pedro up top.

Chelsea scored just one goal against Spurs and Juventus, but the thrust provided by right-back Marco Palestra in tandem with first Geovany Quenda and then Estevao was a bright spot for Alonso.

Chelsea continue their pre-season against AC Milan on Saturday, before they host Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge on August 15.

They begin their Premier League campaign at Fulham in the Monday night slot on the opening weekend.

News.title: The underground lab where ‘princess mosquitoes’ are treated like royalty
News.content:
Beneath the grand Art Deco headquarters of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine lies a vast labyrinth inhabited by weird and wonderful creatures.

In this maze of subterranean labs, store rooms and corridors live colonies of disease-bearing insects and arachnids from all over the world, from bed bugs, sand flies and microscopic dust mites to the so-called kissing bugs that spread Chagas disease – a sinister condition that can cause its victims to drop dead of heart failure without warning, albeit decades after the first (silent) infection.

Behind a series of doors, contained in stacks of mesh boxes, you can even find the flies that spread trachoma, the Dickensian eye disease that is still a leading cause of blindness around the world. But be warned: entering the room is not for the faint of heart – the flies feed on human excrement and the smell is impossible to forget.

There are also many varieties of mosquito, including several species of the Anopheles genus that spread malaria, Culex and Aedes mosquitoes that are also vectors for human and animal diseases, and even Toxorhynchites, perhaps better known as the elephant mosquito, a friendly giant which doesn’t bite people but preys on other mosquitoes.

These animals have been studied intensely since the insectaries were established in the building’s vaults in the 1960s, underpinning many breakthroughs in the control, surveillance, and understanding of vector-borne diseases in the developing world.

LSHTM researchers are now looking closer to home. They have established the UK’s first laboratory colony of Aedes vexans mosquitoes, a species native to the British isles, to study whether they could harbour diseases like West Nile virus, Rift Valley fever, Zika or Japanese encephalitis.

News.title: What I saw in a week on the front line of Afghanistan’s hunger crisis
News.content:
May 15 and 16, 2026

It is the weekend, a small moment to rest, although there is still a lot of work waiting for me. A week in the field does not mean that work in Kabul stops. I try to catch up on my emails and have a planned online interview for an international staff position – since in Europe, Friday is a normal working day. I also review parts of new proposals for donors and our financial planning.

On Saturday, however, I take a short break. Together with the base management team in Helmand, we visit a historical site called Qala-e-Bost, believed to have been built around 3,000 years ago. It is a rare moment to step away from work, followed by lunch with the team.

May 17, 2026

Sunday morning, the first working day of the week, we visit Basrhan Sub Health Centre, run by one of our local partners. As a nurse and former nurse trainer, I feel very much in my element in these health centres. It allows me to engage easily with the team and discuss their work.

I speak with the outreach officer and the vaccinator. They explain that this facility supports 18 outreach locations, each visited at least once a month. They provide vaccinations, raise awareness, and connect communities to the health centre. These visits often take place in simple settings, like mosques.

Immunisation is now well accepted. In the beginning, there was some resistance, but trust has grown over time. Every child is tracked, and if a child misses a vaccination, community health volunteers follow up at home. For extra polio vaccinations, this is carefully recorded by marking a finger of the child – helping ensure that no child is missed. The goal is clear: a polio-free Afghanistan.

I also speak with a mother. She is wearing a burka, so I cannot see her face. She tells me she is 22 years old and holds her 12-month-old son on her lap. She came because he has a fever, but I see a healthy child – something that stands out after my time in the TFU.

She brings her child regularly for follow-up and growth monitoring and the child has never been in a treatment program for malnutrition. She speaks positively about the services. “We are lucky,” she says. “The staff treat us well, and we have access to care in our community.”

News.title: World’s first seahorse hospital fights to protect them from extinction
News.content:
With careful precision, marine biologist Linda Albonetti extracts a 10cm-long injured seahorse – a heavily pregnant male – from an aquarium tank to apply healing ointment to its wound.

Linda, 29, coordinator at the world’s first specialist seahorse hospital, is currently caring for around 50 of these tiny creatures, all of which were brought in by local fishing crews after becoming snagged in their nets.

The seahorse will be kept for a few more days before it is released back into the Adriatic Sea, giving it time to recover from the cut to the soft, bony plates that form its outer carapace.

What the team here are doing is a literal drop in the ocean, a small attempt to fight back against the potential extinction of these remarkable fish.

In Europe and around countries like Indonesia, they are being poached in their millions for sale to a voracious Asian traditional medicine market where they are consumed as an aphrodisiac and alleged cure for impotence, asthma and kidney problems.

“There is definitely a downward trend in the overall seahorse population because they are being collected for the Asian market,” says Linda. “Technically, they cannot be exported to countries such as China, but there is no specific law preventing that trade. They do not have the same protections as sea turtles, for example.

“It is not happening in this part of Italy yet, but it is further south, off the Mediterranean coast. That is why it is so important that we monitor their numbers and maintain a good relationship with the local fishermen.”

News.title: The 13 best castle hotels in England
News.content:
Few places capture the imagination quite like a castle, and England is home to some of the most remarkable places to spend the night. If it’s not the romance of waking up in a canopied four-poster bed, or losing ourselves in centuries-old tapestries and visceral oil paintings, we are lured by tales of brave knights and plotting dignitaries, duplicitous royals and ghosts parleying secrets in the hallways.

Part of the magic is spending an afternoon wandering grounds and gardens followed by evenings in front of a roaring fire, or dining in a banquet hall that may have hosted medieval kings and queens. While not every castle has crenellated battlements, glistening moats or royal connections, each stony stronghold on our list has something special that makes it worth travelling for. In this modern age that might include a spa, fine-dining restaurant or extra touches like free admission to exhibitions and museum tours. Here’s our pick of the best castle hotels in England.

Sports.title: Barcelona to go toe-to-toe with hated rivals Real Madrid for Rodri that could spell bad news for Man Utd transfer plans
Sports.content:
BARCELONA are ready to battle bitter rivals Real Madrid for Manchester City midfielder Rodri in a transfer war that could have huge consequences for Manchester United.

The Spain midfielder is entering the final year of his City contract and is understood to be keen on returning to his homeland.



City have already offered the 30-year-old fresh terms, but know he wants to explore a move back to Spain before committing his future.

Real Madrid had looked to be leading the race after Rodri captained Spain to World Cup glory and picked up the tournament’s Golden Ball award.



But Barcelona have now officially entered the chase as they look to tempt Rodri with the chance to become the latest Spain international to join Hansi Flick‘s side.

Rodri is said to be attracted by Barcelona’s project, with many of his Spain team-mates already at the Camp Nou.

The Catalan giants also arrive full of confidence after beating Real Madrid to the last two La Liga titles, while beating them in six out of seven meetings in all competitions during that time.

Rodri is being tipped to step into the shoes once occupied by his former teammate Sergio Busquests, who became a master of his craft in defensive midfield.

Whoever wins the battle to sign Rodri may well gain a psychological advantage in the war – which is the showdown for the 2026/27 La Liga title.

Real Madrid still lead the race, and move to the Spanish capital could also trigger a domino effect involving Manchester United.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

It was revealed last month that Jose Mourinho is prepared to sell Aurelien Tchouameni if it helps fund a blockbuster move for Rodri, with United having already made enquiries over the France international.

Michael Carrick is understood to be keen on adding a specialist holding midfielder alongside summer arrivals Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, while Tchouameni’s age, experience and availability make him an attractive option.

But if Barcelona manage to hijack Real’s pursuit of Rodri and he goes to Catalonia, then Real Madrid will have no intention of selling Tchouameni to United.



Real, meanwhile, are also closing in on tying Vinicius Jr to a new long-term contract after positive talks this week.

According to Fabrizio Romano, negotiations are understood to be in their final stages, with only the final details remaining before Mourinho gets his wish of keeping one of Madrid’s biggest stars at the Bernabeu.

Sports.title: ‘Never arrogant’ – Man Utd cult hero Chicharito reveals people have wrong perception of Cristiano Ronaldo
Sports.content:
MEXICO’S all-time top scorer has torn apart public misconceptions about his former teammate Cristiano Ronaldo.

Javier Hernandez developed an intimate relationship with Portugal‘s greatest ever player during a 2014-15 loan spell at Real Madrid, and joked that Ronaldo is “competitive even when he has dinner”.



However, as Chicharito was quick to stress: “This competitiveness is not about arrogance.”

Contrary to popular perceptions of football‘s leading goal scorer of all time, Hernandez was unequivocal that Ronaldo “was never arrogant”.



Having once been assisted by Ronaldo in the Champions League quarter finals, Hernandez had a unique insight into CR7’s public persona.

In a recent interview with Rio Ferdinand, the two-time Premier League champion revealed: “He wants to be right, not to prove you that he’s better than you.

“It’s because there’s a switch in him… and there’s no on and off. It’s on all the time.

“To become the best of the best, you need to be the best of the best every single day, so you can hold the pressure of being the best.”

Because the ultra ambitious teammates “always” used to stay late after training, Hernandez “had the pleasure to spend time with [Ronaldo] alone”.

Sports.title: Shameless Argentina create special day to mark World Cup win over England after fury over Falklands banner antics
Sports.content:
ARGENTINA have shamelessly created a special day to mark their World Cup semi-final win over England amid outrage over their Falklands banner celebration.

Lionel Messi and Co completed a dramatic turnaround victory over Thomas Tuchel‘s men in stoppage time last month.



Enzo Fernandez and Lautaro Martinez both struck in the final seven minutes to seal a memorable 2-1 win after Anthony Gordon‘s opener.

But there were controversial scenes after the final whistle as a handful of Argentina players were seen holding up a banner that read: “Las Malvinas son Argentinas.”



That translates to “The Falklands are Argentinian.”

The banner, which players said was passed down to them by fans in the stands, is a reference to the conflict between England and Argentina over the Falkland Islands in 1982.



It was sparked by an Argentine invasion of the islands after a sovereignty dispute and lasted 74 days, leading to the deaths of 655 Argentinians and 255 Britons.

There have been calls for Argentina players who held up the banner to face bans and Fifa have already opened an investigation.

Argentina went on to reach the final before being beaten 1-0 by Spain.

But the country savoured its win over England so much that it has created the National Football Teams Day to mark the occasion.

It will take place on July 15, which was Argentina’s first World Cup win over England since Diego Maradona‘s ‘hand of god’ goal inspired them to a 2-1 win in 1986.

The Argentine FA said: “The date was chosen to commemorate the Albiceleste’s great and historic victory over England in the semi-final of the 2026 World Cup.

“The team, led by Lionel Scaloni, were trailing the English side by a single goal but, thanks to goals from Enzo Fernández and Lautaro Martínez, managed to turn the result around and send the whole country into a frenzy, with people flooding the streets in celebration.”

Argentina stars are under fire after also brawling with Spain players after their World Cup final defeat.



Ugly scenes at the MetLife Stadium following Spain’s win saw Leandro Paredes, Nahuel Molina, Thiago Almada and assistant coach Roberto Ayala all involved.

Paredes had been seen brawling with and then grabbing the throat of Spanish star Eric Garcia.

According to Fifa’s disciplinary code, the disciplinary and ethics prosecutor had the power to enforce a global ban.

However, Argentina will not play a World Cup qualifier for the 2030 tournament as they are co-hosting – so a ban might not come in until the first game of the tournament.

Somerset side Bridgwater United won 2-1 at Clevedon Town last night to go top of the Western League Premier Division after four matches.



The visitors earned an early two-goal lead, before hosts Clevedon pulled one back before half-time.

Bridgwater held on in the second period to earn a priceless three points, much to the delight of their owner Ian Davis.



After the game, Davis sat down for an astonishing interview with the club’s social media team alongside captain Mark Armstrong and player-assistant manager Dave Thorne.

The charismatic club chief began: “Here we go. Here we go. Firstly, Clevedon, f***ing absolute joke. Money money money and can’t do f*** all because they’re a bunch of mugs. So there’s that one out the window, we’ll get that one out the way first.”

As Armstrong and Thorne smirked, Davis continued: “They’re telling everyone how they’re going to walk this league, bash everybody. ‘We’re gonna do this, we’re gonna do that’. Yep, alright, well they haven’t done that tonight to Bridgy.

“No man of the match tonight for Bridgy, but here’s a thousand pounds, Mark, the captain will take the thousand pounds.”

At this point, Davis incredibly shoved a huge wad of cash into Armstrong’s hands.

As Armstrong held the cash up, Davis went on: “That’s for the man of the match, that’s for the whole team towards the end of the season.

Davis then piled pressure on Clevedon by claiming that their owners should take drastic action.

Sports.title: Fight to oust shameless Gianni Infantino is just starting - UEFA must not let up
Sports.content:
In case you are interested, the Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) game in Rabat’s Al-Madina Stadium on Wednesday night produced a 2-1 win for Zambia over Malawi. Alas, Nigeria’s 6-2 victory over Egypt in Rabat’s Olympic Stadium meant Zambia have not qualified for the knockout stages, having been pipped on goals scored.

It was quite a dramatic denouement to Group C but the headlines were all about one man in the stands for the Malawi-Zambia game. Sat next to Mattias Grafstrom, FIFA’s general secretary, was Gianni Infantino, brazening it out after receiving support from a meeting of as many of the organisation’s management board as could be bothered attending.

Outside of Africa, the WAFCON is unlikely to get extensive coverage but the point is that Infantino was a major distraction from what should have been the main attraction. The football.

And that, apart from a myriad other things, should tell him that hanging on to power is doing the game a disservice. The FIFA statement released on Wednesday night, and signed by Infantino and Grafstrom, refers to the ‘successful delivery of the FIFA World Cup 2026’.

‌



And to the extent that it happened and a lot of people watched it, they are right. But when players and fans should be reflecting on the kaleidoscope of emotions felt in the wake of a great tournament, they are instead occupied by Infantino’s sell-off scheme, the subsequent backlash and the ramifications of him staying in power.

If you operate on an ‘every cloud/silver lining’ basis, then it spares some nations a bit of soul-searching into their World Cup performances. For example, we are now more concerned about what the Football Association is going to do about Infantino rather than what it is going to do about an extravagantly-paid manager who completely blew it at the crucial moment.

View 3 Images Spain's magnificent achievement has been overshadowed by the controversy generated by Gianni Infantino (Image: Evrim Aydin/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Thomas Tuchel can thank Infantino for taking away some of the heat. But Infantino’s ill-fated, money-making project has significantly coloured how we now look at World Cup 2026 and its compelling characters on the field of play.

‌



The heroics from Vozinha, the Cape Verde keeper? The brilliance of marquee players such as Kylian Mbappe and Lionel Messi? Erling Haaland announcing himself on a World Cup stage?

The continuing thrill provided by Lamine Yamal? That epic Mexico-England game in the Azteca? Memories fade but these have been banished in an instant by Infantino’s behaviour.

It now feels like World Cup 2026 was just a sales pitch from Infantino to billionaire private investors. World Cup 2026 goes down in immediate history as the World Cup that was a test drive for private ownership.

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino's behaviour has relegated the players' deeds to World Cup sub-plots (Image: Justin Setterfield, Getty Images)

‌



It goes down as a grand finale to an Infantino plot. That plot was foiled and assumptions that Infantino would have no choice but to resign now look decidedly misguided.

Which means the fight to force him out is only just starting. It is a fight that should be led by UEFA, whose nations contributed so much to World Cup 2026, only for their efforts and achievements to be subsequently overshadowed by Infantino’s secret proposals.

There can be no letting up. When one administrator is throwing shade over the brilliance of footballers - whether that be at the World Cup or WAFCON - he simply has to be forced out.

Sports.title: Man Utd forced to fork out millions as Marcus Rashford benefits from contract loophole
Sports.content:
Man Utd forced to fork out millions as Marcus Rashford benefits from contract loophole

Manchester United face losing up to £5million due to past mistakes over contracts with Marcus Rashford expected to benefit

View 2 Images Marcus Rashford is set for a seven-figure bonus on top of his hefty Manchester United wages (Image: (Photo by Carl Recine/Getty Images))

Marcus Rashford is set to pocket an extra £4million if he stays at Manchester United due to a clause in his contract which has been activated because the club are back in the Champions League. The England international is among three players that can receive such a windfall with his current deal signed before United changed the structure of bonuses in contracts.

‌



Prior to the arrival of Sir Jim Ratcliffe, players would automatically receive a 25 per cent wage increase upon Champions League football being secured. Such terms were included in the sizeable long-term deals signed by Mason Mount and Andre Onana in the summer of 2023, which was exactly when Rashford penned a new five-year deal.

‌



United failing to play in Europe last season resulted in pay cuts but Champions League football for the new campaign has seen them go back up. For Rashford and Mount, who are still at the club, it is particularly beneficial because of the clause in their legacy contracts.

‌



Marcus Rashford primed for Ruben Amorim reunion after Man Utd transfer twist READ MORE :

The chance for a salary increase still exists in United deals for first-team players but they now have to earn it, as per The Telegraph, which is done through playing in over 60 per cent of the minutes in the proceeding campaign. That requires players to have been on the pitch in the Premier League for just over 2,000 minutes.

Rashford and Onana spent the campaign on loan elsewhere while Mount played just over half of the total required, but it is something that none of the trio have to worry about when it comes to receiving bonuses.

With Rashford taking in roughly £16million per-year, United's return to elite European football means he will be receiving an extra £4million on top of his weekly wage.

‌



United are also being forced to pay Mount in excess of £1m annually and while Onana's wages for the season are being covered by Trabzonspor, his salary has increased as well with this loan far less beneficial financially due to the clause.

View 2 Images Manchester United look to have managed to avoid paying Andre Onana an extra £1.5million

Both Rashford and the latter have been made available for permanent transfer but United have had problems selling either, largely due to their wages and the bonus in their contracts.

‌



Despite impressing at Barcelona, who opted against signing him permanently for financial reasons, that is likely why United were so eager to sell Rashford. A significant U-turn has since been completed on that stance, however, with it now looking more likely he will stay at Old Trafford.

Given the unnecessary outlay, United's summer plans are being impacted with deals for top targets deemed too expensive. The club were able to strike clever deals for Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos but missed out on signing Elliot Anderson and Mateus Fernandes.
