World.title: Senate committee set to vote on whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress
World.content:
Senate committee set to vote on whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress

toggle caption Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

Anthony Fauci, the 85-year-old retired health official who helped lead the U.S. government's response to the coronavirus pandemic, faces a contempt-of-Congress vote Thursday.

The punitive measure under consideration by the Republican-led Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee comes after he refused to answer lawmakers' questions in a hearing last week, citing his Fifth Amendment right to avoid self-incrimination.

In an opening statement, Fauci said that the committee chairman, Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., has "an unhinged obsession" with him and suggested the hearing was convened in an attempt to trick Fauci into lying under oath.

Sponsor Message

"Therefore, although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress," Fauci said, "under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions."

Fauci told the committee he had answered many of their questions already during previous testimony.

Fauci, the United States' leading infectious disease expert during the pandemic, has long sparred with Paul over the origins of the pandemic. In the days leading up to last week's hearing, Paul released more than 1,000 pages of Fauci's private diary entries, pointing to them as evidence that he masked private uncertainty about what caused the pandemic.

toggle caption Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

During that hearing, Paul indicated that Fauci shouldn't be concerned about testifying, given his immunity from prosecution over pandemic-era conduct. That immunity stems from a pardon that Fauci received from President Joe Biden for conduct between 2014 and January 2025 — a pardon that the then-president described as "preemptive" given Republican scrutiny of Fauci.

The 2025 pardon wouldn't protect Fauci from any prosecution stemming from conduct after that date, including any remarks made during present-day congressional testimony.

If Republicans do vote to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress, the Justice Department will then decide whether to pursue a criminal prosecution. While prosecutions are rare, two former Trump advisers — Steve Bannon and Peter Navarro — were imprisoned on contempt-of-Congress charges during the Biden administration.

Sponsor Message

Many Democrats now see a similar risk for Fauci, pointing to the prosecution of other former government officials whom President Trump is critical of, including his former FBI director, James Comey.

World.title: Drone with explosives found at German airport, official sees 'new quality' of threat
World.content:
Drone with explosives found at German airport, official sees 'new quality' of threat

toggle caption Hendrik Schmidt/DPA via AP

BERLIN — A drone with explosives was found at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport and the device was defused, authorities said Wednesday, in an incident that the country's top security official said posed a "new quality of danger."

Both the runways at the major freight hub were closed and several flights, including one passenger plane, were diverted to other airports after a flying object was sighted nearby shortly before midnight Tuesday. An anti-explosives robot was deployed to check an object near the south runway.

Regional police and prosecutors later said an airport employee discovered a drone near the airport's south runway with "an unknown explosive device," and the object was examined by police. They removed its detonator.

Sponsor Message

That the drone was carrying explosives "is a new quality of danger," German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters at the airport after interrupting his vacation to travel to the scene.

"Drone sightings, drone threats including in a hybrid context, are something we know from the past," he added. "That a drone armed with explosives is at an airport is a new threat scenario."

Dobrindt described what happened as "a hybrid attack scenario," but didn't offer more details of authorities' assessment or specify who might be responsible.

He said questions about details of the explosives, the origin of the drone and who was behind the incident were a matter for the ongoing investigation.

The regional interior minister of Saxony state, Armin Schuster, said authorities were looking for parts of a possible second drone.

Police and prosecutors said an apparent second flying object collided with a freight airplane after it aborted a landing at Leipzig/Halle because the runway was closed. The plane flew to another German airport, Hannover, about 200 kilometers (125 miles) to the northwest, where officials found slight damage.

The north runway at Leipzig/Halle was reopened after about two hours. The south runway was scheduled to be out of action for maintenance on Wednesday. Authorities said there was no danger to passengers or airport employees, and flights weren't affected during the day.

Sponsor Message

Photos from the scene showed police technicians with an explosives-disposal robot near a Ukrainian plane. The airport is a leading cargo hub and the planes located there include Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft.

NATO said it was aware of the incident but referred queries to German authorities.

In 2024, an incendiary device ignited at a logistics center at the airport and set fire to a freight container, part of a plot that Western security officials suspect Russian intelligence was behind. The flight it was supposed to take was delayed.

Western officials have accused Russia and its proxies of staging dozens of attacks and other incidents across Europe since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago.

World.title: Ousted Bangladeshi leader vows to return from exile despite facing a death sentence
World.content:
Ousted Bangladeshi leader vows to return from exile despite facing a death sentence

toggle caption Rajesh Kumar Singh/AP

Ousted Bangladeshi leader Sheikh Hasina said she plans to return to her country despite being sentenced to death by a court there during her two-year exile.

In her first public address since fleeing to India after a violent crackdown on a youth-led uprising in 2024, she said: "Whatever fate awaits me, I will return to my people."

Hasina added: "I may be detained, I may be sent to prison, they may try to enforce verdicts issued in fabricated cases, but fear cannot decide my duty to the people."

The 78-year-old, who served five terms as Bangladesh's prime minister, made the announcement in an audio address at the Foreign Correspondents' Club of South Asia in New Delhi on Wednesday. Her son, Sajeeb Wazed, also joined via video link from Washington, D.C.

Sponsor Message

Hasina's speech marked the second anniversary of her ouster. She fled Bangladesh by helicopter following weeks of protests in 2024 that left nearly 1,400 people dead, according to the United Nations.

Hasina has denied any wrongdoing during that period.

Hasina blames uprising on 'coordinated assault'

Enlarge this image toggle caption Rajib Dhar/AP Rajib Dhar/AP

Instead, Hasina on Wednesday blamed the violence on the protesters. "From the beginning, my government tried to resolve the issue peacefully, but it became a coordinated assault on the constitutional order, driven by hidden instruction, organized violence and propaganda," she said.

Analysts dispute that characterization. Ali Riaz, a professor of political science at Illinois State University, said the uprising was a response to Hasina's decades-long draconian rule.

"The U.N. report proved that state machinery was used against civilians. Killing 1,400 people in less than three weeks demonstrates the ferocity of the actions taken by her government and under her direct instruction," Riaz said. "Her narration of history is simply ignoring the facts of what happened on the ground."

Following her departure, Hasina's Awami League party was banned. And in 2025, a tribunal in Dhaka sentenced her to death in absentia for alleged crimes against humanity, among other charges, for her role in the crackdown during the protests. Hasina has dismissed the verdict as legally void.

Sponsor Message

Hasina announced Wednesday that she intends to return to Bangladesh in December.

Riaz said her return would trigger immediate legal action. "This is a legal requirement. Her conviction stands, there was no appeal, and she is a fugitive. She will have to be taken immediately to jail," he said.

Hasina strains Bangladesh-India relations

India's Ministry of External Affairs said it had no involvement in organizing the press conference. Bangladesh's Foreign Ministry said in a statement that Dhaka "deeply regrets" that the event took place in India despite its objections.

Hasina's exile has strained relations between the two countries, despite India's recent statements that it wants to restore ties.

World.title: 'Shell-shocked': Residents of Alberta town shaken by large white supremacist training meetup
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Residents of a small town outside Calgary are shocked to learn that Canada's most prominent white supremacist group held its second annual national meeting — where masked group members participated in military-style drills — at a volunteer-run community centre in early July.

"My first reaction is: that scares me," Lou Kuiack, a Millarville-area resident, told a CBC Calgary reporter. "I didn’t think that would come to our small little town, in our backyard."

Using visual clues in videos posted by the group, Second Sons Canada, CBC’s visual investigations team identified the location of the gathering roughly 70 kilometres southwest of Calgary, near the hamlet of Millarville, Alta.

Second Sons Canada was formed in 2024 and has chapters across the country.

Founded by Jeremy MacKenzie, Second Sons describes itself as a "men’s nationalist club." But it more closely resembles the " active club" -style model favoured by the global white supremacist movement. Second Sons' leaders have welcomed neo-Nazis into their ranks, called for mass deportations "at gunpoint" of non-white people from Canada and said Canadian politicians should be executed as traitors.

WATCH | Residents react to white supremacist group meetup: Locals 'shell shocked' by white supremacist group training in Alberta hamlet | Duration 2:16 Second Sons, Canada's predominant white supremacist group, held a large meeting in July where masked members participated in military-style drills. CBC's visual investigations team and CBC Calgary uncover the location of the meeting and speak to residents of the small Alberta hamlet of Millarville, shedding light on a recurring strategy for white supremacist groups: booking unsuspecting community centres.

Videos and images from the Alberta event, posted by Second Sons on its social media accounts, show more than 60 members participating in exercises including army crawls and marching with cots. MacKenzie, an Afghanistan veteran, led a military-inspired chant that referenced fighting the Taliban and included a Second Sons slogan: "Our people, our home, our future."

Group members also wore shirts with the slogan "old stock enforcer" emblazoned with crossed swords behind an old-school goalie mask.

"When they say 'old stock,' they mean white and European people," said Evan Balgord, executive director of the Canadian Anti-Hate Network.

"When they label themselves as enforcers, it’s tied to their belief that they will have to use culture, politics and violence to achieve their goal of a racist mass deportation of people who aren’t old stock Canadian."

Exposing the location

Second Sons routinely publishes visuals of its exercises but its members are often masked or digitally obscured, and the group does not publish the precise locations of its gatherings. The group did not identify the exact location of its July meetup, only saying that it took place in the "foothills of Alberta."

In a Telegram post published weeks after the gathering took place, MacKenzie praised the group's members and said they had spent the weekend in activities that included "friendly combat sports competition, organizational training, promotions, awards, excellent food and social time."

Second Sons Canada founder Jeremy MacKenzie delivers a speech to members inside Square Butte Hall. (Second Sons Canada/Telegram)

In a video posted to Telegram recapping the weekend, Second Sons members can be seen holding a banner with the traditional active club slogan "Tribe and train" over an overpass on Highway 2 near Okotoks, Alta., a town about 47 km south of Calgary.

An illustration shows matching elements between an image released by Second Sons Canada and Google Streetview imagery. (Illustration: Froilan Untalasco/CBC; Second Sons Canada/Telegram, Google Maps)

Using that clue as a lead, CBC matched the community centre used by the group that weekend with Square Butte Hall near Millarville, located approximately 43 km from Okotoks.

A distinctive welcome arch belonging to the hall can be seen in shots of Second Sons members arrayed in their ranks outdoors.

CBC News matched images from the Second Sons video, like this welcome arch, to the Square Butte Hall. (Illustration: Froilan Untalasco/CBC; Second Sons Canada/Telegram, Google Maps)

Similarly, interior details of a clip showing MacKenzie leading members in a chant related to the war in Afghanistan match photos of the hall that can be seen on the venue's Facebook page.

Square Butte Hall is a volunteer-run space that hosts community events like dances, recipe exchanges and fire prevention training.

Second Sons Canada members stand outside Square Butte Hall near Millarville, Alta. (Second Sons Canada/Telegram)

"The organization that booked the hall did not identify itself to us in any way," said Shanna Dunne, president of the hall’s board of directors, in an emailed statement to CBC.

"The Square Butte Community Association is committed to providing a respectful and inclusive community space, and our volunteers work hard to support the many positive events and activities that bring our community together."

In a phone call with a CBC Calgary reporter, Dunne said an RCMP officer contacted the hall and asked for information about the Second Sons meetup.

In a statement to CBC, the RCMP said it does not confirm or deny investigations, but that it is "aware of the Second Sons."

It emphasized it does not "investigate movements or ideologies," focusing on criminal activities by individuals or groups. But it said it is "actively monitoring the rise of hate-motivated crime and incidents across the country."

Residents shocked

Millarville residents who spoke to CBC said they didn't know the Second Sons meetup had taken place, and were concerned about the group’s presence in the community.

Leanna Bridgeman, manager of local coffee shop Miss Marple’s, said she was "absolutely shell-shocked that something like that would happen out here," calling it "completely disturbing."

Leanna Bridgeman, manager of a coffee shop in Millarville, says she was 'shell-shocked' after learning that Second Sons held a meeting in her community. (CBC News)

Tim Babey, owner of the Millarville General Store, said he was "really surprised."

"People out here are pretty accepting, but I think they'd still be quite shocked at seeing something like that going on," he said.

Tim Babey, owner of the Millarville General Store, told CBC that he was surprised to learn of Second Sons’ presence in town. (CBC News)

CBC reached out to the Foothills County reeve — a position similar to mayor — for comment.

"Foothills County recently became aware of activities that are reported to have occurred on private property," said Reeve Rob Siewert. "At this time, the county has not received any formal complaints and is not aware of any calls having been logged with staff regarding the matter."

Second Sons Canada’s use of the community hall fits a pattern CBC has observed elsewhere in Canada, where they book spaces like recreation centres without disclosing the full scope of the group’s planned activities or overall aims.

Last September, CBC News tracked a similar meeting in southern Ontario to a Lions Club in Caledonia, Ont. The hall told CBC at the time that if staff had been aware that Second Sons was behind the booking, it would not have been approved.

"Booking community spaces under false pretenses is normal for white nationalist movements, because most spaces wouldn’t agree to hold their events," said Balgord of the Canadian Anti-Hate network.

Second Sons Canada did not respond to a request for comment from CBC.

World.title: More B.C. wildfire activity expected with air quality warnings across Lower Mainland
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The latest on the wildfires:

A new wildfire broke out in Metro Vancouver on Wednesday afternoon, roughly one kilometre southeast of Sasamat Lake's White Pine Beach. As of 6:47 p.m. PT on Aug. 5, it is burning over an area 1.5 hectares in size.

in size. Air quality warnings are in effect for much of the Lower Mainland, including an orange warning for the eastern Fraser Valley and a yellow warning for Metro Vancouver and central Fraser Valley.

of the Lower Mainland, including an orange warning for the eastern Fraser Valley and a yellow warning for Metro Vancouver and central Fraser Valley. A pilot was taken to hospital after a helicopter crash while fighting fires in the South Cariboo.

after a helicopter crash while fighting fires in the South Cariboo. As of 10 p.m. Wednesday, the B.C. Wildfire Service says "hot and dry conditions return for the majority of B.C." and there is potential for increased fire activity . It expects to see holdover fires and lightning-caused fires in the coming days.

. It expects to see holdover fires and lightning-caused fires in the coming days. There are six wildfires of note currently burning in B.C.: the Wait Creek and Tower Creek wildfires in the East Kootenay region; the Brunswick Creek and Ainslie Creek wildfires along Highway 1, north of Hells Gate; the Pear Lake wildfire north of Cache Creek; the Bradley Creek fire near Okanagan Lake.

Metro Vancouver wildfire spotted

A wildfire was discovered late Wednesday afternoon, burning roughly one kilometre southeast of Sasamat Lake's White Pine Beach in Metro Vancouver's Belcarra Regional Park.

The fire grew quickly to cover an area of 1.5 hectares, according to the B.C. Wildfire Service's latest update .

It prompted tactical evacuations of two properties on Fern Drive, in the nearby Village of Anmore. The village issued an evacuation alert affecting roughly 35 properties at 7:30 p.m. Wednesday.

At this time, the fire is suspected to have been caused by human activity.

Ground crews were permitted to access the wildfire directly after B.C. Hydro cut power to electric lines in the immediate area. (Shawn Foss/CBC)

First responders were not able to immediately access the fire on the ground due to live electric wires in the area, and instead used three helicopters to dump water on the blaze.

Once B.C. Hydro cut the power off to its infrastructure in the area later Wednesday evening, ground crews were able to directly combat the wildfire, according to Metro Vancouver incident commander Brant Arnold-Smith.

"We are very fortunate that the conditions presently are not windy. It's advantageous for our crews. It's also a lot safer for our crews," he said on Wednesday evening.

By Wednesday evening, Arnold-Smith said 40 firefighters were involved in the firefighting effort.

Air quality warnings across Lower Mainland

On Wednesday, air quality warnings were issued for various regions across the Lower Mainland.

An orange warning — indicating very high health risk — covered the eastern Fraser Valley.

In the rest of Metro Vancouver and the central Fraser Valley, a yellow warning was issued, which indicates a high health risk.

In a statement , Metro Vancouver said the warnings are "due to elevated levels of fine particulate matter from wildfire smoke from the South Cariboo, the [southern] Interior, and the complex of wildfires near Boston Bar in the Fraser Canyon."

It added that Metro Vancouver staff will continue to monitor the conditions, as weather and wildfire activity can "rapidly change smoke concentrations."

Overall scope of burning

The Pear Lake wildfire is still the largest currently burning in B.C., at roughly 1,269 square kilometres.

The Thompson-Nicola Regional District says about 120 properties , not including ones in the Village of Clinton, suffered structural loss due to the fire.

Further southeast, near Vernon, the Bradley Creek wildfire covered an area of 28.52 square kilometres.

It has caused at least 200 homes on the Okanagan Indian Band's reserves to be destroyed, according to preliminary estimates from the band.

The Brunswick Creek wildfire is roughly 78 square kilometres in size, burning in B.C.'s Fraser Canyon near Boston Bar.

WATCH | Evacuees see destruction from Bradley Creek fire: Evacuees see destruction left behind by B.C.'s Bradley Creek wildfire | Duration 2:19 CBC News reporter Baneet Braich got on a boat with some fire evacuees to take a look at the destruction on the north end of B.C.'s Okanagan Lake amid the raging Bradley Creek fire. The evacuees took her to an area where multiple homes were destroyed and told her about the panic as they fled.

Road closures

According to DriveBC, several major routes remain closed because of wildfire activity.

Highway 1 is closed between Yale and south of Boston Bar at Uztlius Creek Forest Service Road, and there is no estimated time of reopening. Drivers are being directed to use Highway 3 or Highway 5.

The Big Bar Reaction Ferry, which runs across the Fraser River 72 kilometres west of Clinton, is not currently operating due to wildfires in the area.

Highway 97 is closed through Clinton, for a 60-kilometre stretch between Loon Lake Road and 76 Mile Frontage Road. Traffic is being detoured using Highway 1 through Kamloops, then to Highway 5 and Highway 24. Big Bar Road is also closed between Jesmond Road and Highway 97.

Westside Road along Okanagan Lake is closed between Shelter Cove and Highway 97 north, cutting off a key route for residents to the west of Okanagan Lake. The road is open as far as Shelter Cove, with Highway 97 serving as the alternate route.

Highway 95A near Kimberley is closed in both directions between Thomason Road and the Highway 93/95 Junction.

Toward the U.S. border, Silver Skagit Road is closed south of Flood Hope Road to the Canada-U.S. border because of the Hozomeen Mountain wildfire. Silver Lake remains open, but Ross Lake Campground and Skagit Valley Provincial Park are closed.

World.title: Canadian workers speak out against growing screen time surveillance
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Workers at some of Canada's biggest companies say increased workplace surveillance is taking a toll on their mental health as their employers ramp up the use of software that monitors their screen activity.

TD Bank told employees in its financial crimes and risk management team in June, in a call first reported by Reuters , that it will start tracking their screen time — specifically the time they spend on browsers, internal chat and meeting apps — using a tool called WorkiQ.

TD employees in other departments have raised concerns about this and other productivity tracking tools, saying they cause added stress and unease in the workplace.

"We are all very, very worried about what it's going to do," a TD employee in Edmonton told CBC News.

Companies across a range of industries are increasingly facing pushback from employees over the deployment of software that monitors screen activity. The practice has raised questions about privacy, trust, workers' rights and workplace stress.

In June, Meta paused a program that tracked employees' keystrokes and mouse movements amid concerns about data privacy and staff backlash, including a petition signed by 1,600 employees.

Worker feeling 'extreme unease'

The TD employee, who CBC News has agreed not to name because she fears she could lose her job for speaking out, said she worries the new monitoring tools will come to her workplace soon.

Her managers currently use ControliQ, she said, which is made by ActiveOps, the same U.K.-based company behind WorkiQ. ControliQ tracks time spent on tasks, but not granular details like keystrokes and mouse movements.

Introduced about two years ago, the tool is increasingly used to "shame and belittle" workers by displaying and comparing their "productivity" metrics at meetings, the employee said.

Bosses also use "Active" and "Away" status on Microsoft Teams to gauge work activity, she said, even though much of the work she does requires reading documents and other tasks not reflected by screen time.

As this type of monitoring ramps up, the employee — who has been with the company for eight years — said she and her colleagues are feeling burnout, frustration and "extreme unease."

"It's going to start impacting colleagues, because there's a lot of stuff that we do in our day that isn't recordable or isn't quote-unquote productive, but it's necessary work," she said.

"We run the risk of losing bonuses, losing raises, losing performance ratings — that sort of thing. And then we run a risk of getting written up, and eventually, possibly, losing our jobs."

TD spokesperson Mick Ramos did not answer specific questions about the software or employee concerns in an emailed statement to CBC News.

"Like many organizations, we use workflow tools in some areas of our business to better understand how work gets done and where we can make it simpler and more effective," he said. "Colleagues are informed about their use and purpose well in advance."

An ActiveOps spokesperson said in an email that the company aims to improve workplace environments by giving employers "the visibility they need to plan work and resources." He added that WorkiQ is being rebranded as Application Mining.

Using an internet archive search, CBC News found ActiveOps explicitly called WorkiQ "employee monitoring software" in 2021. It has since changed the language on its website and no longer refers to it as such.

Tracking 'degrading and humiliating': Bell employee

Surveillance and monitoring tools have become commonplace at telecom companies in Canada.

A longtime Bell employee in Toronto told CBC News that WorkiQ sounds "eerily similar" to software that's used at her work.

Bell started using Verint software to track employees' screen time and mouse movements during the COVID-19 pandemic, when everyone was working from home, she said, using "occupancy" or "effectiveness" metrics to track their active time.

A Bell Canada employee in Toronto says the company's screentime monitoring software is hard on her mental health. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

Workers can be punished for not meeting their effectiveness targets, the employee said, first with a verbal warning and then with progressive discipline, up to and including termination.

"The amount of surveillance that's done, it's very hard on your mental health," she said.

"I don't know if the company actually understands how almost degrading and humiliating it is to know that you have to have a babysitter when you're in your 50s, and you've been doing your job for 30 years, and you've been doing it well."

CBC News is also not naming the Bell employee because she fears she could lose her job for speaking out.

The employee said the effectiveness time requirements in her specific workplace have continued to increase since the pandemic, to 85 per cent from 72 per cent.

The current target is "almost impossible" to achieve, she said, and leaves no room for people to have bad days.

"When you do the math, it works out to about 23 minutes a day that you've got that you're able to use the bathroom, go grab a drink of water — or, say, you're reading," she said, adding employees are also allowed one half-hour lunch break and two 15-minute breaks.

WATCH | Benefits and concerns around monitoring tools: Should employers use productivity monitoring software? | Quick Question | Duration 7:21 Anti-surveillance advocate Matthew Mitchell and Jay Godse of Awareness Technologies, whose company develops electronic worker-monitoring software, discuss the benefits and concerns surrounding software that tracks employees while they work.

The Bell employee also worries about repetitive strain injuries from constantly moving a mouse to meet the requirements.

CBC News could not verify the 85 per cent target at the employee's specific workplace, but obtained documents from another Bell workplace showing an 80 per cent effectiveness target.

She said she's heard from managers that Verint is not only monitoring workers, but pulling their work to train AI systems and offshore workers, which she suspects has factored into recent layoffs .

"It's a weapon and it shouldn't be wielded the way it is," she said.

A Bell spokesperson told CBC News in an email that the company does not use Verint to train AI or offshore workers, but did not respond to specific questions about employee complaints or the way the software is used.

"Bell uses call-monitoring and screen-capture software to help customers get the best experience possible. This is standard industry practice for call centres," she said.

A spokesperson for New-York based Verint did not respond to CBC News's requests for comment.

Do the tools even work?

Tara Behrend, a professor at Michigan State University's School of Human Resources and Labor Relations who studies monitoring and surveillance tools, said her research has consistently found two things: these tools increase stress on workers and don't actually improve performance.

Tracking tools tend to narrow workers' focus to the metrics that are being monitored, which can then cause them to ignore other aspects of their job and also create "anti-social incentives," she said, like discouraging them from taking a screen break to help a co-worker.

"When someone starts micromanaging you and babysitting you, it breaks that contract of trust. And so then you just say, 'Fine, if you think all I am is this collection of tasks that you wrote down, then that's what you'll get from me and nothing else," Behrend said.

"It just makes work this really superficial imitation of itself. Work is not just a collection of tasks. Nobody wants to feel like that's what their contribution is."

Nevertheless, she said, these tools have proliferated with recent transitions to remote work and accelerated as part of a general societal push toward more data gathering and algorithm training.

Increased worker monitoring has led to negative physical and psychological consequences for workers in some industries, Behrend adds, citing a 2024 Oxfam report that found Amazon and Walmart warehouse workers suffered from pain and dehydration, and were afraid to take bathroom or hydration breaks because of intense surveillance.

Roch Leblanc, a national representative for Unifor, a union that represents 19,000 Bell workers across Canada, raised alarms about growing worker surveillance in telecoms when he addressed the House of Commons committee on industry and technology in April.

WATCH | Ontario employers have to disclose tracking software: Is your boss watching you work? Some Canadians are about to find out | Duration 1:56 In Ontario, employers must now disclose if they have been using productivity tracking software to keep tabs on their employees. Experts say while this may address transparency concerns, businesses should be tracking output instead.

Unifor has also raised concerns to Bell's management about Verint software specifically.

Leblanc tells CBC News the software is "invasive," has created significant stress in the workplace and does not always represent the true picture of a worker's productivity.

"The work intensification is at such a level now, there's no ups and downs in the work on a daily basis," he said. "It's constantly intense, constantly frustrating."

World.title: Ontario police watchdog no longer investigates most off-duty sex assault complaints
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Special Investigations Unit's sexual assault caseload has been declining ever since new legislation narrowed the police watchdog's mandate and diverted complaints involving off-duty officers to local and provincial law enforcement.

CBC News compiled and analyzed data from a decade of SIU cases involving suspected sexual assault by police officers. The independent civilian oversight body in Ontario is responsible for investigating police officers and recommending charges against them for potential criminal misconduct and is mandated to release reports on the status of their investigations. In cases involving sexual assault allegations, some identifying information may be excluded for privacy reasons.

The Special Investigations Unit Act , which came into effect in December 2020, limited the watchdog's ability to investigate sexual assault allegations involving off-duty officers. Though there are dozens of ongoing cases so far this year, the figures have mostly been trending downward since 2021.

What's not clear is if local police services are making up the difference by investigating cases that no longer go to the SIU.

Though some experts suggest law enforcement agencies are better equipped to investigate police-perpetrated sexual assault allegations, advocates say people could be more reluctant to report such crimes to police forces investigating their own officers. They also warn that the changes could limit our understanding of the scope of the issue — unless police forces do a better job of collecting and sharing data.

CBC News asked the Police Association of Ontario, a policing advocacy organization that represents thousands of police personnel from 46 police associations across the province, if police-led investigations into off-duty officers accused of sexual misconduct have risen correspondingly as a result of the changes to the SIU Act.

Mark Baxter, the organization's president, told CBC News in an email that there was no "comprehensive, publicly available" province-wide data detailing the number of those allegations, their investigations or charges.

WATCH | Reporting 'can be a real challenge for survivors,' PAO president says: Ontario policing advocacy organization acknowledges sexual assault reporting challenges | Duration 1:18 Police Association of Ontario president Mark Baxter says the group supports 'any policies that make it easier to report a sexual assault.'

He says SIU data shows the number of sexual assault allegations reviewed by the unit peaked in 2021, the year after the SIU Act came into effect.

"That immediately tells me that nothing changed. That actually, it made it easier for victims to report allegations of sexual assault," Baxter said.

He said he "didn't know what to make" of those numbers decreasing in subsequent years.

Power imbalance

Researchers like Danielle McNabb, an assistant professor of political science at Brock University who co-authored a study on police-involved sexual assaults using SIU data from 2005 to 2020, caution the changes to the SIU Act could limit the public's ability to understand the scope of police-perpetrated sexual violence.

"Basically, the SIU is now empowered to investigate far fewer sexual assaults, and so I think that's why you're seeing that decline," said McNabb. "It's my view that this legislative change has been highly problematic."

Ava Williams, a Toronto-based lawyer who has worked on cases involving police-perpetrated sexual violence, says the change could result in people being less inclined to report police-involved sexual assaults to law enforcement.

"The SIU helps defuse the power imbalance between victims or survivors" and police, Williams said. She noted that she experienced a sexual assault in Ontario in 2010 that she then reported to law enforcement.

Williams says in her experience as a lawyer, a perpetrator being a police officer "just adds another element or layer to how scary it might be to discuss a traumatic event that happened to you."

WATCH | 'People who report want to feel safe,' lawyer says: SIU helps address power imbalance between victims and police, lawyer says | Duration 0:54 Toronto-based lawyer Ava Williams says changes to legislation governing Ontario's police watchdog could result in people being less inclined to report police-involved sexual assaults to law enforcement.

Gaps in reporting

In reference to the apparent decrease in sexual assault cases reviewed by the SIU, a spokesperson for the unit, Kristy Denette, told CBC News in an email that the overall number of reports they receive fluctuates "for a variety of reasons."

In their 2022 study, McNabb and Kate Puddister, an associate professor in the political science department at the University of Guelph, found that more than 40 per cent of all sexual assault allegations investigated by the SIU between 2005 and 2020 had to do with off-duty police conduct.

Puddister says their research identified cases where officers would meet their victims through their police work, then carry out assaults off duty.

"All of the concerns that we have about the power imbalance, the coercion that's possible, all of the deeply troubling things that are related to police sexual violence, are still relevant when the officer is off duty," she said.

Danielle McNabb, left, an assistant professor of political science at Brock University, and Kate Puddister, an associate professor in the department of political science at the University of Guelph, co-authored a 2022 study on police-involved sexual assaults using SIU data. (Submitted by Danielle McNabb and Kate Puddister)

According to a 2021 Statistics Canada analysis , sexual assault is "vastly underreported" in Canada. A 2014 study found the majority of sexual assault incidents — 83 per cent — were not reported to police.

StatsCan also found that the number of sexual assault incidents in Ontario's general population increased by approximately 37 per cent between 2020 and 2024.

McNabb says their research suggests underreporting is due to survivors fearing police won't believe them.

"This is part of why I see this change as problematic," she said.

Their 2005-2020 study showed that in rare instances where the SIU laid sexual assault charges against an officer and the case went to trial, convictions were exceptionally uncommon.

Of 689 SIU reports of sexual assault by on and off-duty officers between 2005 and 2020, only 1.59 per cent led to an eventual conviction and sentence.

The analysis of SIU cases by CBC News found that most sexual assault allegations investigated by the unit resulted in no charges, or were terminated without a full investigation, which could indicate the case fell outside their jurisdiction.

Sunny Marriner, a prominent Canadian sexual assault advocate whose work focuses on how survivors experience the criminal justice system , says the fact that there are numerous oversight bodies in Ontario handling police-involved sexual assault allegations creates a "fractured" information ecosystem.

That data is "probably in 10 different places" that might report it in different ways, Marriner said.

She says what's needed is a centralized database of investigations into police-involved sexual misconduct to provide the kind of data that allows for progress on the issue.

"The violence itself is what we have to look at, not who's addressing it."

Police, ex-SIU director weigh in

Howard Morton, who headed the SIU from 1992 to 1995, says limiting the independent body's mandate to exclude some off-duty conduct was "a huge mistake."

"The imbalance in power that the offender has over the victim is contributed to by the fact that that person is a police officer," Morton said.

While it's impossible to determine the variables involved in the number of allegations, former Ottawa police officer Gregory Brown says it's reasonable to think the number of SIU cases would decline due to changes in the SIU Act.

Brown, now an adjunct research professor at Carleton University whose work focuses on criminal justice, says police agencies are better equipped than SIU investigators to investigate off-duty sexual assault allegations now under their purview because they have dedicated sexual assault units.

Gregory Brown, an adjunct research professor at Carleton University whose work focuses on criminal justice, says police agencies are better equipped than SIU investigators to investigate off-duty sexual assault allegations. (Submitted by Gregory Brown)

"If we want the truth, we need the best possible investigation … which is in the best interest of an alleged victim and alleged accused person," he told CBC News.

As of May 2025, 70 per cent of SIU employees are ex-police, including forensic investigators.

Clayton Campbell, the president of the Toronto Police Association, told CBC News in an email that removing off-duty conduct allegations from the SIU's responsibility have not reduced the level of oversight.

"In fact, we would argue, the changes have drawn clearer lines of responsibility, making the pathway to accountability more precise," Campbell wrote.

World.title: Rebalancing or retreat? Canada's peacekeeping legacy fades away
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Department of National Defence calls it "rebalancing" but others believe we are witnessing the death of Canada's contribution to peacekeeping with the winding down of a series of long-standing overseas missions.

The country has — for years — contributed only a handful of soldiers to United Nations-sanctioned missions around the world. But in mid-July, late on a Friday, the department quietly announced it was closing four missions and reducing its commitment to a fifth non-UN force in Egypt.

Up to 60 military members were assigned to the peacekeeping forces, a sharp drop from 1993 when almost 4,000 Canadians served with various UN forces, most of them at the time in the former Yugoslavia.

The department said the closing of operations KOBOLD (Kosovo), SNOWGOOSE (Cyprus), SOPRANO (South Sudan) and CROCODILE (Democratic Republic of Congo) and the reduction to Operation CALUMET (Sinai) will take place over the next two years.

The decision was made to "better align CAF resources with current defence priorities," which include the NATO deterrence mission in Latvia and possible future missions in the Indo-Pacific region, the department said in a statement.

"This approach focuses personnel and capabilities where they have the greatest impact, while sustaining commitments, maintaining readiness for emerging challenges and enhancing operational effectiveness with allies and partners."

In the case of the deployment to Cyprus, Canadian troops first set foot on the Mediterranean island in March 1964 and military expert Walter Dorn said closing down the mission is the end of an era.

WATCH | Canada ramping up defence spending: Canadians 'expect us to be sensible' around ramped up defence spending, Carney says | Duration 2:55 Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canadians 'expect us to be sensible' around increased defence spending. Carney said what matters is what Canada is spending the money on, pointing to a pay increase for military members.

"This looks like the death of Canada's contribution because it's very hard to revive once you've closed out a mission," Dorn said, suggesting that an important part of modern Canadian heritage was being allowed to wither and die.

"Peacekeeping is part of the Canadian identity. It is something that we are uniquely qualified to do as opposed to the United States. It's a major role for middle powers in the world where the great powers are having their competition.

"The role for peacekeepers is really a great one for middle powers because they can be more impartial. They don't have the colonial baggage."

Military says troops will be ready and relevant

In his now famous speech to the World Economic Forum last January, Prime Minister Mark Carney urged middle powers to co-operate more closely in a globe that is being divided by great powers.

Dorn said peacekeeping was a perfect vehicle to help implement Carney's vision because international values are being backed up by "boots on the ground."

Peggy Mason, president of the Ottawa-based Rideau Institute, said the decision is a major mistake.

"This is very bad news indeed and shockingly tone deaf when it comes to the increasingly empty Davos promise of Canadian leadership when it matters," said Mason, who served as Canada's ambassador for disarmament from 1989 to 1995.

An old UN helmet is seen during a commemoration for the 60th anniversary of Canada's contribution to the UN peacekeeping force in Cyprus in 2024. (Petros Karadjias/The Associated Press)

When the decision was announced, the country's top military commander said Canadian troops made lasting contributions to peace and stability through peacekeeping missions over many years. Gen. Jennie Carignan, the chief of the defence staff, said rebalancing the missions is meant to keep the force "ready, relevant and positioned to meet current and future operational demands.”

But Dorn said he doesn't buy the notion that the Canadian military can't spare the troops in a time when recruiting has turned a corner and the Defence Department is receiving billions of dollars in new funding.

Canada was one of the world's most active contributors to UN peace operations down the decades. In total, more than 125,000 members of the Canadian military served in dozens of peacekeeping and peace support missions, alongside more than 4,000 Canadian police officers, diplomats and civilians. Roughly 130 Canadian peacekeepers have been killed on various missions.

Troop contributions have been dwindling for almost two decades and Dorn argues that much of Canada's hard-won influence in the developing world is now being ceded to Beijing.

"China wants to have a major role in peacekeeping. It's contributing in a major way whereas the United States is not," Dorn said.

"If we, as Western countries, as the Canadian nation, decide to withdraw from peacekeeping — as we currently decided to do — then we're ceding more rights and more territory for China to take over leadership."

Many in the Canadian military are deeply skeptical, even openly hostile, to the peacekeeping legacy, mostly because of the deep frustration related to UN restrictions and bureaucracy that contributed to civilian deaths, including the 1994 Rwandan genocide.

Over the years peacekeeping has evolved from traditional Cold War ceasefire monitoring to more dangerous "peace support" operations in failed states, where peacekeepers often found themselves amid active combat and ethnic violence.

Even still, well into the early 2000s, the mythology over Canadian peacekeeping operations persisted. At the height of the Afghan war, Defence Department public opinion surveys consistently showed a desire for the country to return to its "traditional role" of peacekeeping.

World.title: Perez Hilton livestreamed apparent self-harm. How did TikTok let this happen?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Warning: This article contains details about self-harm, suicide and violence.

Celebrity gossip blogger Perez Hilton was hospitalized Tuesday night after livestreaming a disturbing TikTok video that appeared to show him engaging in self-harm.

TikTok has since taken down the video, but not before viewers watched the blood-covered blogger holding a knife while in what seemed to be mental distress. Some participating in the livestream yelled at him to stop, while others said to call 911.

As the video circulated, social media feeds were flooded with people shocked by what they had just seen, calling it "horrific" and saying they were "terrified." Clips from the video, which CBC News has viewed, were visible on other social media platforms such as X.

"I genuinely can't even believe what I just saw," one person posted on TikTok on Tuesday night.

"How or why TikTok allowed that livestream to go on for so long is still baffling to me," someone else posted.

"I was in the livestream and am traumatized," another viewer commented.

TikTok's policies clearly forbid content showing suicide or self-harm, and its automated content moderation system, which includes AI, is meant to prevent videos like Hilton's from ever being posted.

In its most recent transparency report, TikTok said it suspended 50.7 million live sessions between January and March this year alone for violating its rules. This year, it also removed 99.8 per cent of videos violating its mental health community guidelines before anyone ever saw them, a company spokesperson told CBC News.

So how did Hilton's livestream continue for what TikTok confirmed was about 15 minutes?

"If I was TikTok, I would definitely be revisiting how they could have sped up this process ... because what you want to see is much quicker intervention," Emily Laidlaw, the Canada Research Chair in Cybersecurity Law and an associate professor at the University of Calgary's law faculty, told CBC News.

The TikTok spokesperson added that its automated moderation systems flagged the livestream within minutes and routed it to its U.S. human moderation team for review.

TikTok said it c losed several subsequent streams within 90 seconds and banned the account.

Members of the media crowd around the home where Hilton was found after he appeared to harm himself during a TikTok livestream, in Westchester, Fla., on Wednesday (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

No solution will ever be perfect

Tuesday's TikTok livestream is far from the first time disturbing, even horrific, events have been broadcast live on social media.

There was the 2019 massacre at two mosques in New Zealand that was livestreamed on Facebook for about 17 minutes, for example. Fifty people were killed. And in 2022, a gunman livestreamed his racially motivated shooting at a grocery store in Buffalo, N.Y., on Twitch. He killed 10 people.

And so many people have broadcast their own suicides on social media that there's a term for it: livestream suicide.

Trying to address problems when they happen on a livestream is incredibly difficult, both in terms of detecting it and acting quickly, Laidlaw said. But since the social media platforms designed the spaces, they have to take responsibility for putting safety measures in place, she said.

Many social media companies have different safeguards, she said. TikTok, for example, uses different AI detection tools that might look for certain behavioural indicators (like changes in affect), language (like explicit statements of finality) and visual (such as blood or weapons).

It also relies on people to report what they see, Laidlaw added.

WATCH | TikTok allowed to continue operations in Canada: TikTok allowed to continue operations in Canada under new rules | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 5:23 The social platform is allowed to continue operating in Canada after agreeing to new security measures for users. Canadian TikTok content creator Justin Veneema shares how the federal government's decision affects his digital business.

"There's no way the solution is ever going to be perfect," she said. "You need to proactively think through what those measures are going to be, but things are always going to be slipping through the cracks."

As for Hilton's apparent self-harm, artificial intelligence can "absolutely" help detect this type of content, but it isn't foolproof and is very unlikely to ever be a complete solution, said Peter Lewis, the Canada Research Chair in Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence and an associate professor of computer science at Ontario Tech University in Oshawa, Ont.

"What is needed are robust and well-resourced processes at the platform level, so that action can be taken swiftly when such content is detected or flagged," Lewis said in an interview.

TikTok said it proactively alerted law enforcement to the situation with Hilton.

Miami-Dade sheriff’s deputies are shown at Hilton's home on Wednesday. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

'I made a lot of mistakes'

Police in Miami responded on Tuesday after receiving " multiple calls regarding an individual who was livestreaming acts of self-harm on social media," the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office confirmed in a statement to CBC News.

"Deputies quickly located the individual’s residence, where they spoke with family members on scene and confirmed he was alone inside," the sheriff's office said.

Hilton was safely recovered and transported to a local hospital, where he's receiving medical attention.

His agents, Dante Rusciolelli and Rebekah Kochan, shared a statement on Instagram asking for his privacy to be respected.

"Our primary concern is Perez's health and well being, as well as the well being of his family. Until we have confirmed information, we will not speculate or comment further."

Born Mario Lavandeira Jr., Hilton, 48, began his popular celebrity gossip blog in the early 2000s, which he called "Hollywood's most-hated website." He often calls himself "the original influencer."

Hilton became notorious for his unfiltered, controversial posts, as well as for several high-profile celebrity feuds. But in recent years, he has expressed remorse and apologized for his "selfish behaviour" after a medical scare earlier this year.

"I made a lot of mistakes in my past. We all have. Nobody's perfect," Hilton said in a video posted April 2.

"But my mistakes are very public. The internet is forever. Receipts are forever. I carry with me deep shame and regret. I'm sorry, I will continue to apologize. I have also reached out to make amends. I have apologized publicly and privately to dozens of people."

World.title: Britain's 'exceptionally serious' drought tests a country famous for its rain
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Standing in a field on his southern England farm, James Baird pointed to the ground where the earth had split into deep fissures.

"You'd lose your arm down some of these cracks," Baird, a "nature friendly" crop farmer in West Sussex, said Tuesday.

Baird, 56, has farmed for four decades, but he said he's never seen a summer like this one. His cereal harvest finished weeks earlier than usual. Crop yields at his farm, Stroodelande, are down 25 per cent.

"Most people would think, 'Oh, well, the U.K. is such a rainy place' … we're kind of famous for it."

But in the past five years, the country has seen successive droughts, making it "difficult to deny patterns are emerging," Baird said. "This is by far the the driest summer that I've farmed in."

What is normally, by early August, a country defined by its lush countryside and patchwork of emerald fields has become parched after successive heat waves and weeks without rain.

A drone view shows All Saints’ Church surrounded by parched grassland at Blackheath Common in London, England, on Aug. 1, after Britain’s Environment Agency declared seven areas of England to be in drought. (Toby Melville/Reuters)

Half of England and all of Wales are officially in drought after what the United Kingdom's Environment Agency described last week as an "exceptionally serious" dry spell. In July, England received just seven per cent of its average rainfall for the month. Southern England received one per cent, with just 0.7 millimetres of rainfall.

Britain is famous for drizzle, with its moody climate and an average of 135 precipitation days a year long considered a defining trait.

"We're known as a temperate climate," said David Christensen, a dairy farmer in Oxford.

"England's green and pleasant land," he added, repeating a well-known lyric from Hubert Parry's hymn Jerusalem. "But we may have to change our techniques."

This year's drought has not only called into question English ways of life, but has also renewed concerns over Britain's long-term water security.

The Environment Agency and water companies have estimated that by 2050 England faces a water supply shortfall of five billion litres a day . It has also prompted fears over possible food shortages the National Farmers' Union has warned could be on the horizon.

The prolonged heat has scorched crops, shrunk rivers and canals and fuelled wildfires. More than 20 million people (roughly a quarter of the population of England and Wales) are under hosepipe bans — where water companies impose restrictions on the use of garden hoses, sprinklers and other similar watering devices with steep fines if broken.

WATCH | James Baird shows the effects of drought on his farm: ‘A very, very bad start’: U.K. farmers facing historic drought | Duration 2:15 It’s been the driest summer James Baird has experienced in his nearly 40-year career as a farmer. He’s one of many farmers across the U.K. who are struggling to break even following severe drought conditions during what has been the hottest July on record for the country. For some, crop yields are down by a quarter and it's forcing those in agriculture to either get creative or get out of the business.

The drought has also brought another danger for farmers.

On July 19, Eleanor Gilbert was harvesting grain with her stepfather at Rookery Farm in Hampshire when she spotted flames in a neighbouring field.

The pair grabbed fire extinguishers and raced toward the fire. When that wasn't enough, they climbed back into the combine and began cutting around the flames to create a firebreak before firefighters arrived.

"It's almost becoming a new normal with this dry weather," Gilbert said of fires threatening farmland.

A fire broke out July 19 in a field on Rookery Farms, where Eleanor Gilbert works with her stepfather in Newbury, west of London, England. (Submitted by Eleanor Gilbert via BerkshireFarmGirl/Instagram)

Across England and Wales, firefighters responded to nearly 400 wildfires in July, making it the busiest month on record, according to the National Fire Chiefs Council.

"We've had this triple whammy," said Claire Barnes, an extreme weather researcher at Imperial College London and a member of World Weather Attribution.

Extreme heat has dried vegetation across much of Western Europe, she said, creating ideal conditions for wildfire.

"There's a really clear causal chain going from heat to drying to flammability," Barnes said. "Then it only takes a spark."

Gilbert, 24, said the increasingly difficult seasons are making her question her future in farming.

"I absolutely love it. It's my favourite thing ever."

But rising costs and the stress she sees her stepfather go through have made her question how she'll pay off her 80,000-pound ($150,000 Cdn) student debt, said Gilbert, who also runs a pumpkin patch and posts about life on the farm online as Berkshire Farm Girl .

"I do need to think carefully about what's coming."

Adapting crops and animals

Many, including Gilbert and her stepfather, and Baird, are trying to adapt by adding organic matter to their soils so they retain more moisture.

Christensen, of Kingston Hill Farm in Oxford, said he is shifting from planting maize to wheat, which doesn't grow as quickly but is more hardy.

"What we're doing at the moment is replacing efficiency with resilience."

Christensen said his cows are producing less milk this year, too, because of the stress of the heat and lack of grass to graze.

David Christensen's cows at Kingston Hill Farm in Oxford, England, have been feeling the heat. (Submitted by David Christensen)

The wetter winters are also taking a toll on them. Last winter, they were hit by a strain of pneumonia, which Christensen said was "a first for us in 58 years." He is introducing vaccines for bluetongue and pneumonia, previously unseen diseases for his farm's herd.

Water companies, which oversee Britain's water management, plan to build 10 reservoirs in England, but the first are not expected to come online until the early 2030s.

At the same time, critics have questioned government proposals for dozens of new data centres, which require significant amounts of water for cooling.

"It's baffling when you're being told to save water, save water, but then the government are putting through all of these data centres that are going to use so much water," said Charlotte Bownass, who lives on a wide-beam houseboat on London's canals with her partner and their seven-month-old baby.

Low water levels in canals and rivers

The drought is reshaping more than Britain's farms, with low water levels forcing closures in some parts of the country's vast, 200-year-old network of inland waterways many now call home.

Charlotte Bownass, right, a scenic painter, and her partner, Mike, left, are seen on their wide-beam houseboat near London. (Submitted by Charlotte Bownass)

Bownass said her family chose to live on the boat for its affordability and tranquility, but she worries what wetter winters, which have caused canal breaches, and dryer summers will mean for that lifestyle. Their boat has already been stuck a few times.

"It's just quite scary, these two extremes," she said.

Outside London, many people holiday on the narrowboats that navigate canals and rivers that were used to transport coal before railroads.

For Nici Griffin and her partner, Sharon Bull, who are cheesemongers travelling between markets on their narrowboat, the Three Sheep Cheese Boat, a journey north from Linsdale to Birmingham this week was complicated by several canal and lock closures.

Narrowboat cheesemonger Nici Griffin spotted a cow amid low water levels near Lapworth on the Stratford-upon-Avon canal headed towards Birmingham on Tuesday. (Submitted by Nici Griffin)

"We're having to take a completely different route than we would have done," Griffin said after a long navigation day Tuesday, when the couple had came across an unusual sighting: a cow drinking from the low water.

But Griffin, in true British fashion, said she's not too fussed about the changing conditions.

"We're boaters, so we just get on with it."

World.title: Israel confirms death of 2 soldiers, striking back in Lebanon
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Israeli military said Thursday that two of its soldiers were killed in an explosion in southern Lebanon in the first Israeli deaths since the implementation of a shaky truce with the Iran-backed Lebanese militant group Hezbollah in June.

Four other soldiers were seriously wounded, the military said. The deaths in the village of Majdal Zoun had been reported by Israeli media a day earlier.

The Israeli army launched strikes Wednesday in southern Lebanon in response to what it described as Hezbollah's violation of the ceasefire and issued a call for residents of the village of Mansouri to flee — the first such warning Israel has issued in Lebanon for weeks.

Lebanon's Health Ministry said one person was killed and 12 wounded in an Israeli strike in the town of Tebnine Wednesday and another eight wounded in overnight strikes on the village of Burj al-Shemali. Artillery shelling also targeted the areas of Mansouri and Majdal Zoun, the state-run National News Agency said.

There was no immediate statement from the Iran-backed Hezbollah.

The escalation came as Lebanese and Israeli negotiators met in Rome to discuss implementation of a June 26 deal under which Israeli forces are supposed to withdraw from areas they occupy in southern Lebanon and allow the Lebanese army to take control, in exchange for Hezbollah's disarmament.

A Lebanese man removes debris from his destroyed house in the village of Zawtar al-Gharbieh, south Lebanon on Wednesday. (Mohammed Zaatari/The Associated Press)

The talks on Wednesday ended early due to the escalation on the ground. The talks were set to resume Thursday.

Lebanon's Health Ministry said one person was killed and 12 wounded in an Israeli strike in the town of Tebnine Wednesday. The state-run National News Agency reported more people wounded in overnight strikes on the village of Burj al-Shemali, but the number was not clear. Artillery shelling also targeted the areas of Mansouri and Majdal Zoun, it said.

Hezbollah not participating in talks

The latest Israel-Hezbollah war erupted on March 2, when Hezbollah fired rockets across the border two days after the U.S. and Israel launched their attacks on Iran. More than 4,000 people have been killed by Israeli strikes in Lebanon since then, including hundreds of civilians.

About 40 soldiers and three civilians — including a military contractor — have been killed on the Israeli side.

A shaky truce between Israel and Hezbollah has largely held since June 20, but Israeli forces have continued to occupy swaths of southern Lebanon and to carry out periodic airstrikes and shelling.

The talks in Rome have focused on implementation of "pilot zones" where Israeli forces would withdraw and the Lebanese army would take control. Implementation began last month with an initial pilot zone in an area that wasn't occupied by Israeli forces but had previously sustained Israeli fire.

The Lebanese army entered the town of Zawtar al-Gharbieh and some civilians returned, although many came only to find their homes destroyed and left again.

Michel Issa, U.S. ambassador to Lebanon, suggested ahead of the three-day talks that no new pilot zones would be immediately implemented, saying that "moving too quickly risks jeopardizing the very civilians this process is meant to protect."

Hezbollah was opposed to the direct Lebanon-Israel talks and was not a party to the deal. The group has accused the Lebanese government of making too many concessions without guaranteeing an Israeli withdrawal.

World.title: Colby Cosh: Democrats’ attempt to limit the presidential pardon power is futile
World.content:
Article content

Again, the basic situation is no different in constitutional monarchies like ours. (Not assigning a pardon power to anyone in particular is an option for a state, but this would make the actions of judges un-revisable by any earthly authority — which, honestly, may be the system of government toward which Canada is speeding.) The founders understood perfectly well that a president might make unscrupulous or self-interested use of the power, especially on the way out of the office; they just expected that republican virtue, along with the popularly elected legislature’s power to impeach, would protect the state from disgusting and obvious excesses at the top. And if it came to that, the American people would retain the power to amend the constitution as it thought necessary — although, again, any solution to the problem must leave the final decision-making power to somebody or other.

World.title: Colombia investigating governors, mayors over $941M corruption racket
World.content:
Prosecutors arrested 13 suspects and asked Colombia’s Supreme Court to investigate seven (former) governors over their alleged involvement in the embezzlement of COP3 trillion ($941 million).

The arrests and the investigation requests are related to the public-private partnership Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund, which was created by Martin Zuleta (U Party) and his family when he was mayor of La Paz, Cesar, in early 2021.

While supposedly serving the interests of La Paz, the Sierra Nevada Mixed Fund allegedly used forged documents to illegally appropriate funds from the General Royalties System with the help of governors from at least five provinces.

“So far, we’ve tracked 3 trillion pesos, of which it has been established that some were misappropriated through irregular contracts,” anti-corruption prosecutor Madeleyne Perez said at a press conference.

Among those whose cases were forwarded to the Supreme Court were the governors of Magdalena, Vichada, Amazonas Guaviare an Vaupes.

Former Governors Rafael Martinez of Magdalena and Alvaro Leon of Vichada will also be investigated by the Supreme Court.

Among those who were arrested is the mayor of Maria la Baja, a contractor and multiple (former) directors of the mixed fund.

The non-profit has been investigated since 2024 when authorities found irregularities in the construction of a high school in the Huila province, funds for school transport in Casanare and funds meant for indigenous reserves in La Guajira.

A report by the now-defunct radio station W from that year showed that Sierra Nevada had been hired by authorities from throughout Colombia for a wide variety of projects, avoiding any open bidding procedure.

W found more than 100 contracts between mainly local and regional government authorities and the non-profit.

According to Caracol, Zuleta was taken to hospital after his home was raided by prosecution officials and would be available to cooperate with the prosecutors investigating his alleged involvement in corruption.

World.title: Colombia’s left presents evidence suggesting De la Espriella won through fraud
World.content:
Colombia’s President Gustavo Petro and data analysts presented evidence suggesting that President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella won the election through the mass manipulation of tally sheets.

During a two-hour presentation, Petro claimed that almost all tally sheets that had been shared with his political party, the Historic Pact “lacked the Hash security lock,” which is inserted into official PDF documents to guarantee they can’t be changed.

The absence of a hash file implies that the so-called E14 tally sheets may have been altered, which appears to have happened, according to data analysts who accompanied the president.

Legal expert William Villanueva said that original tally sheets were scanned and subsequently reprocessed, removing the metadata that would allow them to determine whether the E14’s were uploaded or introduced digitally.

“We found documents marked ‘confidential’… and others that said ‘not digitized’ on a blank page, which—and this is important—were later republished with different information,” said one of the computer scientists.

The investigation, which was carried out by 75,000 “digital witnesses,” found that 95 municipalities had more voters than inhabitants. In all of these municipalities, the E-14’s gave De la Espriella landslide victories with more than 70% of the votes.

The president-elect’s opponent, leftist Senator Ivan Cepeda, achieved not a single victory in hundreds of towns where the electoral census was larger than 85% of the population.

In 1,350 polling centers in capital cities, the researchers found that block patterns in which De la Espriella won the first half of the voting booths and Cepeda won the second half.

According to a consulted statistician, this result would only be probably in some 80 polling stations, said Carlos Oñoro, one of the digital witnesses.

“This order is mathematically impossible for human voters,” Petro stated, arguing that automated software replaced actual citizen ballots.

The findings of the digital witnesses will be added to a lawsuit that seeks to nullify the election of De la Espriella and force the Council of State to order a recount of the votes.

Following the presentation, Cepeda said in a post on social media network X that “the competent authority must impartially examine our demands of nullity.”

World.title: De la Espriella says he won’t allow Colombia’s left to “destabilize democracy”
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella said that he won’t allow his country’s left to “destabilize democracy” through civil disobedience against his US citizenship.

In his weekly address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that after Friday he will be president and “with the force of the constitution and the law” ensure that his power will be upheld.

The civil disobedience announced by leftist opposition leader Ivan Cepeda “is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy,” said De la Espriella.

“I will not allow it,” said the president-elect.

I am the president of all Colombians, and I will ensure, through the power of the Constitution and the law, that what the Colombian people decided—which was to elect me—is upheld. My call to the entire nation is that we stop normalizing what is wrong, illegal, and corrupt. Let’s call things by their proper names and confront them for what they are. This so-called “civil disobedience” is nothing more than a euphemism for an attempt to destabilize democracy, and I will not allow it. Abelardo de la Espriella

According to De la Espriella, the left “combined all forms of struggle,” a term used by the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC to justify the violence used by the insurgents, “and lost.”

Cepeda called on his followers to peaceful civil disobedience in response to the president-elect’s refusal to renounce his US citizenship.

The incoming opposition leader and his political party, the Historic Pact, support legal efforts to challenge De la Espriella’s election on claims that fraud concerns have not been tackled.

More radical elements within the Historic Pact, including outgoing President Gustavo Petro, have sustained that the far-right won the elections through deceit and fraud, but have failed to present evidence that would confirm a criminal conspiracy.

World.title: As De la Espriella takes office, his US-backed security policy for Colombia is raising questions
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella assumes office on Friday, after elections with a razor-thin margin. He brings with him promises to wield “iron fist” policies against non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and organized criminal organizations in the country.

He has also promised to dismantle ongoing peace talks initiated by outgoing leftist President Gustavo Petro, including groups that are currently disarming. De la Espriella made scores of hardline promises on the campaign trail, many of which he will likely not be able to achieve with a minority coalition in the legislature, such as withdrawing Colombia from the United Nations.

On security issues, however, Colombia’s constitution grants the president broad unilateral powers. De la Espriella has promised to “end” armed groups within a month, an extremely unlikely goal. Despite the broad powers of the presidential office, De la Espriella faces historical and logistical limitations.

Despite claims from right-wing parties that Petro has gone easy on armed groups, Colombia’s military has been fully deployed against NSAGs in the country for the last two years.

As conflict expert Thomas Garrison reported for news website Pirate Wire Services in June, Colombia has ongoing and large military operations against FARC dissident group Estado Mayor Central (EMC), the National Liberation Army (ELN), and EMC splinter-group EMBF.

Colombia’s security forces are “already operating on all cylinders,” and “stretched to their limit,” according to the International Crisis Group. It isn’t clear how deployments can be increased without increasing the numbers of security forces themselves — hardly a goal that can be achieved in his first month in office.

Nonetheless, there are strategic changes that de La Espriella can impose to chart a more aggressive course. As part of those plans, the president-elect has promised to implement a “Plan Patriota remixed”, an allusion to highly aggressive US-backed military operations against armed groups under then-President Alvaro Uribe in 2003.

Uribe’s allies to this day hail Plan Patriota as a great success that forced the FARC to the negotiating table in 2016.

Critics, however, point to rampant human and civil rights violations, including working with paramilitary forces to kill thousands of civilians and frame them as guerrilla fighters to increase casualty counts.

The US, however, is pushing Latin America towards increased military spending and Bukele-style crackdowns on organized crime, and de la Espriella plans to comply.

What was Plan Patriota and how will Abelardo’s version be ‘remixed’?

Plan Patriota involved aerial bombardments, large-scale military deployments in FARC-controlled areas, and aggressive intelligence gathering against FARC guerrillas at the height of Colombia’s civil war.

Although paramilitary groups were not officially part of Plan Patriota, they cooperated closely with regular military forces during the operation, functioning as spies, informants, and death squads — ostensibly killing alleged guerrillas, but just as often murdering leftists in general, as well as non-politically involved civilians.

The operation, which continued until 2010, weakened the FARC considerably, but at a great price: gross human rights violations including massacres, torture, and using sexual violence against civilians as a weapon of war.

Paramilitary structures were also greatly empowered across the country, sowing the seeds of groups that still exist today, such as the Ejercito Gaitanista Colombiano (EGC) — often referred to in Western media as ‘the Clan del Golfo.’

The full extent of the atrocities committed by both sides of the war would not become clear until Colombia launched its Truth Commission in 2017. (De la Espriella wants to disband the Truth Commission as well as the Colombian Peace Court, which prosecutes the worst offenders of the civil war.)

Any new version of Plan Patriota would look very different. Colombia is not the same country it was in the early 2000’s. Modern armed groups are not interested in clashing with state forces on the battlefield. Most are not interested in overthrowing the state at all, and certainly not via military victory.

Technology has also advanced considerably. Drone warfare is a dangerous new weapon in the arsenal of NSAGs who wage asymmetrical attacks on state forces as well as one another. Digital surveillance and satellite optics also mean that unlike the FARC, which often relied upon jungle canopies to hide large training and logistics camps, modern NSAGs instead blend into civil society in the communities where they operate.
