03

What to See & Do

THURSDAY IN RIO

TODAY’S PICK — ART & ARCHITECTURE A Two-Stop Cultural Pilgrimage in Centro In a city shaped by its coastline, Centro’s dense cultural cluster offers a rare, walkable concentration of world-class museums. Start at the Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil (CCBB) on Rua Primeiro de Março, a stunning neoclassical rotunda now hosting rotating contemporary exhibitions. Entry is completely free, and the air-conditioned galleries offer a cool refuge between 9 am and 8 pm. A five-minute walk away, the Museu Nacional de Belas Artes on Avenida Rio Branco is in a partial reopening phase. The ground-floor galleries are accessible, showcasing 19th-century Brazilian masters and travelling exhibitions, with free admission during this period. Note the reduced collection due to ongoing renovations upstairs. Both sit near Cinelândia metro station (Lines 1/2). The single journey fare is R$7.90. You can seamlessly weave between the two spaces and still have time for a proper lunch nearby. For the best European-style coffee in the district, walk three blocks to Confeitaria Colombo on Rua Gonçalves Dias. The belle-époque mirrored salon is unmissable. Expect to pay around R$35 for a pastel de nata and an espresso at the counter, or a bit more if you sit down for the full afternoon tea service.

OUTDOORS — A POSTCARD VIEW The Easy Urban Hike to Parque Lage With zero rain forecast and perfect visibility, the Jardim Botânico neighbourhood calls. Parque Lage opens its gates at 8 am for free, offering the city’s most direct portal to the base of Corcovado. The mansion courtyard is the draw — an Italianate palace with a pool reflecting the Christ statue above. It is a zero-effort, high-reward photo opportunity. Combine it with the Botanical Garden next door (R$40 for residents, R$80 for foreigners), which is also open today.

COFFEE & WHERE TO WORK — CENTRO & LAPA Reliable WiFi in the Historic Core If you need to set up a laptop, skip the hotel lobby and head to Curto Café on Rua da Candelária. It specialises in single-origin Brazilian beans, has fast WiFi, and buzzes with a remote-worker crowd until 7 pm on weekdays. A quieter choice two blocks back from the VLT tracks is Café Secreto on Rua do Ouvidor. Tucked in a gallery courtyard, it’s ideal for deep work before the after-school rush hits around 4 pm.

THE CONTRASTING PLAY — A WATERSIDE WANDER A Beach-Bar Afternoon in Urca If museums feel too enclosed, let the geography do the work. Take an Uber to the Urca neighbourhood and walk the 2.2km clockwise loop around Morro da Urca. Stop at Bar Urca on the seawall for a late lunch. Sit on the low wall with a cold chopp and a plate of their famous empada de camarão, watching paddleboarders drift across Guanabara Bay. The sea breeze is steady and the sunsets here, at 5:34 pm, are quiet and majestic.

TONIGHT, AFTER 7 PM Samba, Tapas and Small Plates Thursday night in Lapa is the weekend’s dress rehearsal. The Arcos da Lapa area fills early with street parties, but for a seated affair, book a table at Bar da Gema, where a choro or samba circle typically kicks off near Rua Mem de Sá. For a more polished dinner in Santa Teresa, Aprazível offers terrace dining with the city lights pooled below. It’s a splurge (mains around R$90–R$150), but the roasted palm heart and lush treehouse terrace justify it. If you’re staying in Zona Sul, Botafogo’s Baixo Copa district has small-plate energy tonight. Canastra Bar on Rua Jangadeiros is a reliable bet for great natural wines and grilled sardines with a young, chatty crowd.

ALSO ON TODAY Museu de Arte do Rio (MAR) — Praça Mauá — Thu–Tue 11 am–6 pm; R$20 (free on Tuesdays). Expansive view from the rooftop belvedere. Paço Imperial — Praça XV — Tue–Sun 12 pm–6 pm; free. Historical colonial palace with rotating installations. Real Gabinete Português de Leitura — Rua Luís de Camões — Mon–Fri 10 am–5 pm; free. A breathtaking neo-Manueline reading room. Museu do Amanhã — Praça Mauá — Tue–Sun 10 am–6 pm; R$30 (half R$15). The Santiago Calatrava-designed science museum. Theatro Municipal Guided Tour — Cinelândia — Wed–Sat; R$20. An opulent, Parisian-style opera house interior tour. Centro Cultural dos Correios (closed today) — Check ahead: closed today. Exhibitions here remain suspended indefinitely.

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

All Metrô lines (1, 2, and 4) and the VLT light rail are running normally today. The single-journey fare is R$7.90. The transfer between the Cinelândia and Carioca stations is your best route between the museum cluster and Lapa.

With the clear weather, the seafront Ciclovia from Leme to Barra is fully open for bike rentals via the Itaú bike scheme. If you rely on ride apps, surge pricing typically kicks in near the Centro business district around 6 pm as the office crowd disperses.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Lunch: For a classic downtown lunch, sit at the stand-up balcony of Bar Luiz (Rua da Carioca) for a cold draft beer and a German-style salsichão with potato salad — expect to pay about R$70. For a lighter, airier setting, Beta, a contemporary Brazilian kitchen inside CCBB, serves a thoughtful prix-fixe menu starting around R$65.

Dinner: Make for Puro in Jardim Botânico, where the tasting menu featuring fresh Atlantic fish sits around R$160 a head — book a garden table for the full effect. In Centro, before heading to Lapa, São Braz is a no-fuss, old-school spot for a final chilled lager and a bowl of their famous barreado stew.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Carry a reusable water bottle and sunglasses — UV levels are high even in winter. Cards and Pix are universally accepted in Centro, but keep a small R$20 note for the occasional street-vendor coffee.

Book a table for dinner ahead if you are aiming for Aprazível or Puro; these fill up fast on clear, warm nights. The Museu do Amanhã and MAR stop entry at 5 pm sharp — plan your Praça Mauá route to arrive by 4 pm at the latest.

Safety note: stick to the well-lit main streets of Centro and Lapa after dark. Rua Primeiro de Março and the immediate CCBB plaza are safe, but avoid empty side streets near the Praça XV ferry terminal after 8 pm.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

The weekly Mundo Lingo language exchange is on tonight at Ipanema’s Shenanigan’s from 7 pm — a perfect, informal spot for a new arrival to practise Portuguese over a drink. Check their official Facebook page for this week’s flag-code.

The Digital Nomads Rio WhatsApp group often organises a co-working morning at Curto Café on Fridays; if you’re scoping out tomorrow’s plan, introduce yourself on the thread. Many members also gather for the Saturday morning running club at Lagoa.

08

Game Day

A QUIET MIDWEEK WINDOW

It is a rare clear night on the domestic fixture list. No Campeonato Brasileiro matches are scheduled for this Thursday evening for Rio’s big four clubs.

The Maracanã and São Januário stadiums are silent tonight, but the weekend looms. Flamengo’s next training session is attracting attention ahead of their Sunday away fixture.

For those still needing live sport, the Botafogo de Futebol e Regatas clubhouse in General Severiano is open to members, and the big screens will likely carry international football replays.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

Wall Street closed the last session with divergent momentum — the Dow edged upward while the Nasdaq lost ground, and expected volatility gauges pulled back, as shown on the WEEK IN FIGURES board. The market mood remains one of cautious sector rotation rather than outright risk aversion.

The appetite for added volatility has fallen, leaving portfolios slightly steadier — a tone mirrored by mixed moves in Latin American equity markets. Investors are parsing the tight labour market signals against the need for gradual monetary easing.

Looking ahead, the drop in the US dollar index suggests a cautiously weaker greenback, which could provide near-term relief for emerging-market currencies. Traders are now eyeing the next US weekly jobless claims data for clues on the rate path.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

THE DAYS AHEAD FRI 7 — Sunny, 29°C — perfect for an early morning at Praia Vermelha before the Paço Imperial at noon. SAT 8 — Hot and clear, 30°C — secure a chair early at Posto 9, then explore the Feira Hippie de Ipanema. SUN 9 — Light cloud, 27°C — watch for football fixtures; a bike ride around Lagoa Rodrigo de Freitas is top choice. MON 10 — Warm, dry start to the week — the Real Gabinete Português de Leitura is open and serenely quiet. TUE 11 — Free Tuesday at MAR (R$0) — a budget-friendly art fix in Praça Mauá.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

What is the best way to get from Zona Sul to Centro without getting stuck in traffic?

The Metrô is your fastest friend. Board at any Line 1 station in Copacabana or Ipanema — General Osório is a central hub — and ride directly to Cinelândia station in Centro. The journey takes under 20 minutes and the fare is R$7.90. Avoid the Aterro do Flamengo road route by car between 8 am and 10 am, as the inbound lanes clog severely. The VLT is also a smooth option for the final leg once you are above ground in Centro.

Are there any major closures or exhibitions I should know about today?

Yes. The Centro Cultural dos Correios (closed today; currently closed) is closed indefinitely — so skip it for today. The Museu Nacional de Belas Artes is only partially open, meaning you can see the ground level but not the upper-floor permanent collections. On the plus side, CCBB is free and fully open. There is no temporary exhibition in its final weekend — just the larger, long-run programme.

How much cash should I carry, or can I pay with cards everywhere today?

You can survive entirely on cards and contactless Pix today. Virtually every venue recommended — CCBB, Belas Artes, Confeitaria Colombo, and all dinner spots — accepts debit and credit cards. Keep a single R$20 note in your pocket. It will cover any coconut water from a beach vendor or an impromptu pasteis de feira from a street cart that might not have a modern POS machine.

01 The session in one read

Colombia’s stock market fell squarely into the red on Wednesday, with the COLCAP index losing 1.26% to settle at 2,344.80. The drop was anchored by anxiety around crude oil, the country’s most important export and a barometer for the national oil company Ecopetrol, whose weight in the index makes it the tape’s main engine.

The peso told a different story, strengthening 1.07% against the dollar to close at 3,207 pesos per greenback. In a typical session for a commodity exporter, a firming currency and falling stocks can seem contradictory, but Wednesday’s split points to a local equity market spooked by energy prices rather than a broad vote of foreign-investor confidence.

Trade was extremely concentrated. Only two names generated meaningful turnover: Novo-B, which slumped 4.3% on $1m in volume, and DSV, which fell 1.5% on the same $1m. No major stock eked out a gain among the session’s most-traded, painting a cleanly negative picture.

Behind the moves sits an economy still tightly bound to oil. With global crude prices under pressure, Ecopetrol’s earnings outlook dims, and the broader index—packed with banks and insurers sensitive to the same macro health—follows it lower.

Assessment — Oil drag overrides currency relief MEDIUM The session’s dynamic—a sliding equity index beside a rising peso—is unusual for a commodity-exporting market and suggests the equity sell-off was driven more by commodity-price anxiety and local positioning than by a broad flight from Colombian assets. The complete absence of a single advancing stock among the most-traded names reinforces that Wednesday was decisively risk-off for equities. The critical variable to watch next is whether crude prices stabilise, which would be the quickest path to steadying the COLCAP and any rebound in Ecopetrol’s shares.

This currency strength meant that for a foreign investor converting returns back into dollars, the local-currency equity loss was partially cushioned. Still, the day’s equity price action was decisively negative, and no counter-trend buying emerged in the main large-cap names.

03 Why it moved — crude oil anchors the gloom

The session’s downward tilt began with oil. Colombia’s public finances and its current-account balance rise and fall with crude prices, and Ecopetrol—the state-controlled oil giant—is by far the heaviest single stock in the COLCAP. When oil softens, the market tends to reprice not just Ecopetrol but also the banks and utilities that depend on a healthy, oil-fuelled domestic economy.

Wednesday offered a textbook case of that transmission. With global crude prices under pressure, investors marked down Ecopetrol, and the selling bled into Bancolombia, Grupo Sura and other financial names. The currency’s simultaneous rally likely reflected positioning or offshore flows into Colombian fixed income, but it wasn’t enough to lift equities.

Latin America’s broader interest-rate landscape added a layer of caution. Central banks across the region, including Brazil’s, have been cutting rates only gradually because inflation remains sticky—and oil is a big reason why. That backdrop keeps pressure on rate-sensitive sectors and makes it harder for local stocks to mount a sustained rally, even when the peso firms up.

Wednesday’s volume was strikingly thin. Novo-B fell the most among verified movers, losing 4.3%, while DSV dropped 1.5%—and together they accounted for the session’s most meaningful trading activity, each with just $1m in turnover. No stock on the most-active list posted a gain.

Ecopetrol, Bancolombia, ISA, Grupo Sura and GEB—the traditional heavyweights—all felt the downward pull, even if exact percentage moves aren’t available from the public tape. The one-way traffic and threadbare volumes suggest that neither local institutions nor foreign desks had conviction to buy the dip.

Colombia’s 1.26% decline was the steepest drop among the region’s main benchmarks on Wednesday, though the Merval in Argentina came close with a 1.02% fall. Brazil’s Ibovespa slipped a marginal 0.09%, while Mexico’s IPC lost 0.48%, showing that the cautious mood was broadly shared.

Chile’s IPSA bucked the trend with a strong 1.47% gain, and Peru’s BVL rose 0.81%, reminding investors that the region’s commodity-linked markets do not always move in lockstep. Still, Bogotá’s underperformance stood out, underscoring the weight of oil in Colombia’s equity narrative.

06 The technical picture — peso tests the bottom of its range

The Colombian peso’s push to 3,207 per dollar brings the 52-week low of 3,122 into view as the next major support level for the USD/COP pair. A break below that floor would mark the peso’s strongest level in over a year and signal a powerful run of currency appreciation.

For the COLCAP, the technical picture is bleaker. With the index declining to 2,344.80 and volumes fading, it lacks a nearby catalyst to reverse the slide. Traders will be watching whether the index can hold above any psychologically important round number—and whether crude oil can find a floor to stop the energy sector’s bleeding.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the COLCAP?

It is Colombia’s main stock index, tracking the largest and most liquid companies listed on the Bolsa de Valores de Colombia, similar to the S&P 500 in the US or the Ibovespa in Brazil.

Why did the COLCAP fall when the peso strengthened?

The peso likely rallied on foreign inflows into Colombian bonds or currency bets, but stocks sold off because falling oil prices hurt the earnings outlook for Ecopetrol and the broader economy.

What does USD/COP 3,207 mean?

It means one US dollar buys 3,207 Colombian pesos. The rate dropped 1.07%, so the peso became stronger—it takes fewer pesos to buy a dollar than before.

Why is oil so important for Colombian stocks?

Crude oil is Colombia’s biggest export. Ecopetrol, the state oil company, is the heaviest stock in the COLCAP, and oil revenue funds a large slice of the government’s budget.

Today’s Focus Argentina’s stock market took a breather on Wednesday. The S&P Merval index slipped 1.02% to 3,156,332 points, easing back after a powerful rally driven by President Javier Milei’s free-market overhaul. Traders locked in profits on the very banks and energy companies that have come to symbolise the country’s reform trade. The Argentine peso barely budged, with the official USD/ARS rate finishing at 1,496, just a whisper from its 52-week low of 1,500 touched on 28 July. In a market where local investors constantly seek to protect wealth by moving into dollars, the steady currency provided a calm backdrop for an otherwise cautious equity session. Trading screens showed a clear theme: the most-loved names of the recent bull run were the ones getting sold. Energy producer YPF fell 2.0% on a meaty $12 million in volume, while bank Grupo Galicia lost 1.3% with $9 million changing hands. The moves weren’t panic-driven—they looked like methodical profit-taking in a market that had raced ahead of short-term economic reality. When a narrative stock like YPF, Argentina’s state-controlled oil and gas company, falls 2.0% on the heaviest volume of any local name, it suggests institutional investors were trimming positions rather than retail investors bolting for the exits. The $12 million turnover tells you big money was moving, calmly.

Banking stocks softened in sympathy. Grupo Galicia, one of Argentina’s largest private financial conglomerates, lost 1.3%. The logic is straightforward: financial shares are a leveraged bet on the economy, and they had run up sharply on hopes that Milei’s reforms would end the era of capital controls and forced government lending.

Country risk, the extra yield investors demand to hold Argentine debt over US Treasuries, is the invisible hand shaping these moves. Any hint that the reform process is stalling sends this risk gauge higher, and the whole equity market wobbles in response. Wednesday’s measured selling suggests the market is waiting rather than worrying.

01 The session in one read

The S&P IPSA — the benchmark that tracks the 29 most liquid stocks listed on the Santiago Stock Exchange — notched a clean 1.47% gain on Wednesday, closing at 11,158 points. That left the index just 4% below its 52-week peak of 11,628, a threshold traders increasingly treat as the next bullseye.

Liquidity gathered around lithium giant SQM and the country’s two largest retailers, Falabella and Cencosud. SQM-B, the most accessible local listing of the world’s No 2 lithium producer, rose 2.4% with $16 million in turnover, extending a run that has made it one of the IPSA’s most consequential names.

Retail reflected a broader consumer optimism. Falabella, a department-store group with regional reach, added 1.4% on $30 million of volume. Rival Cencosud rose 1.7% on $14 million. Shopping-centre operator Mallplaza outperformed both, gaining 2.6% on $27 million.

The Chilean peso did not share the equity market’s cheer. The dollar bought 913.57 pesos at the session close, a 0.28% increase that nudged the exchange rate a little further from the 851.67 low of the past 52 weeks. Global dollar weakness, visible in the DXY index slipping 0.18%, failed to pull the peso along for the ride.

Assessment — Domestic strength, peso softness MEDIUM The session’s pattern — equities rising while the peso edged lower — suggests local real-money buyers were active in retail and lithium shares, while offshore investors may have trimmed modest peso exposure. With the IPSA at 11,158 it remains 4% shy of its 52-week high of 11,628, leaving clear air if the incoming inflation data prints benignly. The variable to watch is Thursday’s CPI: a reading below the 3.7% estimate could ignite a run at that record ceiling by convincing traders that rate cuts are nearer.

03 Why it moved — lithium optimism meets consumer strength

SQM-B’s 2.4% gain with $16 million in turnover was the session’s most telling datapoint. As one of the world’s largest lithium producers, supplying battery-grade chemicals to the electric-vehicle supply chain, SQM acts as Chile’s proxy for the global energy transition trade. Wednesday’s buying suggests investors see near-term value even as the stock has been volatile alongside lithium spot prices.

The retail bloc — Falabella, Cencosud and Mallplaza — posted gains on heavy volume, a pattern that often signals local institutional conviction. Falabella traded $30 million, the second-heaviest print of the day, while rising 1.4%. Mallplaza, the shopping-centre operator, surged 2.6% on $27 million. Together they paint a picture of a market betting on domestic consumption holding up.

The peso’s 0.28% slip to 913.57 is the puzzle piece that does not quite fit the equity narrative. With the US dollar index down 0.18% and copper — Chile’s export lifeblood — firm in global trade, a stronger peso might have been expected. The mild depreciation suggests that some corporate dollar demand or portfolio outflows created a counterweight to what should have been a supportive external setup.

The move lower was carved out not by a wave of selling across the board, but by painful single-day plunges in a few of the nation’s most widely held consumer and telecom names.

While the index fell, the currency market told a different story. The Mexican peso actually strengthened, pushing the USD/MXN exchange rate — the number of pesos needed to buy one US dollar — down 0.19% to settle at 17.23 pesos, helped by a softer US dollar that retreated against most major currencies.

The sharpest pain was felt by shareholders of Walmart de México (Walmex), the country’s dominant supermarket and discount-store chain, which slumped 3.2%, while billionaire Carlos Slim’s América Móvil, the telecoms colossus, fared even worse with a 3.5% drop.

These deep losses were partially offset by a fierce rally in precious-metals miners, led by a 5.4% surge in Peñoles and a 2.2% gain in Grupo México. The buying was fuelled by a sharp upward move in gold, which jumped 5.03% to $4,277.69 an ounce, and silver, which shot 4.65% higher, as the US Dollar Index slipped 0.18%.

Assessment — Selective selling, not a broad rout HIGH The session’s damage was highly concentrated in specific large-cap consumer and telecom stocks, which fell significantly harder than the broader index, while the peso actually strengthened and global precious metals rallied. This pattern points to a thematic or flow-driven rotation out of select high-weight defensive names rather than a systemic negative shock to the Mexican market. The key variable to monitor tomorrow will be whether Walmex and América Móvil find buyers at these lower levels or whether the selling pressure indicates the start of a broader repositioning.

03 Why it moved — heavyweights hit by a rotation

The driving force behind the index’s decline was a pronounced rotation out of some of its most defensive, consumer-oriented pillars. Walmex’s 3.2% tumble stood out, particularly on notably heavy turnover — the kind of volume that suggests a significant institutional seller was active. Consumer-facing peer Femsa, the operator of OXXO convenience stores and Coca-Cola bottler, dropped 1.8% on even heavier turnover.

The selling in América Móvil, down a steep 3.5%, raised eyebrows given its role as an index heavyweight and its normally bond-like trading pattern. The telco’s move felt connected to a broader reassessment of high-valuation defensive plays as global funds shifted overnight, though no Mexico-specific regulatory trigger was apparent.

On the other side of the ledger, the mining sector acted as a powerful counterweight. Peñoles, a major precious-metals producer, leapt 5.4% while industrial mining giant Grupo México added 2.2%, both feeding off a global rush into gold and silver. Gold’s 5.03% surge above $4,277 per ounce, driven by a falling US dollar, offered an unusually strong tailwind.

The heaviest percentage bleeding among blue chips came from América Móvil and Walmex, which fell 3.5% and 3.2% respectively.

Against that tide, silver and gold miner Peñoles rocketed 5.4% to dominate the gainers’ list, while Grupo México’s 2.2% advance and a 1.8% rise in regional bank BanBajío provided a reminder that pockets of serious strength existed. Financial heavyweight Banorte managed a 0.6% nudge higher, suggesting pessimism had not spread to the banking sector.

01 The session in one read

The Ibovespa, Brazil’s main stock index, ended the day on a flat note, dipping 0.09% to close at 177,726 points. The real, Brazil’s currency, inched ahead by 0.15% to 5.1206 against the US dollar, mirroring a small bout of softness in the greenback globally.

It was a session of fine margins. The index traded in a narrow band, with the weight of a declining Petrobras—the most-traded stock on the B3 exchange—effectively neutralizing modest gains in other pockets of the market.

The day’s action felt more like position-tweaking than a directional bet. Copom’s decision was still hours away when the bell rang, so traders simply refused to commit capital ahead of it.

Assessment — A directionless drift with defensive undertones HIGH The session’s tight trading range and fractional index move point to a market in wait-and-see mode, digesting a recent easing cycle by the central bank but lacking fresh domestic triggers. Gold’s 5.03% leap and silver’s 4.65% jump were the day’s real story, and Brazil felt it through its miners rather than its index. The key variable now is what Copom says next, after cutting the Selic to 14.00% once the B3 bell had already rung.

03 Why it moved — a waiting game without a spark

Nothing seized control of the Brazilian market during trading hours, because the one headline that mattered was still pending. Copom was in its second day of deliberations, and the room simply waited.

Wall Street’s main indices did nothing to help. While the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.49%, the broader S&P 500 slipped 0.17% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 0.83%. This left Brazilian fund managers without a clear lead from overseas.

Locally, everything was on hold for Copom. The committee cut the Selic to 14.00% after the close, a fourth straight quarter-point step that traders could only position for, not react to.

The heavyweight battle defined the scoreboard. Petrobras’s 1.3% drop, on a meaty $264 million in turnover, was the single largest weight pulling the index lower. This came despite a surge in precious metals, which boosted miner Aura Minerals by 13.7%.

The financial sector was divided. Itaú Unibanco managed a solid 0.7% gain as the day’s most influential bank, but that positive impulse was diluted by a 0.8% fall at Bradesco and a flat performance from B3, the exchange operator itself.

Chile’s IPSA index was the undisputed regional standout, charging 1.47% higher and breaking away from the pack. Peruvian equities also had a strong session, rising 0.81%.

The rest of Latin America painted a more subdued picture. Mexico’s IPC dipped 0.47%, while Colombia’s COLCAP suffered a sharper 1.26% decline, leaving Brazil roughly in the middle of a region that couldn’t agree on a common direction.

06 The technical picture

The Ibovespa remains in a corrective phase after peaking at its 52-week high. The failure to reclaim 178,000 points in a meaningful way keeps the near-term trend capped, with the index more than 10% below that top.

A positive sign is that the index hasn’t threatened its lower support levels, remaining well above the 132,971 low-water mark. For momentum to shift, traders will need to see the index push above its recent congestion zone with conviction, pulling it further from the gravitational pull of the 10% correction mark.

The Ibovespa — Brazil’s main stock barometer — is indicating a broadly flat open, mirroring a global mood that has turned cautious after a soft close on Wall Street’s Nasdaq.

The real, Brazil’s currency, held steady just below the 5.12 per dollar mark in the last session. The pair’s quietness underscores a market that is adjusting to the new 14.00% Selic level — at least until the next piece of the inflation puzzle drops.

Assessment — A holding pattern with a dovish tinge MEDIUM The evidence from recent macro releases paints a picture of an economy that is slowing but not collapsing, with inflation easing only grudgingly towards the 4.5% upper tolerance band. In this environment the central bank cut the Selic rate to 14.00% on 5 August, its fourth straight cut, while signalling that its next move will depend on the data. The balance of risks is skewed, however, by a heavily restrictive real rate that is becoming increasingly hard to justify as GDP growth slips below potential. The key variable to watch is any last-minute consensus shift in the BCB Focus survey, which could signal a change in the market’s collective mind after the August cut.

Today’s calendar is conspicuously light on the top-tier inflation and activity reports that usually whip the B3 tape into motion. The most potent release is arguably the IGP-DI, a wholesale and consumer price composite that, while not the central bank’s primary target, often moves market expectations around administered-price changes.

Beyond the data, the corporate radar is equally thin. With no major earnings expected before the open, attention turns to the turnover leaders from the prior session — particularly Petrobras (PETR4), Itaú (ITUB4) and Vale (VALE3) — for any sign of block trades or early positioning ahead of next week’s heavier reporting cycle.

04 Copom and the macro backdrop

The August meeting of the Copom — the central bank’s Monetary Policy Committee — is the gravitational centre of every conversation in the Brazilian financial market this morning. The Selic, the benchmark interest rate, currently sits at a level that the government’s own macro monitors describe as sufficiently restrictive to keep a lid on prices, yet inflation has proven stubborn.

Headline inflation is idling just below the upper tolerance band of 4.5 per cent, while core measures remain stickier than policymakers would like. At the same time, Brazil’s economic activity is visibly downshifting. The IBC-Br, a monthly proxy for GDP growth, has already shown a January contraction, reinforcing the view that the economy is cooling towards its potential growth rate of around two per cent.

This collision of stickier prices and softer demand creates a genuine dilemma. The wager on the trading desks is finely balanced: the 25-basis-point cut to 14.00% acknowledged the growing slack in the economy while keeping the fight against inflation firmly in view. For foreign investors holding Brazilian assets, the decision is pivotal — it will determine whether the real maintains its attractive yield cushion or starts to see that carry-trade advantage eroded.

The market will parse every word of today’s data, however peripheral, for clues about how far the BCB’s nine-member committee will take its easing cycle. The IGP-DI print, in particular, will be watched for any early sign of a new disinflationary impulse that helped underpin the cut to 14.00%.

05 Corporate stories to watch today

With the macro calendar offering little immediate direction, the spotlight falls on individual names that carved out big moves in the last session. The retailer CVCB3 led the B3 gainers with a 12.3 per cent surge on modest turnover, while fellow consumer names PCAR3 and RADL3 also notched strong gains, hinting at a potential rotation into beaten-down domestic cyclicals.

On the flip side, the healthcare operator HAPV3 slumped 5.7 per cent, and homebuilder POMO3 fell over four per cent, suggesting that yesterday’s market was aggressively differentiating between sub-sectors of the domestic economy. Turnover leaders Petrobras, Itaú, Bradesco and Vale will remain the bellwethers; their early pricing will set the directional bias for the broader Ibovespa.

A notable exception to the domestic-consumption story was the rise of gold miner GOLD11. Its four per cent gain tracked a surge in bullion prices to $4,131 an ounce, a theme that could extend into today’s session if global haven demand persists, offering a rare commodity hedge inside the local index.

06 The levels to watch at the open

B3 traders will be fixated on the Ibovespa’s immediate reaction around the 177,000-point zone, a level that has provided a temporary floor in recent sessions. A clean break below this support would open the way for a test of the index’s 52-week low near 132,971 — a distant but psychologically potent line in the sand that would signal a serious deterioration in risk appetite.

On the currency front, the real’s resilience below 5.12 per dollar is the thin end of the wedge. If the IGP-DI prints below expectations and reflects the backdrop to the August rate cut, the currency could test the 5.10 handle. Conversely, any inflationary surprise would shatter the calm and send the pair lurching back towards the 5.15 resistance level, punishing the country’s large banking and consumer names.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Ibovespa?

It is Brazil’s benchmark stock index, tracking the most representative and liquid companies listed on the B3 exchange in São Paulo.

Why does the Copom meeting matter for stocks?

The Copom sets the Selic, Brazil’s key interest rate. Higher rates tend to support the real but hurt domestic cyclical stocks; lower rates do the opposite, making the decision pivotal for the whole market.

What is the key data release today?

The IGP-DI inflation index at 11:00 BRT is the main event. It measures a mix of wholesale, consumer and construction prices and is a key gauge for contractual adjustments.

How does USD/BRL affect my Brazilian stock position?

A stronger dollar (higher USD/BRL) hurts returns for foreign investors by reducing the dollar value of local shares, and it can also signal capital flight that pressures the stock index lower.

The Mohamed Salah Trabzonspor talks are the transfer story of the Turkish summer. The Egypt captain, 34, is negotiating a two-year deal worth a reported €17 million (US$19.6 million) a year, and Turkish media say an agreement is in place.

Multiple Turkish outlets reported over the weekend that Trabzonspor had reached an agreement with the most decorated African footballer of his generation. The club has not yet issued a formal announcement, and the final signature is still pending.

That has done nothing to dampen the mood in Trabzon. Supporters have flooded social media with welcomes, turning the negotiation itself into a public event.

The numbers on the table

The reported structure is a two-year contract at €17 million per season, roughly US$19.6 million. For a player of 34, that places Salah among the best-paid footballers ever recruited by a Turkish club.

A commitment of that size would rank among the largest salary packages in Süper Lig history, underlining how far Trabzonspor are stretching to win the race.

Notably absent from the reporting is any transfer fee. The package being discussed centres on salary and contract length, pointing to a deal built around the player’s own negotiating position.

Salah’s commercial gravity explains the premium. He brings one of the largest followings in world football, spanning the Arab world, Africa and beyond, and shirt sales alone would recoup a share of the outlay.

The structure also explains the player’s side of the ledger. A two-year guarantee at elite wages offers security that incentive-heavy extensions elsewhere could not match at this stage of his career.

The player Trabzon are buying

Salah’s résumé needs little embellishment. He is a two-time CAF African Player of the Year, a Champions League winner in 2019 and a multiple Premier League Golden Boot winner during a decade at the top of English football.

With Liverpool he collected Premier League titles in 2020 and 2025, becoming the most productive African forward in the competition’s history. With Egypt he twice reached the Africa Cup of Nations final, in 2017 and 2021, losing both but carrying the hopes of a football-mad nation.

At 34, he is no longer a resale asset. What Trabzonspor would be buying is performance, leadership and a global brand that few clubs outside Europe’s richest five leagues could previously afford.

A statement window in Trabzon

The Salah pursuit caps an aggressive rebuild at Papara Park. Trabzonspor parted with veterans Anthony Nwakaeme and Edin Visca and reinvested across the attacking line.

The club has already paid €11.5 million (US$13.3 million), including bonuses, for 22-year-old left winger Noah Saviolo. It has also tabled a €15 million (US$17.3 million) offer for Milan’s Nigerian international Samuel Chukwueze and explored a loan for Leicester City’s Ghanaian winger Abdul Fatawu.

Adding Salah to that recruitment would transform an ambitious window into a statement of intent. The 41,000-capacity Papara Park would host the biggest name ever to wear the claret and blue.

What it says about African talent

The move underlines how the market for elite African players keeps widening. Turkish clubs, long a home for solid African professionals such as Trabzonspor’s own Paul Onuachu, are now bidding for the continent’s global superstars.

It also lands at a moment when African football’s institutional weight is rising. The Rio Times documented that shift in its report on Africa’s 54 votes and the US$4.2 billion FIFA fight, and tracks the game across North Africa.

For Egypt, a high-profile move keeps the national team’s talisman in weekly European competition ahead of the next Africa Cup of Nations cycle. For the Süper Lig, it is a marketing coup measured in broadcast interest from Cairo to Lagos.

African federations watch such moves closely. Visibility in a competitive European league shapes sponsorship income, and national-team commercial deals increasingly follow where the continent’s stars play their club football.

What to watch

First, the official announcement. Until Trabzonspor confirms the signature, the agreement remains a report, however well sourced.

Second, the medical and presentation. Turkish clubs traditionally unveil marquee signings in mass stadium ceremonies, and Papara Park would deliver a spectacle.

Third, the dominoes. A completed Salah deal could free or freeze moves for Chukwueze and Fatawu, reshaping the market for African wingers across Europe, within the shifting economics of the New Scramble for Africa in 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Mohamed Salah joining Trabzonspor?

Multiple Turkish media outlets report that Trabzonspor have reached an agreement with Mohamed Salah, and the club is in negotiations with the Egypt captain. A formal announcement from the club was still pending at the time of writing.

How much would Salah earn at Trabzonspor?

The package under negotiation is a two-year contract worth a reported €17 million per year, about US$19.6 million. No transfer fee has been reported as part of the discussions.

Who else have Trabzonspor signed this summer?

Trabzonspor paid €11.5 million (US$13.3 million) for winger Noah Saviolo and bid a reported €15 million (US$17.3 million) for Milan’s Samuel Chukwueze, while exploring a loan for Abdul Fatawu. Veterans Anthony Nwakaeme and Edin Visca left the club.

Why is the Salah deal significant for African football?

It would be the most high-profile transfer by an African player in the current window, confirming Turkish clubs as bidders for the continent’s biggest stars. It also keeps Egypt’s captain in top-level European competition.

World.title: Sanitation worker killed after falling into path of school bus on Lord’s Bank Road
World.content:
Sanitation worker killed after falling into path of school bus on Lord’s Bank Road

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have detained a school bus driver following a fatal traffic accident that claimed the life of a sanitation worker on Lord’s Bank Road in the Belize District.

The accident occurred at approximately 1:15 p.m. on Wednesday, August 5, 2026. Police say Andrew Smith was standing near the left rear of a garbage truck that had been parked along the roadside when he allegedly fell into the traffic lane.

Smith was subsequently struck by an approaching school bus and died from his injuries. Public reports have identified the victim as 39-year-old Andrew Alexander Smith. (Facebook)

The bus driver was detained, and urine samples were obtained as part of the standard investigative process. Police have not indicated whether impairment is suspected.

Investigations into the circumstances surrounding the fatal accident are continuing.

The cause remains framed as preliminary, since police are still investigating how Smith fell into the roadway.

World.title: F**k Around & Find Out: Delivery truck man shoots two robbers who held him up
World.content:
F**k Around & Find Out: Delivery truck man shoots two robbers who held him up

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Two men are receiving medical treatment under police guard after they were shot during an armed robbery on Mahogany Street in Belize City on Wednesday afternoon.

According to police, the incident occurred at approximately 1:00 p.m. while a salesperson was seated inside a parked delivery truck. Two armed men reportedly approached the vehicle and demanded the sales proceeds in the salesperson’s possession.

The salesperson complied with the demand initially then subsequently fired upon the alleged robbers, shooting and injuring both men. Earlier reports confirmed that police had responded to a robbery and shooting involving a delivery truck in the area.

The injured men were transported for treatment and remain under police guard. Their identities, medical conditions and the amount of money stolen have not yet been disclosed.

Police investigations into the incident are continuing.

World.title: Jimmy Rojas remanded after allegedly climbing lamp post and damaging nearly $49,000 in police camera equipment
World.content:
Jimmy Rojas remanded after allegedly climbing lamp post and damaging nearly $49,000 in police camera equipment

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Jimmy Rojas was remanded to the Belize Central Prison on Wednesday after being arraigned on two counts of damage to property involving government-owned surveillance cameras in the Saint Martin de Porres area.

Police allege that cameras and related equipment valued at approximately $49,000 were damaged at the corners of Tibruce Street and Croton Lane, and Flamboyant and Lavender streets, during the early morning hours of August 1.

Investigators said surveillance footage showed a slim-built man climbing the camera posts and repeatedly striking the equipment with an object resembling a knife. Police reportedly identified the man as Rojas.

Rojas appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate and pleaded not guilty to both charges. Although he was offered bail on the new allegations, the court revoked his bail in a separate burglary case after finding that he had allegedly breached his curfew and failed to attend a scheduled court appearance.

He was consequently remanded to prison until September 14, 2026, when both the damage-to-property and burglary cases are scheduled to return to court.

Rojas was previously charged with burglarizing the security booth at Saint Luke Methodist Primary School in March. He had also been charged in connection with the 2024 murder of Jose Matus, also known as “El Whapo,” but that charge was later withdrawn on the instructions of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

World.title: Lennox Gentle remanded for murder of Kiffer McKenzie
World.content:
Lennox Gentle remanded for murder of Kiffer McKenzie

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Twenty-four-year-old Lennox Linsford Gentle was arraigned on Wednesday for the murder of Kiffer Alexander McKenzie, who was fatally shot in downtown Belize City on June 13.

Gentle, a resident of Vernon Street, was escorted to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court under heavy police security. He appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate, who explained that no plea would be taken because the charge is an indictable offence. Bail could not be granted at the Magistrate’s Court level, and Gentle was remanded to the Belize Central Prison until October 1, 2026.

McKenzie was seated inside his blue Jeep near the corner of Albert and Orange streets with his two children when a gunman approached the driver’s side and fired several shots. The shooter reportedly escaped on a motorcycle.

Despite being injured, McKenzie drove along Albert Street before colliding with a parked vehicle near Tropicana. He was transported to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he was pronounced dead shortly after 10:20 a.m.

Police recovered several expended 9mm shells and bullet fragments from the primary scene. Investigators also collected a blood sample from McKenzie’s vehicle.

According to police, information obtained through the department’s Fusion Center and a statement from a female Special Constable helped investigators identify the alleged shooter and eventually led to Gentle’s arrest.

McKenzie was the son of the late George “Junie Balls” McKenzie.

World.title: ‘The Dog-Gone Girl Is Mine’: Love triangle lands man in court after allegedly kicking ex-girlfriend’s new man off his cycle and throwing bottle at ex
World.content:
‘The Dog-Gone Girl Is Mine’: Love triangle lands man in court after allegedly kicking ex-girlfriend’s new man off his cycle and throwing bottle at ex

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man accused of attacking his former girlfriend and injuring her new boyfriend in two separate incidents has been granted bail after appearing in the Magistrate’s Court.

Raheem Tray Gibson, 22, a runman of North Front Street, was arraigned on charges of aggravated assault and harm when he appeared unrepresented before a Senior Magistrate on Tuesday. He pleaded not guilty to both charges.

The aggravated assault charge relates to an allegation made by Gibson’s former girlfriend, a 24-year-old sales clerk.

Yearwood reported that at about 6:30 p.m. on Sunday, August 2, she was at a park on Matron Roberts Street with her five-year-old son and her current boyfriend when Gibson arrived on a motorcycle.

She alleged that Gibson stopped several feet away, cursed at her and threw a glass pint bottle in her direction. The bottle reportedly missed her, and Gibson then rode away.

The harm charge stems from an incident reported by the woman’s current boyfriend, a 24-year-old security guard.

He told police that on the morning of Saturday, August 1, he was riding his motorcycle toward Douglas Jones Street when another motorcyclist began following him.

He alleged that the rider drove directly behind him and kicked the rear tyre of his motorcycle, causing him to crash. Flowers reportedly suffered abrasions to his right palm, elbow, ankle and hip.

His motorcycle was also damaged, including a bent handlebar and front wheel, as well as broken lights, indicators and a rear-view mirror.

Flowers identified the alleged attacker as Gibson, whom he knew as his girlfriend’s former boyfriend.

There was no objection to bail, and Gibson was offered bail of $1,500 for the aggravated assault charge and $1,000 for the harm charge. He was required to provide separate sureties for each matter.

His bail conditions include staying at least 100 yards away from Yearwood, her home and workplace, and avoiding all contact with her, her relatives and prosecution witnesses, including through social media.

Gibson must also report to the Queen Street Police Station every Wednesday and must not be charged with any other offence while on bail.

Both matters were adjourned until September 16, 2026.

World.title: National Commission for Families and Children launches child protection training
World.content:
National Commission for Families and Children launches child protection training

By Zoila Palma: The National Commission for Families and Children (NCFC), with the support of the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology, launched the first child protection training session for teachers from Wesley College, Excelsior High School, and Gwen Lizarraga High School.

The NCFC explained that as mandatory reporters and a critical line of defense for vulnerable children, teachers play a vital role in recognizing signs of abuse, reporting concerns, and safeguarding children’s rights and well-being.

This initiative will strengthen educators’ knowledge of child protection, safeguarding, and their responsibilities under Belize’s child protection framework, with a total of 80 teachers expected to be trained to help ensure every child is protected, heard, and supported.
