World.title: Germany: 10 years of 'Integration Act' for refugees
World.content:
The German Integration Act aimed to regulate the integration of recognized refugees following high levels of immigration, facilitating access to the labor market in return for integration efforts.

In early August 2016, a phrase began circulating in Germany that would shape political and societal discussions for many years to come: "the divided society."

There were still many Germans who remained committed to welcoming hundreds of thousands of refugees who had begun arriving the previous year, mainly from Syria. However, an increasing number were more skeptical of immigrants and foreigners, especially following the mass sexual assaults involving young men with immigrant backgrounds that took place in Cologne on New Year's Eve 2015–2016.

Under the leadership of Chancellor Angela Merkel, the coalition government of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)/Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) sought to calm the polarized mood in Germany by introducing an integration act , a law designed to appeal to all sides through the guiding principle of "support and challenge" ("fördern und fordern").

Some thought it offered too many giveaways; others felt it imposed too many demands.

Germany relies on Syrian workers amid return debates To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

'Support and challenge' means squaring the circle

"For someone in favor of strong regulatory policy, the integration law offered too much assistance while demanding far too little. One example is the fact that a rejected asylum application did not necessarily lead to deportation," says Holger Kolb, of the Expert Council on Integration and Migration (SVR).

"For someone very concerned with integration policy, on the other hand, the requirements were far too high, especially regarding temporary residence permits for vocational training. They believe this creates far too many obstacles to successful integration."

Providing support for new arrivals meant massively expanding integration and language courses, allowing new arrivals to enter the labor market more quickly. A vocational training permit for refugees whose individual asylum applications had been rejected, but whose home countries were still categorized as unsafe, allowed them to complete a three-year vocational training program followed by two years of employment in the field they trained in.

On the other hand, it was made obligatory to participate in language and integration courses. Sanctions were imposed in the form of welfare benefit cuts for those who refused to participate. Also, the refugees were distributed evenly across Germany to prevent over-concentration in major cities.

German village struggles to unite amid migration challenge To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Criticisms of the residence requirement

This "residency requirement" had a very negative impact on integration, says Herbert Brücker, head of the Research Department for Migration, Integration and International Labour Studies at the Institute for Employment Research (IAB).

"People were distributed disproportionately to economically weak regions with high unemployment. If we restrict people to regions where the economy isn't doing so well, that naturally has negative effects on labor market integration," Brücker explained.

However, he has a positive assessment of the vocational training policy, which allowed rejected refugees to finish their vocational training. He argues that it always makes sense to offer those who integrate well the prospect of staying: They put more effort into learning the language and finding employment and ultimately contribute to the social security systems.

Integration in Germany is better than many think

And it turns out, integration in Germany isn't going nearly as badly as has often been claimed, says Brücker, even if refugees are entering the labor market much more slowly than other immigrants.

"Ten years later, we're now seeing employment rates of 65% to 67% — just 3% below the national average. This puts Germany at the top of the European rankings, alongside Norway. This is also due to the fact that we've offered integration courses, language programs and vocational training to actively promote integration."

How migration to Germany changed after 2015 refugee arrivals To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Federal Ministry of the Interior and the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees (BAMF) has partially scrapped plans to severely restrict free access to integration courses to only those with "good prospects of remaining in the country." Since June 2026, Ukrainians and EU citizens have once again been able to participate in the courses — including those without a secure prospect of remaining.

Brücker points out that integration courses are a relatively inexpensive tool for integration. "They increase employment rates by five to ten percentage points once people complete the course. Cutting funding for integration courses delays integration into the labor market and prolongs reliance on benefits. This doesn't save money — it actually costs us a lot of money."

Room for improvement

Were Brücker able to refine the Integration Act, he says he would relax the residency requirement after asylum proceedings are concluded, begin integration courses just one month after arrival and expedite asylum proceedings in order to integrate people with protection status more quickly while also being able to deport those without protection status more quickly.

Kolb, however, wants to see more coordination between the federal government and the states, and a simpler regulatory framework.

The Integration Act of August 2016, he says, does not really deserve that name. "People expect the Integration Act to provide comprehensive regulations governing the integration of people who are already here," he says.

"In reality, however, the Integration Act is specifically designed for people who have come here as refugees. It would have made more sense to manage expectations better, and establish regulations that are significantly simpler."

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Middle East: Hormuz deal near, IDF soldiers dead in Lebanon
World.content:
08/06/2026 August 6, 2026 Iran says Hormuz deal in 'final stage'

Iran's Foreign Ministry on Thursday said that a deal with Oman regarding control over the Strait of Hormuz is in its "final stage" and will soon be in place "if certain parties do not obstruct this process."

Though not mentioned by name, the inference is that US President Donald Trump — who triggered the shutdown of the all-important waterway when he launched his war with Iran on February 28 — will again scupper a return to shipping flow.

"The factors making the Strait of Hormuz insecure still exist on the part of the United States, particularly the naval blockade and other aggressive and threatening actions against Iran and its interests," Iran's Foreign Ministry said.

Mediator Pakistan praised Oman's role in making the Tehran-Muscat deal a reality, adding that it would pave the way for comprehensive peace negotiations between Iran and the US.

The strait agreement could see ships traveling through Iranian and Omani waters and paying fees for safe passage.

Iran has insisted that it will exert control over the international passageway — through which roughly one-fifth of global oil and gas supply generally flows — but the US has insisted traffic must flow freely and without fees, as it did before Trump ordered US attacks on Iran.

Currently, the US has a blockade on the blockade, with Iran controlling the movement of ships through the narrow passage and the US maintaining a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

As the world economy sputters under the increased economic strain brought on by the US war, Trump has faced growing pressure from his Republican underlings in Congress to end the unpopular, price-busting conflict before November's mid-term elections.

World.title: Germany arrests Ukrainian suspected of spying on arms firm
World.content:
Investigators say the suspect photographed a Bavarian defense site for a foreign intelligence service in preparation for possible sabotage.

German authorities have arrested a Ukrainian man suspected of spying on a defense company in Bavaria to prepare possible acts of sabotage.

Investigators suspect he took photographs of the premises of a Bavarian defense company in June and passed them to handlers working for a foreign intelligence service.

What do we know about the case so far?

The 33-year-old was detained in the eastern state of Thuringia on Sunday and is now in pretrial detention, Munich prosecutors and Bavaria's State Criminal Police Office said on Thursday .

A Munich court issued an arrest warrant on Monday and the suspect is now being held in pre-trial detention in Bavaria.

Authorities described the man as a so-called "low-level agent," a term used for people recruited by foreign intelligence services to carry out relatively simple tasks.

Prosecutors said he was suspected of acting as an agent for sabotage purposes.

The arrest followed cooperation between security and intelligence agencies coordinated through Germany's recently established Joint Center for Countering Hybrid Threats, known as GAZ-Hybrid.

Authorities did not identify the foreign intelligence service allegedly involved and said no further details could be released while the investigation continues.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

Tarun Tejpal, who founded Tehelka, a magazine known for its investigative journalism and sting operations, has been sentenced to 10 years in prison and fined 10 lakh rupees (€9,100) for the rape of a woman journalist in 2013.

The Bombay High Court convicted Tejpal, overturning the acquittal granted by a Goa sessions court in 2021.

Before the sentence was pronounced, Tejpal sought leniency, citing his age and family.

The court has given Tejpal two weeks to surrender, according to a report by the Indian Express newspaper.

The high-profile case sparked a nationwide debate about the harassment of women in the workplace, and the underreporting of such incidents due to fears of job loss and victimization.

World.title: Why is Russia selling its gold?
World.content:
Russia has become one of the world's biggest sellers of gold over the past 12 months. It's an attempt to raise cash in the face of budget issues, but not necessarily a sign of a looming financial crisis.

Russia has sold significant volumes of its gold reserves so far in 2026 as the Kremlin seeks to raise cash to offset a big budget deficit.

The Russian Central Bank announced recently that its gold reserves stood at 73.4 million troy ounces, or 2,282 metric tons, as of the start of July. That represents a decline of around 43.5 metric tonnes since the start of 2026.

It means Russia's gold reserves are now at their lowest level since before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022.

Gold prices hit record levels earlier this year, with prices averaging around $4,800 (€4,210) per ounce in the first four months before falling back to a current level of around $4,000 per ounce. Moscow's sell-off is likely to have raised more than $5 billion.

"The fact that they're selling gold means that they're running out of other more liquid assets," Elina Ribakova, an economist with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW. "So there is pressure on the deficit and also pressure on the sources to finance this deficit."

Budget problems

Russia's budget has been under serious strain in recent years due to its massively increased defense spending, which funds the war in Ukraine.

Earlier this year, the Financial Times reported that the country's finance ministry had warned the cabinet in a letter that overspending on the war would be at least $28 billion in 2026, with further overspends expected in 2027 and 2028. Defense spending has more than quadrupled since 2021. It totalled around 16 trillion rubles in 2025 ($204 billion; €178 billion).

Chris Weafer, a Moscow-based financial analyst with the consulting firm Macro-Advisory, says that while the Russian gold sell-off is significant, it is not a case of panic selling.

"It's an extraordinary situation, but it's a relatively normal trend," he told DW. "It doesn't represent any element of Russia going broke, running out of money, not having anything else and literally selling the household silver."

He says that the gold Russia has offloaded has mostly been sold by the country's finance ministry, via its National Welfare Fund (NWF), rather than the Russian Central Bank.

"Since early 2022, gold was one of the assets that the National Welfare Fund could buy, because US treasuries and bunds weren't available to them (as a result of sanctions following the invasion of Ukraine)."

Weafer pointed out that the asset had become a key liquid component of the fund, which, he said, was precisely what a national welfare fund is intended for: to be sold when funds are needed, particularly during difficult times. "To that extent, one can argue it is serving the intended purpose."

The fund's gold sale is intended to replenish its so-called liquid assets. Weafer estimates that the fund is worth approximately $150 billion, with around $50 billion of that being described as "liquid."

"The Kremlin doesn't want that buffer to go down because that would lead to maybe more speculation about financial crisis or economic difficulties, and it would undermine the Kremlin's geopolitical position," said Weafer.

"It likes to portray the country as being very stable and very strong, and that $50 billion of cash is an important part of that."

He says another important factor to consider is that as one of the world's biggest producers of gold, Russia can replenish stocks it has sold relatively quickly by buying from its domestic producers. Russia holds the fifth-largest reserves in the world, around the same level as China, France and Italy, and significantly behind the top two, Germany and the US.

Ribakova agrees that this offers Russia a significant buffer.

"Russia has an advantage," she said. "It does produce gold itself. So when it was worried about sanctions, it allocated part of the money into the gold purchases, which they were buying from the domestic producers."

Funding the war for the foreseeable future

The fact that Russia has become one of the biggest sellers of gold has raised further questions about its budget deficit and what that says about wider economic stability.

Russia's defence budget has increased dramatically Image: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Sputnik/AP Photo/picture alliance

Russia's federal budget spending and deficit could exceed official plans by more than 1 trillion roubles ($12.85 billion) in 2026, according to ​recent government data. The budget deficit is currently projected to be 1.6% of GDP for 2026, which is approximately $40 billion, and could yet grow.

However, improved revenues from oil and gas, boosted by higher oil prices due to the war in Iran, has helped Moscow to offset the budget difficulties so far in 2026.

Ribakova says everything comes back to the prices and revenues Russia gets from its oil and gas, calling it the "real limit" on Moscow's capacity to finance the four-and-a-half-year-long war in Ukraine.

"Everything hinges on that," she noted. "When the oil price is high, Russia gets revenues. It's easier to borrow, its domestic financial system is healthier. If the oil price drops, say, to sixty or forty, then you immediately have a crisis."

Both she and Weafer caution that despite the obvious economic difficulties the Russian economy has at present, it can continue to fund the war for the foreseeable future by cutting back on non-defense spending.

"Putin can continue going for years in the current environment," said Ribakova. "Maybe not making any progress on the front line, which we haven't seen any progress for the last couple of years, but still being able to throw resources at the war with Ukraine."

Could Russia save the global economy? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Even if the deficit continues as is, Russia can still find the money and really won't be in any sort of a financial crisis or a weak geopolitical position over the next 12 to 24 months," said Weafer.

Yet he points to obvious longer-term damage being done to the economy and the trouble that may bring further down the tracks.

"It is creating this huge distortion in the economy and creating this longer-term negative picture that's now creating divisions in government," he said.

He added that the situation had a divide between those responsible for economic growth and the Kremlin. Their message, he said, is that the current approach could not be sustained, "if you want the economy to go back to a more normal trajectory after peace. That's the bottom line."

Edited by: Rob Mudge

Skip next section Germany's heat death toll rises to nearly 12,000

08/06/2026 August 6, 2026 Germany's heat death toll rises to nearly 12,000

Nearly 12,000 people have died from the effects of extreme heat in Germany this year, according to new estimates from the Robert Koch Institute.

The German public health institute put the number of heat-related deaths between April 6 and July 26 at around 11,900, already well above any full-year total since 2016.

The previous annual high was around 9,000 deaths in 2018.

Around 9,600 of this year's deaths were linked to the exceptionally hot week from June 22 to 28.

Average temperatures across Germany reached 26.4 degrees Celsius (79.5 degrees Fahrenheit) that week, while daytime temperatures topped 40 degrees C (104 degrees F) in many places.

The institute described the latest total as a conservative estimate, meaning the true figure could be higher.

People aged 85 and above accounted for around 6,000 deaths, while almost 3,000 victims were aged between 75 and 84.

Around 1,800 deaths were recorded among people aged 65 to 74, while about 1,100 were among those younger than 65.

Heat rarely kills directly. More often, extreme temperatures worsen existing illnesses or put additional strain on the cardiovascular system.

World.title: El PP reconoce que acogerá a los menores en sus comunidades: “El Partido Popular siempre cumple la ley, en esta ocasión, también”
World.content:
La pregunta planea cada rueda de prensa que ofrece un dirigente del Partido Popular desde el jueves pasado, cuando 72.000 personas entraron a Ceuta. ¿Acogerán las comunidades, en su mayoría gobernadas por el PP, a los menores llegados aquel día? ¿Y aquellas que comparten el Ejecutivo con Vox después de haber firmado acuerdos en los que se oponen precisamente a su tutela? En el inicio de la crisis, Alberto Núñez Feijóo esquivó la cuestión cuando compareció desde la ciudad autónoma. “Conocen nuestro plan de inmigración”, respondió con evasivas el líder del PP, el sábado. Cinco días después, Génova reconoce que sus autonomías realojarán a los niños y menores extranjeros, aunque los barones protesten y se opongan con todo tipo de trabas al considerar que el reparto obligatorio es injusto. “El Partido Popular siempre cumple la ley; en esta ocasión, también. Nosotros y nuestros gobiernos”, ha asumido el vicesecretario de Política Autonómica y Municipal, Elías Bendodo, este jueves. La norma obliga a darles cobijo cuando otro territorio exceda por tres su capacidad de atenderles, como es el caso de Ceuta. Y “cumplir la ley” implica aceptar ese reparto.

En Extremadura, Aragón, Castilla y León y Andalucía, los cuatro pactos suscritos por PP y Vox comprometen a las dos formaciones a no aceptar más menores no acompañados. Pero la avalancha de Ceuta ha puesto a prueba estas alianzas ante una crisis humanitaria sin precedentes. “En los documentos firmados se habla de que cumplirán la ley en materia de inmigración”, ha recordado Bendodo. “Vamos a cumplir la ley, pero es un problema que tiene que arreglar el Gobierno porque lo ha generado directa o indirectamente”, ha añadido el vicesecretario del PP, que ha vuelto a cargar contra Pedro Sánchez, a quien responsabilizan de la llegada de miles de personas en un día a la ciudad autónoma. “El presidente está tumbado en la hamaca y quiere que las comunidades del Partido Popular resuelvan la papeleta”, ha aseverado.

Así, fuentes de los distintos territorios gobernados por el PP avanzan que opondrán todo tipo de trabas a la ley de extranjería —reformada en marzo del año pasado mediante real decreto para incorporar el reparto obligatorio—, como recurrirla en los tribunales, pero no se negarán a cumplir la ley. De hecho, desde que en agosto pasado se estableció la distribución numérica de plazas por comunidades autónomas, más de 1.750 niños y jóvenes han sido derivados desde Canarias, Ceuta y Melilla a la Península y Baleares. Traslados que se estaban dando al menos hasta mediados de julio pasado, incluso después de los pactos del PP y Vox. Del lado de la extrema derecha, el secretario general de su grupo parlamentario ha sostenido que “España tiene una obligación internacional de devolver a los menores con sus padres”, ha dicho José María Figaredo en Cuatro, donde ha descartado que en esta ocasión rompan las coaliciones con el PP.

Frente a la resistencia de sus compañeros de partido, el presidente de Melilla, el popular Juan José Imbroda, pidió anoche al resto de barones autonómicos un “gesto de solidaridad” en la acogida de menores. “Entiendo a mis compañeros del PP, pero ahora mismo hay que hacer ese gesto de solidaridad y hay un real decreto que cumplir, te guste o no. Vamos a poner pie en pared y vamos a empezar a arreglar esto desde el origen. No podemos traer a todos los menores de Marruecos”, afirmó Imbroda este miércoles en la Cadena SER. A Melilla entraron 140 menores más coincidiendo con la llegada masiva a Ceuta, pero el dirigente melillense ha subrayado que primero hay que aliviar la situación de la otra ciudad autónoma.

Comparecencias en el Congreso

En paralelo, el Partido Popular ha solicitado este jueves la comparecencia urgente del ministro de Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska; de Defensa, Margarita Robles; de Exteriores, José Manuel Albares, y de Justicia y Relaciones con las Cortes, Félix Bolaños, en el Congreso en distintas comisiones por la crisis de Ceuta. Para ello, al estar en período inhábil por ser agosto, los populares piden a la Mesa que convoque a la Diputación Permanente para calificar dichas peticiones. Algo improbable, considerando que el PSOE y Sumar tienen la mayoría en el órgano de Gobierno de la Cámara baja.

Las solicitudes de comparecencia se suman a la ya formalizada la semana pasada por los populares, que exigen a Sánchez dar explicaciones en un pleno extraordinario en el Congreso. El PSOE ha hecho caso omiso ya también a esta petición. “Clama al cielo que el presidente, después de que 72.000 personas hayan violentado nuestras fronteras, esté a la bartola en la playa”, ha criticado al respecto Bendodo. “Si tú eres el presidente del Gobierno y tienes una avalancha de 72.000 personas, no puedes irte de vacaciones y tumbarte en la hamaca”, ha insistido. Quien sí será previsiblemente interrogada en sede parlamentaria es la ministra de Defensa. Pues el PP ha solicitado la comparecencia de Robles en el Senado, donde tienen mayoría absoluta, para que sea interrogada este mes de agosto.

World.title: Vox y Sumar coinciden al pedir que se excluya a Marruecos de la organización del Mundial 2030
World.content:
La entrada de 72.000 migrantes por la frontera de Ceuta ha dejado una imagen insólita en el Congreso: Vox y Sumar han presentado sendas propuestas que buscan que se estudie la exclusión de Marruecos de la organización del Mundial 2030. Este jueves, el partido de Abascal ha registrado una proposición en la Cámara baja solicitando que la Comisión de Deportes discuta su exclusión como país coorganizador, mientras que la coalición izquierdista ya había registrado un documento similar un día antes. Además, fuentes del partido de ultraderecha señalan que estarían dispuestos a apoyar la propuesta de Sumar si esta “llegase a pleno o a comisión”.

“Los gravísimos acontecimientos registrados en Ceuta los días 30 y 31 de julio han quebrado por completo los presupuestos de confianza y cooperación sobre los que necesariamente descansa una candidatura compartida”, subrayan desde el partido de ultraderecha. “No es un socio leal, ni para organizar un evento deportivo de esta magnitud ni para ninguna cuestión de vecindad”, añaden en su proposición no de ley.

Asimismo, insisten en que las llegadas de migrantes suponen “gravísimos ataques a la soberanía nacional” y a la “integridad territorial”. Esto, según exponen, levanta “serias dudas sobre la capacidad de Marruecos para ofrecer las garantías que exige un acontecimiento de la dimensión de la Copa Mundial de 2030”. Por ello, los de Abascal piden “que el Ejecutivo defienda el protagonismo y los intereses de España en la organización del campeonato y promueva ante la FIFA la revisión de la participación de Marruecos como Estado organizador”.

Esto coincide con lo expuesto el día anterior desde Sumar. El principal socio de Gobierno aseguraba en su escrito que “mientras persistan dudas tan graves sobre el uso político de vidas humanas”, Marruecos no puede “obtener el prestigio, los beneficios económicos y la legitimación internacional de un Mundial”. Ambas formaciones difieren en la forma, pero no en el fondo, ya que desde Sumar señalan que “la cooperación migratoria no puede funcionar como una llave que se abre o se cierra en función de intereses diplomáticos”. En su propuesta, se quejan de que, a su juicio, “las personas migrantes no pueden ser utilizadas por el Gobierno marroquí ni criminalizadas al llegar a España”. Aun así, Vox estaría dispuesto a apoyar esta propuesta.

Vox y Sumar no han sido los únicos que han defendido que Marruecos no debe organizar el torneo. También lo ha hecho el secretario de organización de Podemos, Pablo Fernández, desde su cuenta de X: “España no debería organizar el Mundial con una dictadura como Marruecos que no respeta los derechos humanos, y que es responsable de la muerte de más de 140 personas en una operación contra España”, ha escrito, antes de concluir que la Copa del Mundo se tendría que organizar “solo con Portugal”.

Esta respuesta de los partidos políticos llega en un momento de incógnitas, tanto en la FIFA como en la organización del torneo. La mayor es el estadio en el que se disputará la gran final. Según las palabras en enero del presidente de la RFEF, Rafael Louzán, la final se disputará en España, con el estadio Santiago Bernabéu como punta de lanza. Pero el estamento del fútbol aún no ha tomado una decisión. Marruecos también quiere la final y está metiendo presión para conseguirla. Para ello impulsó el proyecto de reforma de su gran estadio, el Hassan II de Casablanca, con capacidad de 115.000 espectadores, de la mano del estudio encargado de la última reforma de Wembley.

La ministra de Deportes, Milagros Tolón, fue preguntada por la propuesta de su socio de Gobierno en los micrófonos de la Cadena SER, y aseguró que mantienen su confianza en la organización del evento. “Nosotros respetamos, estamos en un Gobierno de coalición, a veces tenemos diferencias y, como Gobierno, apostamos por este Mundial”, defendió. En la entrevista, Tolón fue preguntada por la información del diario británico The Times, que aseguraba que el presidente de la FIFA, Gianni Infantino, habría ofrecido la final del torneo a Marruecos a cambio de su apoyo en las elecciones a la presidencia. “Queremos que la final sea en España porque lo merecemos”, confesó la ministra, antes de zanjar que “será la FIFA quien decida”.

World.title: El eclipse une la España vaciada con Marruecos para revelar los secretos de la corona solar
World.content:
El minuto y medio de fama de la España vaciada El primer eclipse de Sol total visible en la Península en más de un siglo pondrá el foco, por un día, en algunas de las provincias más despobladas, donde las condiciones de observación serán idóneas. EL PAÍS recorre hasta el domingo seis puntos de la franja de la totalidad de la España vaciada para contar cómo se preparan para el 12 de agosto O CEBREIRO (LUGO) CUENCA DE CAMPOS (VALLADOLID) PALENCIA QUINTANARRAYA (BURGOS) HITA (GUADALAJARA) ARCOS DE LAS SALINAS (TERUEL)

En la escuela de verano de Frómista, niñas y niños dibujan el Sol, como todos hemos hecho alguna vez, rodeado de una corona que casi nadie ha visto. Sin embargo, esa corona existe. Y el próximo eclipse les brindará la oportunidad de comprobarlo por sí mismos y desde casa, a ellos y a los 15 millones de españoles que viven dentro de la banda de totalidad. “Un eclipse solar total es la única posibilidad que tenemos para ver la corona solar con nuestros propios ojos. En mi caso, unos ojos llenos de lágrimas por poder compartirlo con la gente de mi tierra”, explica Eva Villaver, subdirectora del Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias (IAC) y promotora de un experimento que arrancará el 12 de agosto en Palencia.

Su pasión por las estrellas y por la divulgación ha sido clave para llevar a su ciudad natal —y a Frómista, un pueblo de poco más de 700 habitantes en el que pasaba los veranos de niña— la mayor iniciativa de investigación y cooperación del trío ibérico de eclipses 2026-2027-2028. Es el proyecto NATE (las siglas en inglés del Telescopio para el Eclipse del Norte de África), que no solo aspira a iluminar la aún muy desconocida corona solar, sino también a construir un puente científico entre la España vaciada y Marruecos.

Cruzar la provincia de Palencia al atardecer deja claro por qué será uno de los epicentros de este fenómeno astronómico. Al conducir por Tierra de Campos sobre las 20.28, la hora a la que en esta zona comenzará la totalidad, el Sol ya está cerca del horizonte; pero sigue permanentemente a la vista e inunda las plantaciones de girasoles, que miran ahora en dirección contraria al astro rey. En las vastas llanuras de esta comarca castellana —que ha perdido a 6 de cada 10 habitantes desde 1950—, sin apenas colinas, edificios o árboles que tapen la puesta de sol, es fácil encontrar un lugar de observación óptimo. Por eso los cazadores de eclipses tienen esta zona marcada en su mapa desde hace años, y los medios especializados en astronomía colocan la capital palentina en el podio de mejores ciudades para estar el 12 de agosto.

Una pareja camina el 2 de agosto entre campos de girasoles a la salida de Frómista. NICO RODRÍGUEZ

La alcaldesa de Palencia, Miriam Andrés, y su equipo llevan un año preparándose para el denominado “eclipse de la España vaciada”. Ante la previsible avalancha de visitas —las plazas hoteleras para esa noche se agotaron hace mucho tiempo— ofrecen “divulgación, observación del eclipse y, además, investigación científica”, explica la regidora palentina. El Ayuntamiento está preparando una gran zona de observación pública, en la que caben más de 50.000 personas —un tercio de las que viven en toda la provincia—. Allí, una orquesta interpretará las composiciones más míticas de Mike Oldfield para señalar el comienzo del evento astronómico en ese mirador oficial, ubicado entre los dos cerros que dominan las vistas de la ciudad.

En una de esas cimas está el Cristo del Otero, una estatua de 21 metros de altura que durante el eclipse mirará al Sol y dará la espalda a los astrónomos al mando de los telescopios del experimento NATE; entre ellos estará el director del IAC, Valentín Martínez. “Es una importante iniciativa de cooperación internacional que establece un vínculo entre regiones con singularidades muy dispares: la España vaciada, las islas Canarias y el extremo norte del continente africano”, explica. El impulsor del proyecto en Marruecos, Youssef Moulane, investigador de la Universidad Politécnica Mohammed VI, destaca la trascendencia que tendrá para su país, donde espera que perdure más allá del eclipse: “Estamos consiguiendo que estudiantes, investigadores y docentes marroquíes sean protagonistas activos, en lugar de meros espectadores”, sostiene este astrofísico.

La puesta en marcha de NATE ha sido posible por la extraordinaria coincidencia de que dos eclipses totales consecutivos también estén muy cerca geográficamente. Lo de este 12 de agosto en Palencia será, en realidad, una prueba piloto. “Nos va a permitir calibrar los instrumentos y tomar decisiones para usarlos el próximo año”, afirma Martínez. Entusiasmado de poder vivir, por fin, un eclipse total en España, reconoce que este primero no es ideal “para estudiarlo científicamente, pues es demasiado corto —no llega a dos minutos de máximo— y sucede con el Sol demasiado bajo”. El grueso del experimento tendrá lugar en Marruecos durante el segundo, que ocurrirá el 2 de agosto de 2027 y que también oscurecerá por completo Ceuta, Melilla y el extremo sur de Andalucía. Llegará a superar los cuatro minutos de totalidad y tendrá lugar con el Sol hasta cuatro veces más alto de lo que estará ahora en la España vaciada.

Eva Villaver ha visto “miles de veces” la corona solar en imágenes científicas, pero, asegura, nada que se le parezca a la emoción de hacerlo con sus propios ojos. “Una cosa es entender un proceso y otra sentirlo”. Además, explica que “NATE nos permitirá salir de la foto fija y hacer una película de la evolución de la corona durante mucho más tiempo del que dura el eclipse, y con medios muy sencillos”.

Una película más larga de la corona solar

La clave para alargar el eclipse está en una ingeniosa solución: instalar una red de pequeños telescopios coordinados en una decena de localidades a lo largo de la banda de totalidad en Marruecos, lo que permitirá seguir el fenómeno hasta por lo menos 10 minutos. Como en una carrera de relevos, cada modesto observatorio le irá pasando el testigo al siguiente; y, entre todos, al final podrán recrear una grabación de la corona solar mucho más completa y larga de lo que podría conseguir un único gran observatorio de categoría internacional.

Tener una película lo más amplia posible de la corona solar no es un capricho de coleccionista. Según explica Jorge Pérez Gallego, coordinador global del proyecto, cada nueva visualización larga nos acerca más a revelar los secretos de esta capa externa del Sol. “La gran aplicación será hacer mejores predicciones del clima de nuestra estrella, que en la corona genera violentas tormentas solares: cuando nos llegan a la Tierra, generan espectaculares auroras boreales, pero también amenazan la integridad de los satélites meteorológicos y los de telecomunicaciones”, afirma.

A él le fascinan también otras cuestiones más teóricas que esconde esta corona. “Por ejemplo, ¿cómo puede ser que esa parte externa esté a millones de grados de temperatura y la superficie del Sol solo a unos pocos miles?”, se pregunta. “No sabemos por qué sucede”.

Imagen de un taller de astronomía para los alumnos de la escuela de verano de Frómista (Palencia), realizado en las semanas previas al eclipse total del 12 de agosto. Ángel de Francisco Moreno

La divulgación del proyecto NATE irradia desde la capital palentina hacia pueblos de Tierra de Campos, como Carrión de los Condes, Osorno la Mayor, Villalcázar de Sirga, Autilla del Pino y Frómista. En esa última localidad, por la que pasa el Camino de Santiago, Jesús Casañés y Ángel de Francisco preparan actividades relacionadas con el eclipse. El invitado estrella será Pérez Gallego, que impartirá un taller el 11 de agosto en la escuela de verano.

Intentará que los alumnos “se enamoren del Sol y de la ciencia que lo investiga”, planteándoles misterios como el de la temperatura de la corona solar, que él relaciona con el calor que desprende un horno en cualquier cocina. Busca ir más allá de explicarles el eclipse y de insistirles en la observación segura, que también lo hará. Y como siempre en charlas a escolares, va preparado para recibir preguntas que la mayoría de los adultos reprimimos cuando maduramos.

Mientras tanto, sus dos anfitriones aseguran que todos en Frómista, adultos y niños, van a estar pendientes del fenómeno astronómico. Esperan que se les unan los habituales peregrinos y, esta vez, muchos más que llegarán por motivos astronómicos. En cambio, los que se van a perder el eclipse total son los girasoles de sus campos, que a las 20:28:34 del 12 de agosto estarán mirando en dirección contraria y esperando el siguiente amanecer. “Aquí todo el mundo sabe que cuando los girasoles crecen y maduran, pierden flexibilidad y ya no son capaces de seguir al Sol durante todo el día”, dice De Francisco. Sin embargo, los mecanismos biológicos que lo explican eran un enigma para la ciencia hasta hace solo 10 años, igual que ahora lo sigue siendo el funcionamiento de la corona solar.

World.title: Cómo hacer un sencillo bocata de calabacín marinado
World.content:
En verano, la huerta de temporada nos regala ingredientes frescos, jugosos e irresistibles que son altamente susceptibles de acabar entre dos panes

Cuando tengo hambre, lo primero en lo que pienso es en un bocata. Este pensamiento me persigue desde que soy muy pequeña, cuando me acostumbré a desayunar pan recién hecho cada mañana y rápidamente comprobé que las miles de advertencias sobre “no hincharse a pan” antes de comer eran inútiles frente a mi obsesión hacia un producto tan extraordinario. Una debe saber cuales son sus batalla y admitir cuanto antes que el bocata es un amigo incondicional cuya grandeza se debe a tres motivos básicos: es práctico, es accesible, es versátil. Ante uno, todos somos iguales; dentro de uno, la libertad es infinita. El comfort food definitivo junto a un caldo calentito en invierno, unos spaghetti de resaca o un croissant el domingo.

En verano, el deseo de bocata se hace más fuerte y la huerta de temporada nos regala ingredientes frescos, jugosos e irresistibles que son altamente susceptibles de acabar dentro de uno. Por eso, en esta serie veraniega os queremos proponer cinco bocatas vegetales resultones, sencillos y muy ricos que ojalá envolváis en papel de aluminio y disfrutéis al aire libre.

El primero guarda todo lo bueno del verano y se puede preparar en cualquier lugar, ya que no necesita ninguna fuente de calor. El calabacín se elabora en crudo con un marinado express de limón y aceite de oliva virgen extra, la ricotta se tunea con ralladura de limón y queso Parmigiano, el tomate —perfecto en sí mismo— se aliña con aceite de albahaca y la rúcula aporta amargor y un ligerísimo picante nasal. Una barra de pan artesana, de miga suave, absorbe los jugos y el frescor de un bocata que representa el esplendor del buen tiempo, los días eternos y el conformismo sensacional de no necesitar nada más que esto y una bebida refrescante.

Bocata de calabacín marinado

Carlota Badía

World.title: Pistas para un viaje de verano a Portugal: de las playas del Algarve a los azulejos de Lisboa
World.content:
Ciudades y pueblos llenos de encanto, pistas para comer bien y barato y algunos trucos para descubrir el país

Año tras año, Portugal es un destino de vacaciones recurrente. Pero decir Portugal puede tener muchos significados: están las playas del Algarve que acogen a los amantes del surf, los pueblos del centro del país llenos de encanto y calles empedradas o los paisajes que dejan el Duero y el Tajo a su paso por el país vecino. Además del magnetismo de Lisboa y Oporto, dos ciudades llenas de vida y de historia.

Esta es una guía de destinos para quienes este verano viajen a Portugal.

Además, dos pistas gastronómicas para saber dónde comer y qué pedir en Lisboa y Oporto. Así como una visita cultural imprescindible en la capital lusa.

Y la experiencia viajera en primera persona de Paco Nadal, dispuesto a regresar una y otra vez al país.

World.title: Dutch state close to breaking even on ABN Amro bailout
World.content:
The Dutch state is close to recouping the full cost of the 2008 nationalisation of ABN Amro, after a share price rally took the bank’s stock above €40 this week, according to calculations by the Financieele Dagblad.

The finance ministry had long assumed the rescue would be a loss-making operation. In late 2023 it told MPs it was “not realistic” that the state would break even in the short term, projecting a shortfall of almost €7 billion.

Since then the shares have tripled in value, from €13.20 at the time to just over €40 on Thursday. The state, which still owns 20.5% of the bank has now recouped €14.2 billion through staged sell-offs, and its remaining stake is worth some €6.7 billion, the FD said.

That brings the total close to the €21.7 billion the ministry says has been pumped into the bank since 2008.

Slow sell-off

The state bought ABN Amro, Fortis Bank Nederland and the insurer now known as ASR in October 2008 for €16.8 billion to stop parent company Fortis collapsing in the credit crisis, and injected roughly €8 billion more into the banks in the years that followed.

ABN Amro returned to the stock market in 2015, but the share price languished for years and the sell-off repeatedly stalled. Former D66 finance minister Sigrid Kaag restarted the sales in 2023, and every tranche since has fetched a higher price.

Interest paid on the money borrowed for the rescue has been roughly cancelled out by dividend income over the years, the FD said.

Cost cutting

Morningstar analyst Johann Scholtz told the FD the share price rise is partly due to the state selling its stakes and the bank therefore having more freedom to cut costs, along with investors speculating about takeovers in the European banking sector.

The windfall will not plug the cabinet’s budget gaps, however, as one-off share sales cannot be counted towards the deficit under EU rules.

World.title: Jetten thanks firefighters on visit to site of Limburg wildfire
World.content:
Prime minister Rob Jetten has visited the site of a wildfire that has been raging in Limburg for four days, destroying around a square kilometre of woodland.

Jetten thanked emergency workers for their efforts to contain the blaze in the Boshuizerbergen, in a social media video showing “the huge damage to nature and to the animals and people who have had to be evacuated”.

An emergency order banning people from the area remains in force, but limited train services resumed between Venray and Boxmeer on Thursday morning. Arriva had to lay on buses for commuters after the line through the fire zone was closed.

Firefighters said on Wednesday they had brought the blaze under control, only for it to flare up again twice during the night.

Chinook helicopters dropped 900,000 litres of water on the fire in the first two days, drawing it from the Maas in giant buckets containing 7,600 litres.

Efforts to contain the fire have been complicated by the fact that the area contains unexploded Second World War munitions, which bomb disposal specialists have had to make safe.

“In the next few days the fire service and [nature management service] Limburgs Landschap will focus on completely putting out the last sources of the fire. After that we can make a plan to restore this area,” Jetten said.

“I want to thank in particular everyone who has worked so hard in the last few days to deal with this crisis.”

World.title: Vollering closes in on Tour de France lead with stage five win
World.content:
Demi Vollering closed the gap on Tour de France leader Marlen Reusser to just 12 seconds as she edged out her rivals to claim victory in the fifth stage.

Vollering broke away on the final climb of the 140km stage from Mâcon to Belleville-en-Beaujolais before crossing the line just ahead of Reusser and Kasia Niewiadoma.

Reusser, who took the overall lead in Wednesday’s individual time trial, retained the leader’s yellow jersey, but Vollering reduced the Swiss rider’s lead by claiming the bonus seconds for the stage win.

The trio are the only realistic contenders left for the title after the other hopefuls, including defending champion Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, who lost two and a half minutes on the day and is back in 17th place, five minutes behind Reusser.

Dutch veteran Anna van der Breggen’s hopes of adding a Tour de France Femmes win to her four Giro d’Italia titles also appear to have been dashed after she crossed the line with Ferrand-Prévot to drop back to 12th place with a deficit of just over four minutes.

The next placed Dutch rider is Femke de Vries, Ferrand-Prévot’s team-mate at Visma Lease-a-Bike, in eighth place, 3 minutes 11 seconds back.

It is the fourth stage victory for 29-year-old Vollering in the women’s tour, which has only existed as a separate race since last year. In 2023 she won the mountain stage to Tourmalet, while the following year she won the time trial in Rotterdam and the climb to the summit of Alpe d’Huez.

“I’m so incredibly proud of this victory,” said the FDJ team leader. “Everyone in the team played their part, which makes it all the sweeter.”

On Thursday the riders will tackle the 153km stage from Montbrison to Tournon-sur-Rhône, with the high point, the 1,099m Col de Lalouvesc, coming at the 105km mark.

World.title: Two explosions at Amsterdam nursery, minors arrested
World.content:
Police have arrested two minors after a second explosive device went off at a children’s nursery in Amsterdam West within a week.

The first blast at the nursery on Bos en Lommerweg happened at around 4am on Saturday morning. The second went off at roughly the same time on Wednesday morning. Nobody was hurt and damage was limited in both cases, broadcaster NOS reported.

Officers detained the two suspects nearby shortly after the second explosion. They are being held under full restrictions, meaning they may only have contact with their lawyers and their parents.

Police said all scenarios are being examined, including whether the two incidents are connected. No motive has been established, broadcaster AT5 reported.

A nursery worker said staff had been badly shaken but that it would stay open as normal.

World.title: Dutch houseboat owners left high and dry by falling river levels
World.content:
Low water levels in the Rhine delta are causing problems for owners of Dutch houseboats, with no sign of an imminent end to the drought.

Some houseboats and static barges have been standing dry for over a month, resting on platforms that are not designed to support them out of the water or the exposed riverbed.

The Rhine sank to its lowest recorded level last week of 6.46 metres at Lobith, where it enters the Netherlands from Germany, while the flow in the river is one-third of its normal level for July because of low rainfall further upstream.

“We’ve seen these water levels more often in recent years, but usually not until September, and then it gets better after a few days’ rain,” Peter Broekmeulen, board member of the houseboat owners’ association LWO told broadcaster NOS.

The problems for dried-up houseboat owners go further than being stuck above dry land. Several homes have tilted, causing doors and windows to jam and cracks to appear in walls.

Power cables become strained and water pipes crack as they are stretched by the sinking houseboats.

But the biggest challenge is drainage, as residents have had to create improvised systems to deal with waste water that usually flows into the river.

“Open septic tank”

“When the water is there it flows away, but now they’re standing dry it ends up on the land and you get a kind of open septic tank, which is unacceptable from a public health point of view,” Broekmeulen told DutchNews.

Paul van de Veen, who has lived on Rosandepolder in Arnhem, for 40 years, told NOS: “In the early years our boat once had to be towed away by a sailing boat because the water was too high. Now we’re seeing the other side of the coin.”

Van de Veen’s house is still floating after the council dredged his side of the river in February. “We still have a margin,” he said. “The water around us is around a metre deep.”

His neighbours across the water are less fortunate. Marloes Kraal, whose houseboat is in the neighbouring municipality of Renkum, is on a section of river that dried up months ago. “We have cracks in the wall and the roof and there are more appearing,” she said.

The LWO is calling for councils to be more consistent in their policies for houseboats to avoid postcode lotteries arising. Arnhem paid the dredging of the river bank in February from public funds, but in Renkum owners have been told that removing the clay from the riverbed is their own responsibility.

“They are paying the same rent but get much less value for money,” Broekmeulen said. “Legally the council are in the right, but if one council dredges and the other doesn’t, that leads to inequalities.”

Wild west situation

“That’s the wild west situation that we’re up against. We want it to be better regulated nationally for everyone who has to deal with low water levels.”

Owners also face problems when the river levels rise again, as exposed houses can become stuck to their bases, causing them to flood rather than float.

Gert Schols, shipping expert at insurance company EOC, said: “We advise houseboat owners not to go on holiday in periods of extreme drought or arrange a housesitter. You need to keep an eye on what’s happening when the water rises.”

Without action from the government, living on Dutch houseboats risks becoming unappealing in the long term as droughts become more frequent, Broekmeulen warned: “If your house is lying off centre for six months, you’re going to start thinking about moving into one that stands upright.”

World.title: End of a cycling empire? Bike maker Accell at risk of bankruptcy
World.content:
Accell, one of the Netherlands’ biggest bicycle groups, has been granted protection from its creditors to hold off the risk of bankruptcy.

The move will give the company court-approved breathing space to try to restructure its debts but leaves its future in doubt.

It is not yet clear how this will impact people with an Accell bike, or for the shops that sell and service them. Neither the company nor the courts have said anything about warranties, spare parts, or outstanding claims from the 2024 recall of tens of thousands of bikes, which were pulled from sale over cracking frames.

Accell owns some of the most well-known names in Dutch cycling – Batavus and Sparta city bikes, Koga touring bikes, and the Babboe and Carqon cargo brands – as well as Raleigh, Lapierre, and the German marques Haibike, Winora, and Ghost. It employs around 3,700 people in 15 countries.

Four difficult years

The company was publicly listed in Amsterdam until private equity group bought it for €1.56 billion in 2022.

It has struggled ever since the covid pandemic. Demand for bikes surged during the pandemic but parts were hard to get, and by the time supply chains recovered Accell was left with a mountain of unsold stock. Revenues fell 22% in 2024 to just over €1 billion.

A series of cutbacks followed: its warehouse network was reduced from 85 sites to 28, its Turkish factory was sold, and its Heerenveen plant closed last spring, ending its bicycle manufacturing in the Netherlands. Production moved to Hungary and France.

Earlier this year Accell struck a deal with its creditors, who took ownership of the company. That was always a stopgap, and a search for a new owner began. Accell said it held talks with several interested parties, assessed a number of bids, and sought regulatory approval for a possible merger, but no workable solution emerged.

World.title: Double Dutch victory blows Canadian Open tennis draw wide open
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The top two Dutch tennis players, Tallon Griekspoor and Botic van de Zandschulp, have both claimed major scalps in the second round of the Canadian Open.

Griekspoor, who turned 30 last month, put a wretched season behind him to knock out the world number three, top seed and French Open champion Alexander Zverev in three sets.

Zverev appeared to have overcome an early wobble when he rescued a set point before taking the first set on a tie-break.

But Griekspoor hit straight back to take a 4-0 lead in the second set, going on to win 6-2, before breaking the German twice in the decider to win 6-4.

“This is one of my most special wins,” Griekspoor said on court after the match. “There were times this year when I almost threw in the towel.”

Van de Zandschulp matched his achievement as he overcame blustery conditions to see off the Russian number four seed, Daniil Medvedev, in straight sets.

Multiple breaks

In an opening set that featured six breaks of serve, the 30-year-old Dutchman prevailed 6-3. The players broke each other twice in the second before Van de Zandschulp won the tie-break 7-5 with a sublime pass on his second match point.

“It was difficult for me and Daniil to play this evening and I’m happy that I got over the line in the end,” Van de Zandschulp said.

The results leave the draw wide open after world number one Jannik Sinner and 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic opted to sit out the tournament, while the number two player Carlos Alcaraz is recovering from a wrist injury.

Griekspoor will face the Italian Matteo Arnaldi, who knocked him out of this year’s French Open, in the round of 32, while Van de Zandschulp takes on Poland’s Hubert Hurkacz.

Both players are also likely to rise in the ATP rankings from their current positions of 69th for Griekspoor and 70th for Van de Zandschulp as a result of their wins.

World.title: Bol and De Bijenkorf warn customers of possible data leak
World.content:
Online retailer Bol and department store chain De Bijenkorf have emailed customers to warn that their personal details may have been exposed in a cyberattack on a logistics company both firms use.

Hackers may have gained access to systems at CEVA Logistics, which handles deliveries for both companies. Names, addresses, postcodes, and phone numbers are among the details that may have been taken, broadcaster NOS reported.

Bol said its own systems were not affected and that the incident involves orders from a single distribution centre. Neither company has said how many customers may be affected, and De Bijenkorf has commissioned an external investigation into the breach.

Bol said there is no indication that payment details, passwords, or login credentials were affected and has taken part of its range offline – products handled by the logistics company – cancelled some orders, and stopped exchanging data with the firm as a precaution.

De Bijenkorf blocked access to the systems involved and added further security measures. It says customers may face delays to orders, returns, and refunds, and that email addresses and product information may also have been taken. The chain said it was certain no bank account numbers or passwords had been exposed.

CEVA told Bol about the possible breach on August 1 and the Dutch data protection authority AP was informed on August 3, but customers were only emailed on Wednesday.

A Bol spokesperson told NOS the company wanted to establish first what had happened and who was affected, rather than contacting people repeatedly.

Poland’s top administrative court has upheld a decision by the finance ministry to withhold state subsidies from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party due to campaign finance irregularities. The decision was welcomed by the government, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying that there will be “no money for grifters”. PiS, however, argues that the money is being withheld for political reasons and accuses the authorities of “Russian standards”. Naczelny Sąd Administracyjny oddalił w środę kasacje ws. dotacji i subwencji dla PiS. – Miażdżący dla PiS wyrok podtrzymany! – stwierdził szef MF Andrzej Domański https://t.co/bcL18WbiYf — OKO.press (@oko_press) August 6, 2026 The dispute dates back to August 2024, when the National Electoral Commission (PKW) rejected PiS’s financial report for the previous year’s parliamentary election campaign after identifying around 3.6 million zloty (€838,000) in unauthorised expenditure. As a result, the PKW ordered that PiS should lose 10.8 million zloty from the state subsidies that political parties in Poland receive based on their level of electoral support. The party would normally have received 25.9 million zloty based on its 2023 election result. The decision triggered months of legal wrangling, with PiS arguing that the funding should be restored after the Supreme Court upheld its complaint against the PKW’s decision. However, finance minister Andrzej Domański refused to release the money, saying there were unresolved legal doubts over the ruling. The finance minister has refused to comply with the electoral commission's decision to pay out subsidies to the opposition PiS party He says there are "legal doubts" over the issue. But PiS says he is obliged to pay and will be held criminally responsible https://t.co/ZwIZRqn5tp — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 9, 2025 Those doubts stem from a broader dispute over the controversial and contested judicial reforms implemented by PiS when it ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023. The chamber of the Supreme Court that ruled in PiS’s favour was created as part of those reforms. It has previously been found to not be a legitimate body by both the European Court of Justice and European Court of Human Rights because it contains improperly appointed judges. After the Supreme Court chamber’s ruling, the PKW initially said it would not recognise the decision until the chamber’s legal status was clarified. Two weeks later, however, it reversed that decision and approved PiS’s financial report. Domański still declined to restore the subsidy, arguing that the PKW’s resolution was internally contradictory. While it approved the payments, it also stated that the chamber’s ruling should come from a body recognised as a court and that it was not determining whether the chamber met that standard. PiS challenged Domański’s decision. However, its case was initially rejected by a lower court in June last year, and that decision has now been upheld by the Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), which is the final court of appeal for administrative issues. The NSA found the minister had acted lawfully in withholding the funding. It also said the Supreme Court chamber’s ruling had no legal effect because it had been issued by a body that was not a properly constituted court, reports news website OKO.press. The ruling was welcomed by Domański, who called it a “crushing blow to PiS” and said that “yet another PiS lie has been exposed”. After a ten-year-long investigation, prosecutors have concluded that Poland’s government in 2010 – which was led by current Prime Minister Donald Tusk – was not guilty of “diplomatic treason” in its response to the plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczyński. The national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party – which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023 and is led by Lech’s twin brother, Jarosław – has always rejected the findings of official Polish and Russian investigations into the crash, which found it to have been an accident. Instead, PiS claims that the disaster, which claimed the lives of 96 people, many of them senior Polish state officials, was caused deliberately by Russia and then covered up with the help of Tusk’s government. However, while PiS launched various investigations during its time in power, it has never substantiated its claims. And prosecutors now say that there is no evidence that diplomatic treason, a crime that carries a potential prison sentence of up to ten years, took place. Teraz potwierdzenie @PK_GOV_PL: nie było żadnej zdrady dyplomatycznej ani żadnej intencji jej popełnienia. Oczywiście żaden z kłamców… https://t.co/VKZHlF5xkX — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) August 5, 2026 Wednesday’s announcement by the National Prosecutor’s Office was welcomed by Radosław Sikorski, the current foreign minister, who held the same role in 2010. He condemned the “Smolensk liars”, such as Jarosław Kaczyński, who he suggested had exploited the tragedy for their own benefit. “They brainwashed millions of people, divided families, stirred up hatred within the nation,” he wrote. “They’ll burn in hell for it. But the power, money and satisfaction they gained from spitting on their rivals – that’s theirs.” The idea that Smolensk was an assassination of Lech Kaczyński has been a core part of PiS rhetoric. In 2022, for example, Jarosław Kaczyński said that the decision was made “at the highest level of the Kremlin” and Tusk’s government then “covered up” the incident as part of a “macabre reconciliation with Russia”. Smolensk was an “attack decided at the highest level of the Kremlin”, says Jarosław Kaczyński ahead of the 12th anniversary of the crash. Donald Tusk's government then “covered up” the incident as part of a “macabre reconciliation with Russia”, he adds https://t.co/5ae0gHJj3B — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 4, 2022 The investigation into diplomatic treason – a crime consisting of acting to the detriment of Poland while authorised to represent the country in relations with foreign states or organisations – was launched in August 2016, less than a year after PiS had come to power. Among the individuals who had formally notified prosecutors of a potential crime was PiS deputy leader Antoni Macierewicz, who from 2015 to 2018 served as defence minister. He has been the foremost proponent of conspiracy theories around the Smolensk air disaster. In their notifications to prosecutors, Macierewicz and the others accused Tusk and other officials of, in their relations with Russia, deliberately choosing a legal basis for an investigation into the crash that was unfavourable to Poland by giving it no real influence over how it was run. However, prosecutors now say that, after ten years in which they questioned 488 witnesses, gathered extensive documentation and requested legal assistance from several countries, they have “concluded that no crime of diplomatic treason was committed”. In a statement explaining the decision, the National Prosecutor’s Office said that the legal basis chosen for cooperating with Russia on an investigation – Annex 13 of the Convention on International Civil Aviation – was, in fact, “the most advantageous solution” for Poland. It ensured the participation of Polish representatives in the Russian-led investigation, including access to the wreckage and crash site. Other legal options would have offered no greater benefits and involved significant risks, concluded the Polish prosecutors. They acknowledged that Russia “subsequently failed to fulfil some of its obligations arising from the adopted procedure”, but said this should have no bearing on assessing the decisions that were previously made on setting up the investigation. The defence ministry will notify prosecutors of 41 suspected crimes linked to a commission established by the former PiS government to investigate the 2010 plane crash in Russia that killed President Lech Kaczyński https://t.co/aEAlmk9lDM — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 24, 2024 The prosecutors also found that, not only did Polish officials choose the best legal solution, but there was also “no evidence indicating that individuals authorised to act on behalf of Poland, including the prime minister and members of the Council of Ministers, acted with the intent to harm Poland”. Given that the crime of diplomatic treason requires intent, this finding further reinforced the decision to drop the investigation. However, the prosecutors note that their decision can still be appealed. At the time of writing, neither Kaczyński, Macierewicz, nor other senior PiS figures had commented on the prosecutors’ announcement. However, it is likely they will point to the fact that the current national prosecutor was appointed by Tusk’s government after it had removed the previous PiS-era incumbent in a legally questionable move. The Supreme Court has issued a ruling that effectively found that the government unlawfully replaced a senior prosecutor earlier this year However, the justice minister says the ruling has no legal force as it was issued by illegitimately appointed judges https://t.co/9fCE6d18uy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 27, 2024 In 2020, in a separate civil case, a court ordered Jarosław Kaczyński to apologise for accusing Sikorski of “diplomatic treason” in relation to the Smolensk crash. Two years later, after Kaczyński had refused to comply with the ruling and Sikorski published the apology himself, Kaczyński was ordered to pay the costs. In 2024, an investigation by Tusk’s government found that the PiS administration had wasted tens of millions of zloty on a commission, headed by Macierewicz, that was tasked with re-investigating the Smolensk disaster. It notified prosecutors of dozens of suspected crimes relating to the functioning of the commission. Macierewicz, however, accused the government of spreading “lies and disinformation” designed to “protect Putin”. Poland has urged the European Union to adopt tougher measures in response to the recent migration crisis in Spain’s African exclave of Ceuta, including making migrants who enter the bloc illegally ineligible for obtaining residence rights. During a special meeting of EU interior ministers on Tuesday, Poland shared its own experience of dealing with “weaponised” migration from Belarus, which prompted the Polish government last year to restrict the right to asylum for people who cross irregularly. 🔵 KOMUNIKAT | Polska przedstawiła swoje stanowisko ws. migracji na nadzwyczajnym posiedzeniu Rady JHA w sprawie ostatnich wydarzeń w Ceucie 🇵🇱🇪🇺 Wiceminister spraw wewnętrznych i administracji @MaciekDuszczyk wziął udział w odbywającym się we wtorek (4 sierpnia br.)… pic.twitter.com/glfyiu5ZW3 — MSWiA 🇵🇱 (@MSWiA_GOV_PL) August 4, 2026 Last week, tens of thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, most of them by swimming there from neighbouring Morocco. Dozens died while trying to cross. Among those who managed to enter Ceuta, Spain says that the vast majority have been returned to Morocco. The incident prompted expressions of concern from many European leaders, including calls to restrict Spain’s participation in the Schengen free movement zone (despite the fact that anyone leaving Ceuta for the European mainland is subject to identity checks). Among those to speak out was Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who on Friday called on Spain to “follow our example if Schengen is to survive”. Poland has tightened asylum laws, border procedures, and has built effective barriers on its border with Belarus, which is the eastern border of the EU. We have invested billions of euros and engaged thousands of soldiers, police officers and border guards. Spain must follow our… — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) July 31, 2026 That was a reference to Poland’s response to a crisis on its eastern border, where since 2021 Belarus has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross irregularly into the EU. Both Poland and the EU have accused Belarus and its ally Russia of deliberately “weaponising” migration in an attempt to destabilise European societies as part of Moscow and Minsk’s broader “hybrid threats” against the EU. Tusk noted that, in response, Poland has restricted the right to asylum, invested billions in strengthening physical and electronic barriers along the border, and has deployed thousands of soldiers, police officers and border guards there (who have also been given expanded rights to use firearms). A court has ruled that Poland's recently introduced partial suspension of the right to asylum is justified and lawful. It rejected a complaint by a Sudanese man who had been denied the right to claim asylum after crossing irregularly from Belarus https://t.co/jx3s1AxRgG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 10, 2025 On Saturday, Tusk and 21 other EU leaders jointly signed a letter expressing “serious concern” at the situation in Ceuta and warning that the EU “cannot allow uncontrolled mass border crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration, or other hybrid threats to create the impression that illegal entry…is possible”. While they welcomed Spain’s cooperation with Morocco to send most of the migrants back, they also called for an extraordinary meeting of EU interior ministers to “agree on a coordinated European response, including the rapid mobilisation of available EU instruments and the necessary support to Spain”. At that meeting, which took place on Tuesday, Poland’s interior ministry said that it had expressed the view that “illegal entry into the European Union should automatically exclude the possibility of obtaining residence permits, and therefore the possibility of permanent stay in the future”. While Poland’s statement did not mention it directly, earlier this year Spain’s government launched an amnesty that allowed undocumented migrants to apply to legalise their stay in the country. Over one million people had signed up for the scheme by the time it closed at the end of June. In its statement, Poland’s interior ministry warned that “migration must be fully controlled”, as otherwise it can “be used against the values that guide the EU”. It also called for the “official recognition of migration as a challenge directly linked to security”. It added that during Tuesday’s meeting it had “presented its own experiences with border protection in the context of the instrumentalisation and weaponisation of migration and adapting law to migration challenges”, including restrictions on asylum claims. “The example of Ceuta clearly demonstrates that absolute access to asylum is impossible to maintain in the face of such real threats,” wrote the interior ministry, which said that it “welcomed the shared perspective on migration among a growing number of member states”. In a statement of its own, the European Council noted that there had been a “common understanding of the need to continue relentlessly fighting migrant smuggling networks, to reinforce returns, to strengthen EU borders, to build deep partnerships with third countries, and to improve foresight.” It added that member states “were united in expressing strong solidarity with Spain”, appreciated its “swift and effective efforts” to deal with the crisis, and had also expressed their condolences for the people who died while attempting to cross from Morocco to Ceuta. Despite efforts to discourage and prevent crossings, the figures remained high, with just under 30,000 attempted crossings recorded in each of 2024 and 2025. However, those figures have fallen dramatically this year, with only 235 attempted crossings recorded in the first half of 2026. Meanwhile, the estimated number of successful crossings has been falling, from 12,000 in 2023, to 5,000 in 2024, 1,700 in 2025, and zero in the first half of this year, according to the Polish interior ministry. Last August, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visited Poland’s border with Belarus, where she thanked the Polish authorities for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” orchestrated by Belarus and Russia. World.title: Unexploded WWII ordnance discovered under busy Warsaw street
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Part of central Warsaw was shut down today after unexploded ordnance from World War Two was found buried under a major road during construction work. The discovery, which came just days after the city commemorated the anniversary of its wartime uprising against Nazi-German occupation, led to traffic being diverted and residents being warned to stay away from their windows and avoid going outside while bomb disposal experts worked to safely remove the item. W Al. Solidarności znaleziono niewybuch, najprawdopodobniej z czasów II wojny światowej. ℹ️ Czytaj więcej: https://t.co/Fv6oe84XiM pic.twitter.com/BfjQPZveYZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 4, 2026 The object, reportedly around 70 centimetres long, was found early on Tuesday morning on Solidarity Avenue, a major thoroughfare, during modernisation work on tram lines. “We were digging a trench and I literally just touched it with the tip [of my digger],” the operator of the excavator who found it told broadcaster TVN. Staff working at the site were immediately evacuated to a safe distance. Police later confirmed that the item is unexploded ordnance, and that initial findings indicate it dates from World War Two. Bomb disposal experts arrived at the scene in the afternoon. However, they have not confirmed precisely what type of ordnance was discovered or its origin, reports Polsat News. Warsaw was the site of major fighting during World War Two, beginning in 1939, when Nazi Germany invaded and occupied Poland. In 1943, the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, the largest single act of Jewish resistance during the war, took place. On 1 August 1944, the Polish underground Home Army launched the Warsaw Uprising, which was the largest single act of armed resistance anywhere in German-occupied Europe during the war. In response, the Germans destroyed much of the city, around 85% of which lay in ruins by 1945. Warsaw’s historic Old Town was meticulously rebuilt after the war. But many other parts of the city were redeveloped by the newly installed communist authorities, including Solidarity Avenue (which during the communist era was named after Polish-Soviet Red Army General Karol Świerczewski). Thousands of vehicles drove over the unexploded ordnance every day for decades. “Warsaw is marked by history, and there are many such surprises,” Witold Urbanowicz, spokesman for the city’s tram operator, told news website Interia. After the fall of the Warsaw Uprising – which began 80 years ago today – the German occupiers expelled the city's entire population. However, some survivors decided to remain among the ruins. They became known as "Robinson Crusoes" and this is their story https://t.co/UuVbfbcpQ4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 1, 2024 Unexploded ordnance is regularly found in Poland. In May this year, around 200 anti-personnel mines dating from World War Two were discovered at the construction site of a student dormitory at Kraków’s Jagiellonian University. In October last year, two men were hospitalised after an artillery shell that one of them had brought home from a forest exploded in his apartment while the pair were under the influence of alcohol. Earlier that year, wild boars unearthed 21 mortar shells buried in a forest since the war. In 2023, 72 unexploded artillery shells were discovered during renovation work at a primary school and four pieces of World War Two ordnance were found in the walls of a church undergoing renovation. Wild boars dug up 21 mortar shells from World War Two that had been buried in a Polish forest. The unexploded ordnance has now been safely removed without harm to either the animals or humans https://t.co/W9kaPr1BNw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers.
