Police road blitz launched after young woman's death in SA

South Australia Police is launching a state-wide road safety operation after a young woman was killed and another left fighting for life following a crash at Hallett Cove.

World.title: AFL LIVE: Bulldog boilover: Roos lift in Marvel Stadium stunner; Libba’s telling concussion comments
World.content:
Bulldogs veteran Tom Liberatore has spoken about his battles with concussion on a day when head injuries and player care have been firmly front of mind.

Liberatore told Seven that any talks about his playing future are on hold until the end of the season as he aimed to finish the year healthy and without any more head injuries.

“My main priority is to make sure I don’t have any more,” Liberatore told Seven pre-game.

When asked if he was likely to be still playing next season, this was Liberatore’s answer:

“That’s the discussion after that [he finishes the season healthy].

“The main priority is my health and safety, making sure I look after my future after footy. [I’ll] prioritise that and we’ll go from there.”

World.title: Grand finalists really do face a baptism of fire
World.content:
George Zivkovic of Northmead reckons “talk of the NRL having to move the 2028 NRL Grand Final because of Pope Leo’s visit to Sydney on the October long weekend ignores the possibility of including the pontiff in the bunker for a truly impartial perspective.”

Before we submerge this debate, here’s Col Burns of Lugarno: “Our national underwater hockey team (C8) deserves a catchy, alliterative name that irreverently embodies both reaching the top of one’s game and having a reputation for aquatic invincibility. I’ve left the porch light on for the Harold Holt Hockeyroos.”

It was happy days for Hong Kong resident Richard Cunningham when he realised our quiz compilers get some material from their own backyard: “My first order of business of each day is the Herald Superquiz (I save C8 for lunchtime diversion). While I’m still chasing the elusive perfect 30 score, I have to thank you for providing me with the knowledge to score five of my points on Wednesday’s quiz. Had the questions not seemingly been directly scraped from recent C8 items, I would’ve otherwise been clueless about meatball recipes and underwater team names.”

Crossing certain borders will always cause a scene. Graham Russell of Clovelly recalls that “during our two-person road trip around Europe in April 1971, my colleague and I drove from Spain to Morocco via Ceuta. I was accepted with a smile, but my colleague was rejected because his hair was too long. He had to drive from Ceuta back to a village twenty kilometres away for a haircut. It was a dreadful haircut, but Ceuta accepted him.”

Mary Carde of Parrearra (Qld) finds that some inventions leave her cold: “I’ve been wondering, has there been a more spectacularly pointless invention to date than the single bottle electric wine chiller that was trendy in the early 2000s, and which was about as useful as a solar-powered torch in a cave?”

World.title: ‘The pressure is on Australia’: Eddie Jones fires a shot at the Wallabies. Sort of
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby ‘The pressure is on Australia’: Eddie Jones fires a shot at the Wallabies. Sort of Iain Payten August 6, 2026 — 9:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

He came, he zoomed, he logged off. So went a brief, and only mildly spicy, pre-game press conference from Eddie Jones on Thursday night, as his Japan side prepares to meet the Wallabies on Saturday in Osaka. Eddie Jones at Japan training. Getty Images The anticipation of some verbal fireworks from Jones was only natural. Here is a man who has, over the course of his long career, made an art of dropping a well-placed barb or pressurising critique of a green rival. Sometimes, as it unfolded near the end days of his ill-fated 2023 Wallabies return, those barbs were even aimed straight back at the scribes asking the questions, along with instructions to apply some self-inflicted upper cuts.



Jones departed the Wallabies soon after and landed back in Japan. Almost three years on, Australia are in Osaka to meet his Brave Blossoms. It is not the first meeting - Jones’ side lost to the Wallabies in Tokyo last year - but with residual tension still in the air, a new Wallabies coach and Japan an ever-improving side, the clash on Saturday still carries just as much meaning. And so it came to pass that Jones was sitting at a desk in the Japan team hotel on Thursday night, doing a press conference after naming his side to meet the Wallabies. For reasons not explained, the conference was not in person, but rather conducted on Zoom. A handful of Australian journalists sat dotted amid a group of around 40 Japanese entrants. Japan coach Eddie Jones looks on during a session. Getty Images The fireworks would have to be virtual. “It’s another test match for us to grow and learn and compete against the team in the top eight in the world,” Jones said. “You know, our record against Australia, there’s been seven official Test matches, we don’t have a win yet, so it’s a fantastic opportunity for Japan to create new history.



“And we saw last year that we were getting closer to Australia, and believe that gap, if there’s a gap now, is going to be minimised again on the weekend.” So far, so diplomatic. Jones was asked about the make-up of his team, which surprisingly didn’t contain former Reds big man Harry Hockings in the starting side. Wallabies coach Les Kiss had, just hours earlier, said they’d identified Hockings and captain Warner Dearns as the major threats for Japan. Jones had moved another Aussie, Jack Cornelsen, into the second row to pick Kanji Shimokawa, a mobile backrower tasked with shutting down Fraser McReight. “This is the best 23 and we’ve got the highest confidence that they can do the job for Japan on the weekend at Osaka,” he said. Eddie Jones resigned as Wallabies coach after failing to make it out of the World Cup group stage in 2023. Getty



“The team’s prepared really well. I think we probably had one of our best preparation periods, and we feel like we’re ready to go after Australia. You know, there’s a lot of pressure on Australia.” Here we go. “They got a very experienced team,” Jones continued. “It’s a game that they’d be expected to win. So we want to make sure we’re putting pressure on them right from the start.” Before Kiss, Jones was the last Australian coach to take over mid-season, when he replaced Rod Macqueen in 2001. Did he sense that handover could provide the cracks required for Japan to get that win over Australia? “Les and Joe have had a pretty close relationship going back to when Les was in Ireland, so their thinking would be the same,” Jones said. ”



Eddie Jones talks to Les Kiss in 2019 when the pair were coaching in England. nna\sworthington “There’ll be little nuances they change, but I think it’ll be a reasonably easy transition given also that Les coached the Reds and a number of the players he selected have come from the Reds team. “I see that being a fairly seamless transition. Look, we’re more interested in ourselves than Australia. You know, we believe it’s a team that can beat Australia. And Australia’s got a very experienced team. “If you look at a number of those players, they were young players back in the 2023 World Cup, now they have 50 or 60 caps next to their name. “So they’re coming into their prime stage of their careers. So we’re going to have to be at our best, and we’re prepared to be at our best, so we’re really looking forward to getting the chance to make history.”



Just seven players in the Wallabies 23-man squad were at the 2023 Rugby World Cup, and the trio who now have more than 50 caps - Tate McDermott, Rob Valetini and Taniela Tupou - were 24, 25 and 27 in 2023. Related Article Australian rugby The 310 seconds of All Blacks defence that should give Wallabies fans hope But never mind that. Back to the fireworks. Jones was asked if the heatwave conditions in Japan at the moment could be to his side’s advantage over the Wallabies. “Well, I’ve never gone to France at Stade de France and they put on the heaters for you, have you?” he asked.



No Eddie. “That’s Test match rugby, you know? You go home and away, and you play in the conditions.” And then - 18 minutes into a 30-minute press conference - thanks were offered and the screen went blank. Jones had gone, the Zoom was over and those fireworks had failed to truly pop or crackle. Oh well. There is always game day. World.title: Cheika comeback firms as possibility after Foley and Phipps return to Tahs
World.content:
Two of the heroes of the Waratahs’ only premiership season were unveiled as the club’s new signings on Thursday, and a shock comeback by 2014 coach Michael Cheika could be on the cards as well. As revealed by this masthead last month, Bernard Foley and Nick Phipps will suit up for the Waratahs again after signing one-year deals. Bernard Foley and Nick Phipps are back at the Waratahs. Sam Mooy The coach who recruited them, Dan McKellar, is now gone, having resigned in June. But in an intriguing twist, former NSW and Wallabies coach Cheika has this week firmed as an option to also return to the club he led to its only Super Rugby title.



Cheika is currently an assistant coach at the Roosters, but after missing out on the head coach vacancy at the Dragons recently, the decorated coach is eyeing a probable return to the 15-man game. He said last month he’d not heard from the Waratahs, or their owners, Rugby Australia, about the NSW vacancy, but after lobbying from senior Waratahs players, RA officials have come to appreciate the massive impact of a Cheika return to the Tahs and are now exploring how it could work, according to informed sources. If Cheika returns, another 2014 Waratah and current California Legion coach Stephen Hoiles would likely be involved in the coaching team. “It’s hard to get a hold of the great man [Cheika],” Phipps said. “I do know there’s been lots of really quality candidates who put their name forward [for the NSW job]. Michael Cheika and Michael Hooper celebrate victory over the Crusaders in the Super Rugby decider in 2014. Could Cheika return to lead NSW again? Getty Images



“Like it or not, the Waratahs is probably one of the jewels in the crown of the [Super Rugby] competition; you want to think that lots of players and coaches would want to be a part of it ... “Obviously, it’s disappointing not to go the full way with Dan [McKellar], but I’m certain that whoever comes in next will be great for the squad. “It’ll be good for the guys in there training this week [to know who the coach will be], and there’s a little bit of uncertainty about how it’s all going and what the future and the scheduling leading forward will be with everything going on. “It’d be good to put that to bed early and then let them start to impress coaches and get ready for the next season.” Phipps and Foley were originally sold the dream of returning to the Waratahs for one last dance by McKellar, before an end-of-season review by Rugby Australia sealed the coach’s fate.



McKellar joined the club in 2024 on a three-year deal, but was unable to see out the final season of his contract. Foley believes the Waratahs’ recent lack of success – two finals appearances, in 2022 and 2023, since 2018 – is partly due to the turnover of coaches. “It hasn’t been from a lack of effort, and you know as an outsider you are never really privy to what happens within the walls of this place,” he said. “But I’ll tell you one thing that hasn’t helped is the changeover of coaches and environments. Michael Cheika and Bernard Foley at the Waratahs in 2015. Getty Images “That doesn’t help anyone involved; it doesn’t set you up for success and there’s no longevity in what they’re trying to do. So the amount of change and disruption I’m sure has caused a lot of heartache for a lot of guys and, hopefully, they can set this place up for a long time with sustained success.”



Neither Phipps nor Foley would be drawn on naming their preferred candidate, but Foley did describe the character both veterans want from the Waratahs’ next coach. “A guy who’s going to drive a good standard, but also empower the players to really be themselves to bring their flair each and every day, on and off the field,” Foley said. “We want this to be a place where everyone wants to come to work, everyone wants to turn up and work hard for each other, and be able to express themselves and feel included and enjoy the environment, so yeah it’s just finding a coach that can deliver all those things.” Related Article Australian rugby The 310 seconds of All Blacks defence that should give Wallabies fans hope Foley is also excited to get to work with the NSW backline and is keeping a close eye on Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, who will start for the Wallabies this Saturday in Japan. The five-eighth believes outside centre is Suaalii’s best position, and it is his job to get him the ball as much as possible.



“I’d just love to free him up,” Foley said. “He could be interchangeable ... I’d probably persist with him at 13. “But it’s going to be the nature of the backline and the other players who are available already. But I also don’t think that if you’ve got [jersey] 13 you always have to be in that position. You can start to evolve his game and evolve the backline in that regard.” Foley last played for the Wallabies in November 2022 against Ireland and is keen to compete for a spot at the 2027 World Cup in Australia once he has established himself at the Waratahs. “I’d be lying if I said it’s not on the radar ... a couple of months ago I was retiring [from rugby] and looking at that, so there’s a lot of work to be done, get through a pre-season, get through a Super season and then try and think whether you can do a home World Cup,” Foley said. “There’s not that many players in front of you [at the Wallabies] if you can go and have a good season. I haven’t spoken to anyone involved at the Wallabies, and I’m not really looking at it at the moment, but if I can get the body right and get myself into a good position and have a good Super season, then I might consider it.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Two sides of the coin on government priorities
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Two sides of the coin on government priorities August 6, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Political life’s a gamble. To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. In contrast to the government’s refusal to prioritise public good over private profit when it comes to gambling and gas, Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen’s insistence that data centres invest in renewable energy and pay the price is a welcome display of political fortitude (″⁣Bowen lays down the law to states on data centres″⁣, 6/8). Just as welcome is the agreement expressed by Belinda Dennett, chief executive of Data Centres Australia.

On the other hand, the refusal of the Queensland and Northern Territory governments to give their consent is as predictable as it is disappointing.

The issue that appears not to have been addressed in the debate is the data centres’ immense thirst for cooling water. The supply of clean renewable energy can be planned for and achieved.

How to provide water at scale in Australia’s arid, drought-prone land is a question that is crying out for an answer.

Tom Knowles, Parkville Now, to examine the ‘whales’ of pollution

Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen describes data centres as energy consumption ″⁣whales” predicted to use 10 per cent of the national grid’s electricity by 2050. It’s timely for Bowen to use federal powers to ensure these “whales” pull their weight: that they offset their electricity use with investments in wind and solar energy and storage.

This is good policy that works towards “Australian households and Australian energy reliability being put first”. Surely, the next step for fairness for Australian households is to ensure the “whales” of pollution – our oil and gas companies – pay for the climate consequences of their pollution. It’s only fair that they should pay for the fire, flood and wild weather damage that oil and gas

pollution create.

Karen Campbell, Geelong Labor, do the right thing on gambling

The government’s timid response to gambling reform (“Coalition, Greens force PM to rethink gambling reforms”, 6/8) is presumably explained by lobbying efforts from the gambling and connected industries, highlighting potential job losses. While many people “gamble responsibly”, many do not. The industry needs to be reined in, with advertising restrictions or banning a “no brainer” first step. If jobs are lost because the growth of this industry is curtailed (there is no guarantee that limiting advertising will achieve this), then so be it.

Big business never hesitates to make employees redundant if they can find more cost-effective options such as offshoring or AI. The government should stare down industry pressure and do what they did with the housing tax change legislation – the right thing.

Peter Thomson, Brunswick



Coming to grips with inflation

Australia’s inflation rate has been much higher in the past than it is now. During the 1970s and ’80s, the annual inflation rate was often above 10 per cent. However, governments at that time did not feel the need to offer cost-of-living support in the form of the ″⁣baubles and charms″⁣ dangled in front of the public in the way the federal government and increasingly state governments do now.

As columnist Peter Hartcher suggests (Comment, 1/8), governments now seem fixated on addressing the symptoms of inflation, the so-called cost-of-living crisis, rather than its cause. They don’t want to think about the cause because that would mean government admitting it is, at least partly, responsible for inflation.

No, it’s far easier for government to dangle another sparkly trinket and hope the public falls for it.

Rod Wise, Surrey Hills Cabal is treating Labor as a fool

I’m on board with your correspondent’s conspiracy theory (Letters, 6/8) that a global cabal of fossil-fuel companies is behind the rise of populist parties like One Nation. However, after reading columnist Caitlin Fitzsimmons’ excellent analysis, “Fuel tax rebates undermining climate action goals” (6/8), I can only conclude that same cabal is also supporting the Labor government.

Peter Cook, Essendon THE FORUM Has to be cut-off point

Any ode to the beauty and health benefits of trees always generates correspondence advocating for governments and councils to enforce tree preservation at all costs (″⁣Not too late to provide statewide tree measures″⁣, 4/8).

My perspective urges more consideration for the private home owners’ situation. I have more than 20 trees on my suburban block, most planted by us. However, it has been a pre-existing planting of a Himalayan cedar dominating the front garden close to the house that has proved problematic. Its massive size towers over our heritage home, many limbs have dropped, bringing down power lines on numerous occasions, and risks of further falls prevent any activity under canopy stretching the width of property. Regular reduction via pruning is very costly.

State and local governments need to introduce the criteria enabling removal in exceptional circumstances where the species of trees has outgrown its position in an urban residential garden.

Diana Yallop, Surrey Hills Channelled message

Your correspondent (Letters, 5/8) offers three good and pragmatic reasons not to ignore One Nation in political reporting.

But it is his final sentence that is the most cogent – the proposition that One Nation voters are unlikely to access the nominated media sources. The One Nation organisation seems to have hitched its wagon to the Murdoch organisation’s media – and its supporters’ views and outlook are likely to be influenced by the latter’s content.

Admirable as the letters are in The Age (concerning One Nation), they are messages to similar-minded Australians and not likely to reach those people who currently indicate a voter preference for One Nation.

Brian Kidd, Mt. Waverley



The easy option

It is quite right for One Nation to bar certain media outlets from its media conferences for their continuous asking about the party’s policies and candidates’ controversial views.

In her earlier years, such questions would draw from Pauline Hanson the response of “Please Explain”.

Much easier not to be embarrassed or have to explain at all.

Harry Kowalski, Ivanhoe Premise broken

It’s terrific to see opposition to the premise that all perpetrators of sexual offences need their identity protected for the good of their mental health (″⁣Psychiatrists cast doubt on court orders″⁣, 6/8).

Protecting the identity of perpetrators is often framed as concern for their partners and children, and of course, the victim. Learning that a partner, father or family member has raped someone must be horrifying, complicated and confusing, working through feelings of disbelief, betrayal and grief. But protecting perpetrators is about just that: protecting them, their reputation and their social capital. Their ″⁣concern″⁣ for their family (or the victim) was not front of mind when they committed the crime. They were thinking only about their immediate wants and how they could get away with it.

Protecting perpetrators is about upholding the status quo, and this just leads to more of the same.

Christine Craik, Darraweit Guim Drop in the ocean

Caitlin Fitzsimmons captures Australia’s climate policy dilemma perfectly: we’re bailing out a boat with a teaspoon while pouring water in by the bucket (“Fuel tax rebates undermining climate action goals”, 6/8). The $8.8 billion in diesel subsidies paid to big polluters not only encourages more use of dirty fuel, but it far exceeds what is spent on cutting climate emissions via the Safeguard Mechanism.

And the sheer volume of coal and gas Australia exports easily outweighs the gains we make from installing solar panels and batteries at home. Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen often highlights Australia’s impressive uptake of solar, batteries and EVs, but until the Albanese government begins winding down coal and gas production, these improvements will remain a drop in the ocean.

Larni Dibben, Glen Iris Mystery deliveries

My Bolivian partner was surprised to read about her country’s lack of a functioning postal service in her city, La Paz (“Think the census is annoying? Try a 24-hour lockdown”, 6/8). She is now wondering how all the letters she wrote and received to and from family and friends were magically sent and delivered.

James O’Keefe, Prahran Sign of the times

I applaud the state government’s strategy for saving taxpayers’ dollars in the way it has addressed the “pothole” issue. Instead of wasting money on actually fixing the potholes, it now erects a sign that says, “Rough Surface Ahead.“But the state government has also come up with a new cost-cutting measure. Instead of wasting money on the sign, it simply spray-paints an orange arrow on the road where the pothole is. Marvellous. What will they think of next?

Robert Langworthy, Bayswater North



Take us home . . .

Your correspondent (Letters, 6/8) suggested bringing the Country Roads Board back. Yes, but ensure the board is composed entirely of engineers and ensure that its workload can be organised in the most efficient way, not one that prima facie requires work done by contractors.

Only engineers can ensure we get value for our money.

Laurie Comerford, Chelsea Catastrophes, then, now

Many think the world is in dire straits.

With the senseless Iran war and the Middle East erupting, the man-made climate catastrophes unfolding in Europe and the United States with record temperatures, droughts and fires, people enduring cost-of-living crises, political instability in many countries and populist demagogues on the rise, toxic social media’s extraordinary reach and the uncertain future the consequences of AI pose, the list is endless.

But do we catastrophise the present? Think of the world of the 1940s with Hitler jack-booting his way across Europe, murdering Jews, homosexuals, Jehovah Witnesses, the mad, disabled children and political prisoners and the whole world at war.

We have always lived with world conflict and uncertainty, but is it different in 2026? It is easy to think of the present as dire, but history teaches us that we have lived through many other catastrophes before and survived.

Sandy Jeffs, Christmas Hills Think it through

My dad used to remind me to ″⁣think things through″⁣ whenever I was about to make a momentous decision. The same advice needs to be given to those voters who believe One Nation is the answer to our country’s woes. Nothing could be further from the truth.

At this time of great volatility and uncertainty in the world, the last thing we need is a parliament containing new One Nation members pushing their own far-right barrows of political populism and division with not a positive, constructive idea among them.

Nick Toovey, Beaumaris A nation of migrants

It was a brave thing for Home Affairs Minister, Tony Burke, to defer his speech due yesterday on immigration to allow further internal consultation to more deeply consider flow-on effects (“Opponents circle Labor over delay to migration cut”, 6/8).

Labor intends to reduce migration by 75,000 over the next two years. They are sensible in getting the appropriate and workable numbers of migrants, and Chris Bowen says we need to consider demand for workers.

Migrants have traditionally been small business owners as well as providing labour. They have built infrastructure and enhanced our cultural diversity.

Humanitarian considerations also must play a part in our migrant intake.

Labor must avoid being pushed into actions by the attitude of One Nation and the baying of Liberal politicians for speed in this matter. Government must consider the rights of all constituents, not just the vocal ones.

We are a nation of migrants and multiculturalism, and we should remember and celebrate this.

Jan Marshall, Brighton Need for more rooms

The latest figures from the Coroners Court of Victoria show fatal overdoses in Geelong have increased by 25 per cent compared with the previous year, renewing calls for a medically supervised injecting room.

The evidence from North Richmond is compelling. This service has prevented overdose deaths, reduced public injecting and enabled immediate medical care during overdoses.

Beyond crisis intervention, it provides access to mental health care, housing support and pathways into drug treatment for people who might otherwise never engage with these services.

If we accept the evidence that medically supervised injecting rooms save lives and improve public amenity, why are they confined to so few locations?

Surely, a proven, life-saving health service should be available wherever the need exists, not just in one suburb.

When the evidence is this strong, expanding access to a safe injecting room should be a matter of public health, not politics.

Sue McNamara, Rye



The bankruptcy move

US President Donald Trump has built his commercial empire on never backing down or, when he had to, declaring business bankruptcy to clear the books.

Pity he can’t just pull the whole Iran thing and declare bankruptcy again.

Tom Stafford, Wheelers Hill Photo: Matt Golding AND ANOTHER THING Politics

If anyone has doubts about One Nation and its policies, the article, ″⁣Victorian pick a self-described conspiracy theorist″⁣ (5/8), about Warren Pickering should relegate the party to political oblivion .

Greg Bardin, Altona North What a thrill to have a conspiracy theorist as leader of the Victorian One Nation party. Just what we need. Jennifer Gerrand, Carlton North



Shaun Carney (Comment, 6/8) lauds the Prime Minister, Anthony Albanese, for his leadership. I confess that I am disappointed the PM is being so timid. I wish he would go further on taxation reform, gambling reform and other issues. I had hoped for so much more.

Juliet Flesch, Kew Furthermore

I can handle ″⁣learning″⁣ as a noun, as in ″⁣learning is fun″⁣. But ″⁣learnings″⁣, ″⁣understandings″⁣? No thanks. Lindsay Zoch, Mildura I mustn’t have been betting enough. I was only offered a blow-up doll and a packet of aspirin (″⁣Regulators struggle to curb surge of influencers advocating betting″⁣, 6/8).

Bryan Fraser, St Kilda West If all airlines enforced a strict and reasonable carry-on baggage rule, it would expedite the boarding process for everyone.

Tony Jackson, Fitzroy It is great that Jetstar is to charge up to $52 for passengers to put bags in overhead lockers. For too long, sensible passengers have suffered from those who bring suitcase-size bags on board, clutter the aisles and hog all the lockers.

Reg Murray, Glen Iris



If wholesale electricity prices are falling, Chris Bowen, why aren’t retail?

Ian Anderson, Surrey Hills President Donald Trump has said, again, that Iran and the United States are close to an agreement on the re-opening of the Strait

of Hormuz. Sure. I can’t understand why anyone listens to Trump any more or takes what he says seriously. Robyn Westwood, Heidelberg Heights Finally

Where do I vote for my favourite pothole?

Luise Mock, Tawonga South

World.title: Expansion of citizen's arrest powers to take effect within a week
World.content:
An amendment to the Crimes Act has passed its final reading in Parliament.

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith says the majority of the legislation will take effect within a week.

That includes an expansion to citizen's arrest powers, allowing members of the public to intervene in any Crimes Act offence at any time of day.

A person making an arrest would be allowed to use restraints "when reasonable," but is also required to contact police and follow their instructions.

The bill is intended to crack down on retail crime by allowing security guards to detain thieves.

"Retailers and security guards face abuse and assault that no New Zealander should be subjected to, and we know the economic cost of retail crime is in the billions," Goldsmith said in a statement.

The amendment also specifies a number of new, more specific offences, including for assaulting first responders and front-line corrections workers, and three new offences for "coward punches".

"Where others may flee, first responders and front-line corrections workers run towards danger to help those who need urgent assistance. Assaulting them puts multiple lives at risk, so there must be greater consequences for these terrible acts of violence," he said.

"We know how dangerous coward punches are. People can be killed or suffer lifelong brain injuries, yet perpetrators often receive lenient and insufficient sentences. That changes with this legislation."

Goldsmith said the amendment also strengthened trafficking and slavery laws to close loopholes.

Retailers react

A group representing retailers fears robbers might decide to arm up, as security guards and customers get more powers to carry out citizen's arrests.

But Carolyn Young from Retail NZ said it was not as straightforward as citizens being allowed to make an arrest to stop a crime.

"This may cause offenders to think, 'Ok, in an event that someone might try to stop me and get physical with me, instead of bringing knife, I'm going bring a gun or a butcher's knife or I might bring a machete'. It's just that arming up that we don't want to see in a retail environment."

Young said retailers needed more official direction about the new law.

World.title: NZ Warriors recall Luke Metcalf for crucial NRL clash against Penrith Panthers
World.content:
NRL: NZ Warriors v Penrith Panthers

Kickoff: 8pm Friday, 7 August

Go Media Stadium, Auckland

Live blog updates on RNZ

Departing NZ Warriors half Luke Metcalf has been recalled to the starting line-up for their crucial NRL home clash with Penrith Panthers on Friday.

Incumbent halfback Te Maire Martin, who left last week's win against the Gold Coast Titans early, apparently aggravated a hamstring injury at training this week and has been ruled out 24 hours from kickoff at Auckland's Go Media Stadium.

Metcalf, 27, enjoyed a breakout season in 2025, until he suffered a knee injury that ended his campaign and delayed his 2026 return.

Over the summer, he extended his contract with the club, but in his absence, Tanah Boyd consolidated his grip on the No.7 jersey and, uncertain of his future with the Warriors, Metcalf sought an early release and signed with St George-Illawarra Dragons for 2027.

Although Boyd also suffered a season-ending knee injury, Martin was promoted into the halfback position and has held it since Round 11, impressing with his form and also signing a contract extension for 2027.

Metcalf has played just two first-grade games this season - both losses - and tweaked a hamstring against Cronulla Sharks in April. Coach Andrew Webster has resisted calls to bring him back during a mid-season slump that saw four defeats over seven games.

Metcalf has turned out for the club reserves in NSW Cup and occupied a spot on the interchange bench, without being required to take the field.

World.title: Timeline to implement new school subjects 'unrealistic', teachers' union warns
World.content:
Industry leaders are enthusiastic about nine new secondary school subjects announced on Thursday, but the teachers' union warns the timeline to develop and introduce them is extremely tight.

The government says industry skills boards will develop the subjects for introduction in 2029, when a new qualification replaces the NCEA.

The subjects are:

Next-Gen manufacturing

Applied intelligent systems

Construction and built environment

Energy and infrastructure

Engineering technology

Food and fibre systems

Health services and care

Hospitality, food and beverage

Tourism

Education Minister Erica Stanford announced the subjects with Finance Minister Nicola Willis at Meridian Energy's Mākara windfarm, overlooking Cook Strait.

New proposed subjects may sway number of early leavers Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

She said it was critical that industry helped write the new content.

"They are the people on the ground who know what the skills and knowledge are that they will need for the future," she said. "That is being built into the curriculum, so these young people, when they leave school, will have relevant knowledge and skills to be able to.. walk into either jobs, further training, apprenticeships or through to university."

Stanford said the new subjects would vary less than NCEA subjects, and would better equip teens with skills and knowledge that employers wanted.

She said more industry-led subjects may be added.

Stanford said not all schools would be able to offer all nine subjects, and some might work together or with local trades academies to provide them.

Naenae College students Lydia Campbell, Daytona Falwasser, and Reagan Cronje said the subjects provided good opportunities for future generations, but were not sure they would study them. RNZ/John Gerritsen

"There will, of course, always be some in-school provision as well, and that's why we're working with the likes of the PPTA and the Teaching Council to make sure that we can get those people the pay that they require to be able to teach," she said.

Teachers' union vice-president Kieran Gainsford said the PPTA supported industry-led subjects, but there was a lot to work out before 2029.

"In some cases, schools are going to need very technical learning spaces or technical equipment," he said. "They're going to need specialist staff often from industry and those people are going to have to be recruited... and then we have to keep them in schools.

"There's a lot of work to happen between now and then, and unless we get the details pretty pronto, that timeline does start to look a little bit unrealistic."

Gainsford said who would teach the subjects was not clear.

"We're desperately keen to know exactly what the government's plan is for the delivery of these subjects, because until we see that, we can't get started on making it work for the kids," he said.

Gainsford said some of the subjects could be offered by schools and already were, but others, like applied intelligence systems, would require more teachers.

"There's going to have to be some additions to the teaching workforce to make those possible and that needs to happen really now," he said.

"We want those people in schools before we start teaching this stuff."

Energy and Infrastucture Industry Skills Board chief executive Philip Aldridge was enthusiastic about the new subjects. RNZ/John Gerritsen

Industry leaders at the launch were enthusiastic and said one of the main effects of the new subjects would be to open students' eyes to potential careers in industries they had never heard of, many of which faced serious workforce shortages in future.

Energy and Infrastucture Industry Skills Board chief executive Philip Aldridge said the energy and infrastructure subject would bring entirely new courses to schools.

"This is new," he said. "In my sector - energy and infrastructure - there's nothing at school.

"There's a bit of geology, a bit of physics, but really there's nothing about energy and infrastructure."

Aldridge said the board wanted to see the subject offered in all schools.

He said whether the subject would be taught in schools or in trades academies run by polytechnics or other tertiary providers was yet to be determined.

Some of the new subjects, such as tourism and building, already existed in some form in schools.

Construction and Specialist Trades industry skills board chair David Kelly said letting industry have a hand in what's taught would have several advantages over the current system.

Construction and Specialist Trades industry skills board chair David Kelly. RNZ/John Gerritsen

"One is it raises the status of some trades, so that it gives it equal status within the secondary schools," he said. "Secondly, it does give recognised skills across the country, so when students come out of secondary school, they've got something to show that is a nationally accepted standard that they've achieved.

"It will be more comprehensive and more linked-up, so it's connected to potential employment. At the moment, there are some good courses, but they're not consistent right across the country and really depend on the individual school."

Rotorua Girls High School principal Sarah Davis was seconded to the Education Ministry to work on the subjects.

She said the involvement of industry would ensure the subjects created real pathways to jobs.

Davis said some teachers already had industry qualifications and might be able to teach the new subjects.

World.title: Wellington City councillors vote yes on super-merger proposal
World.content:
Wellington city councillors have unanimously agreed to submit a super-merger proposal to the government this weekend.

Councillors expressed "preference" that Wairarapa be excluded, and for the Hutt Valley, Porirua, and Wellington City to merge. However, they ultimately voted to support a wider regional proposal if mayors agreed on that.

Regional mayors will decide on Friday on the exact model - which could see a Wellington-Wairarapa unitary council - merging 8 councils together.

A layer of community councils could represent the Hutt Valley, Wairarapa, Porirua, Wellington City and Kāpiti.

In an hours-long debate, Councillors discussed whether they should force Upper Hutt into a merged council, whether Wairarapa should be included, or if a referendum should be put to residents.

In the Wellington-Wairarapa region there are currently eight territorial authorities and one regional council. There are 106 elected members, 12 community boards, and 55 community board members in the region.

Councils divided as deadline looms

The backdrop of discussions was fraught before the meeting on Thursday, with councils across the region disagreeing on the model as the deadline for the proposal looms.

Porirua and Lower Hutt city councils, along with South Wairarapa, agreed on a Wellington-Wairarapa council, but Upper Hutt City Council wanted to remain separate.

Masterton and Carterton want to create their own Wairarapa Unitary council, while Kāpiti wanted to remain either its own council or join with Horowhenua.

Mayor Andrew Little said the proposal being considered was "far from perfect", but it was the best the council could do given the rushed timeframe.

The decision was about future generations, he said. Wellington region had been "anemic" economically for some time, and was woefully under-prepared for climate change, he added.

It needed a bigger platform to advocate for itself, he said.

"Put aside Head Start, put aside the dodgy process, can we seriously address those challenges under the status quo?" My view is not."

Councillor Diane Calvert put forward an amendment signalling that councillors wanted four Wellington metro councils to merge, with Wairarapa excluded and forming its own council instead.

She said a survey of Wellington city residents had shown a majority did not want to join with Wairarapa.

Councillor Tony Randle RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Councillor Tony Randle agreed.

He said the Greater Wellington Regional Council was spending $30 million a year more in Wairarapa than it received in revenue from the area - and Wellington city ratepayers were subsidising services.

"What's been missing from this whole thing is the justification, of why Wellington city residents should be funding people who choose to not live in Wellington, but who actually live in far cheaper housing, far far away, and who pay much lower rates."

Little disagreed, arguing that Wairarapa and Wellington were "wholly integrated regions - not just 'rural folks' versus 'urban folks'".

He said excluding Wairarapa would increase transport costs for those residents and have a direct effect on the labour market.

Environmental regulations and management, currently carried out through the regional council, would suffer - to the detriment of the region.

Councillor Jonny Osbourne put forward an amendment - which passed - to seek advice from officials on a possible referendum later on the issue later in the year. It was indicated that central government would not support that.

Porirua and Lower Hutt had already done this, he said.

"If Wellingtonians are not given the same opportunity via a referendum, lingering discord with any significant reform with the way we govern ourselves will exacerbate divisions which naturally occur in communities, but are occurring unfortunately more and more."

That passed, with councillors discussing whether the process had been democratic at all.

What about Upper Hutt?

Councillor Geordie Rogers submitted an amendment that other councils shouldn't be coerced into a merger councillors had voted against.

The comments came after Upper Hutt City Council voted against any amalgamation plans, and mayor Peri Zee said that the city shouldn't be forced into a merger against its will.

Rogers said he was doing this in the interests of Wellington city residents, saying the disagreements between councils could lead to "bad consequences".

The amendment, however, failed.

Upper Hutt mayor urging Wellington councils not to force amalgamation Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Randle conceded four councils didn't want the plan, likening the arrangement to a "shotgun marriage".

"I don't think those marriages really work out," Randle added.

But he ultimately decided not to support the amendment, on the basis that Upper Hutt was part of the region's catchment areas and economy.

What do iwi representatives think?

Kara Puketapu-Dentice presented a letter on behalf of iwi leaders across the region, which urged councillors to think of future generations.

This was not a "restructure of councils", he said, but a chance to build something new.

"The decisions in front of us are mokopuna decisions.

"The people who will live longest inside what we choose are not yet in any of our rooms, and they will not ask which council held which preference in 2026," the letter said.

Kara Puketapu-Dentice RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Councillor Matthew Reweti, representing the Māori Ward, said the Local Government Act and the Head Start process required discussions with iwi.

He said any future model must retain Māori representation.

In Wellington, 68 percent voted to retain the Māori ward, and Porirua, Lower Hutt, Kāpiti, Masterton and South Wairarapa also voted to retain the wards, Reweti said.

"The iwi leaders have come together...and they have asked councils to pursue the Head Start pathway, rather than default to the government's back stop process."

[h] What happens now?

On Friday, mayors will meet to work out the proposal which will go to ministers.

Speaking after the meeting, Little said he was confident an agreement on an amalgamation model could be reached.

World.title: Performance measures linked to reducing emergency housing numbers dropped
World.content:
Highly criticised performance measures linked to reducing the number of people in emergency housing have been dropped by the Ministry of Social Development.

The government had come under intense pressure from the opposition and housing providers in recent months following revelations senior managers at the ministry (MSD) had performance agreements related to reducing emergency housing numbers.

Regional leaders for the ministry have been told, now the emergency housing reduction target was met, the expectation was that they shift their focus to achieving "sustainable housing for people currently in emergency housing and offering other support for those who are not eligible."

But the emergency housing target had already been met before the performance measures were specified last year.

It was revealed in June MSD managers could be pulled into line if they were not contributing to the reduction of people living in emergency housing - something the minister in charge, Tama Potaka, said was a matter for the ministry leadership and not him.

But the MSD boss had defended linking staff performance with cutting emergency housing numbers, saying it's executing the government's policy.

The coalition set a target to reduce the number of households in emergency housing by 75 percent by the end of 2029 - which was achieved early last year - and introduced rules making emergency housing harder to get into, and harder to stay in.

On Thursday, MSD sent out the latest performance letters for the new financial year to regional leadership.

Group general manager for service delivery Graham Allpress said MSD was asking regional leaders to strengthen their focus on helping people secure stable housing after they leave emergency housing.

Allpress also said he expected the number of households in emergency housing to remain "broadly stable over the coming year."

"There are no goals in the letters for regions to reduce the number of households in emergency housing."

Last year, "housing services effectiveness" was a performance measure, with a number of supporting indicators for the overarching emergency housing reduction focus.

This year, the housing monitors performance measure and supporting indicators were now regarding the overarching "sustainable housing support" focus.

The government's emergency housing target was to be maintained, but there were now measures around achieving a target of initial appointments, early intervention and public housing assessment for those in emergency housing.

Five priority areas were also outlined in the correspondence, including consistency of service, accuracy, employment outcomes, effective management of contracted services, and housing support.

These differ slightly from the previous year's letter: effective and efficient commissioning, leadership of regional teams, consistency and efficiency of service, and driving performance.

As well, regional leaders were told last year that performance targets would be assessed quarterly and "where performance does not meet expectations, you will be required to develop and implement targeted improvement plans to address gaps and restore performance."
